Enzyme‑responsive delivery systems Enzyme-responsive delivery systems utilize enzymes as triggers to release the miRNA payload in a controlled manner. The delivery vector is designed to be stable in the bloodstream but sensitive to the enzyme present at the target site. Once the vector reaches the target tissue, the enzyme catalyzes a chemical reaction and leads to the release of the miRNA (Wang X et al. 2019). The choice of enzyme is crucial for the success of these systems. Enzymes that are overexpressed in diseased tissues or present at the target site can be leveraged to achieve precise delivery. For example, proteases are overexpressed in many cancers and can be used to trigger the release of miRNA in tumor cells. Wang et al. showed the controlled release of miR-21 was achieved by enzymatic cleavage of the chitosan/hyaluronic acid nanoparticle, leading to more active osseointegration (Wang Z et al. 2015). Guo and his coworkers constructed a glutathione-responsive polymer to protect the nanocarriers of miR-21 antisense from degradation by Dicer or other RNase in normal cells (Guo et al. 2019). Redox‑responsive delivery systems Based on the redox reaction, redox-responsive delivery systems offer a promising solution, leveraging the natural redox environment of cells to control the release of miRNA (Yu et al. 2017). A self-assembling peptide-polysaccharide carrier was loaded with indocyanine green and miR-34a. When the conjugate entered cancer cells, the intracellular redox potential of glutathione tripeptide caused its disulfide bond to break. This disruption leads to the release of miR34a, which can then carry out its therapeutic function (Deng et al. 2018). Another type of redox-responsive carrier was designed to deliver miR-129 and Dox for treating breast cancer. DL-dithiothreitol could cause carriers to swell, resulting in the break of the disulfide bond. This allowed the two therapeutics to be simultaneously released from the carriers, which showed a promising combination of effective drug and miRNA therapy (Yi et al. 2016).

Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology (2025) 109:247 Page 11 of 14 247 Summary and outlook Since miRNA-based drugs are still in the early stages of development, further preclinical and clinical studies will provide abundant approaches to improve their safety and delivery efficacy. The development of miRNA-based therapeutics requires a deep understanding of the complex networks involving miRNA and their target genes. Identifying the precise miRNA that regulates the expression of diseasecausing genes is crucial for the successful development of therapeutic interventions. Moreover, choosing an appropriate miRNA nano-delivery design is a very challenging task due to the diversity of barriers encountered within the organism. This must be tightly controlled for avoiding off-target effects as well as ensuring optimal therapeutic outcomes. The combination of miRNA with other therapeutic strategies, such as immune modulation or stem cell therapy, is opening up new avenues for disease therapy. By manipulating the expression of specific miRNA, it may be possible to treat a variety of diseases, such as tumors, neurodegenerative disorders, and autoimmune diseases. There is no denying that a few investigations have been halted because of related immune side effects, which could be attributed to the miRNA and its delivery system. The ideal vectors of miRNA should have the following characteristics: (1) keeping the stability of miRNA in the circulatory system and extending its half-life; (2) enhancing their distribution in target tissues; (3) reducing the toxicity and off-target effects associated with miRNA drugs; and (4) promoting transfection efficiency for drug delivery of miRNA, conquering physiological barriers within the body. Recent advances in nanotechnology will pave the way for the clinical translation of the miRNA-based drugs in the upcoming years. What is worth expecting is that miRNA-based therapeutics will obtain approval in the few years to come. The development of new technologies and methods for manipulating miRNA function will further enhance the ability to treat diseases effectively.

The development of new technologies and methods for manipulating miRNA function will further enhance the ability to treat diseases effectively. By harnessing the unique properties of nanoparticles, such as the ability to cross biological barriers and target specific organs, it may be possible to design more effective delivery systems for oligonucleotides. Besides, modification of miRNA-based drugs and better delivery systems will enhance targetability and stability, and improve the controlled release of oligonucleotides. The advancements of stimuli-responsive modes will simultaneously improve the pharmacodynamics of oligonucleotides, allowing for less frequent dosing and reducing side effects. Rigorous clinical trials will be essential to assess the safety and efficacy of these agents in treating human diseases, as well as to determine their optimal dosing and treatment schedules. By addressing these challenges mentioned above, the field of miRNA-based therapeutics has the potential to make a transformative impact on human health in the future. title: MTR4 methylation-dependent degradation activates mTORC1 signaling to promote glioma cell survival under methionine starvation.
text: RESEARCH Amino Acids (2026) 58:3 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00726-025-03495-w Lude Wang and Qiuwen Lou are co-first authors of the article. Communicated by S. Broer Wenxia Xu xuwenxia@zju.edu.cn Minfeng Tong tongminfeng777@163.com 1 Central Laboratory and Precision Diagnosis and Treatment Center, Affiliated Jinhua Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Jinhua, Zhejiang Province, China 2 Department of Neurosurgery, Affiliated Jinhua Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Jinhua, Zhejiang Province, China 3 Key Laboratory of Nutrition and Metabolism Research for Oncology, Affiliated Jinhua Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Jinhua, Zhejiang Province, China 4 Department of Neurosurgery, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China Abstract Methionine is an essential amino acid for the human body. Understanding how tumor cells adjust their signaling networks to evade apoptosis and sustain proliferation in a methionine starvation tumor microenvironment is a significant scien­ tific question that warrants in-depth investigation. This study aims to explore the response mechanisms of glioma under methionine starvation conditions, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for the development of novel therapeutic strategies for glioma. To investigate the response of glioma cells to a methionine starvation environment, we established methionine-starvation-tolerant cells. Our findings indicate that mRNA transporter 4 (MTR4) plays a crucial role in cel­ lular adaptation to methionine starvation. This study employed various experimental approaches, including Western blot­ ting, immunohistochemical staining, and colony formation assays, to validate the expression mechanism of MTR4 under methionine starvation conditions. Furthermore, transfection, quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR), and cytoplasmic-nuclear fractionation techniques were utilized to explore the regulatory mechanism of MTR4 on solute carrier family 1 member 5 (SLC1A5). In response to methionine starvation, glioma cells exhibited a timedependent activation of the mTOR signaling pathway. Transcriptomic analysis revealed a high expression of the methio­ nine transporter SLC1A5, which is regulated at the mRNA level by the nuclear export factor MTR4. Under conditions of methionine starvation, MTR4 undergoes methylation, leading to its ubiquitination. Lysine Methyltransferase 2B (KMT2B) has been identified as the methyltransferase responsible for the methylation of MTR4. In summary, we propose that under conditions of methionine starvation, the enhanced methylation of MTR4 promotes its ubiquitin-mediated degradation. This process facilitates the nuclear export and expression of amino acid transporter mRNA, such as SLC1A5, leading to increased amino acid uptake, activation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) signaling pathway, and ultimately ensuring the survival of glioma cells.

Wang et al. Introduction Glioma is the most prevalent primary brain tumor, account­ ing for 81% of central nervous system (CNS) malignancies (Andersen et al. 2013; Guo et al. 2024; Xu et al. 2020). Among them, glioblastoma (GBM) is one of the deadliest and most relapsing malignant solid tumors, accounting for 57% of all gliomas and 48% of primary CNS malignan­ cies. The standard treatment for glioma involves gross total resection, focal radiotherapy, and adjuvant temozolomide (TMZ) chemotherapy, commonly referred to as Stupp ther­ apy (Karimi-Sani et al. 2024). All gliomas ultimately prog­ ress or recur, and there is currently no standard treatment for recurrent glioma. Therefore, an in-depth investigation of the molecular mechanisms underlying glioma development is crucial for devising new therapeutic strategies for brain glioma. Amino acids are essential nutrients for the body. During tumor development, amino acid metabolism undergoes sig­ nificant changes (Ma et al. 2024). Methionine, one of the body’s essential amino acids, plays a crucial role in pro­ tein synthesis, DNA methylation, and polyamine synthesis (Sanderson et al. 2019; Tassinari et al. 2024). Studies have indicated that abnormal methionine metabolism is linked to the occurrence and progression of various malignant tumors (Jiménez-Alonso and López-Lázaro 2023). The brain, being a highly metabolically active organ, typically exhibits low methionine uptake under physiological conditions, however, this uptake significantly increases in brain gliomas. Based on this principle, 11C-MET PET-CT has been applied in patients with brain gliomas to assess tumor grade (Katsanos et al. 2019), monitor tumor progression, and provide prog­ nostic information.

The brain, being a highly metabolically active organ, typically exhibits low methionine uptake under physiological conditions, however, this uptake significantly increases in brain gliomas. Based on this principle, 11C-MET PET-CT has been applied in patients with brain gliomas to assess tumor grade (Katsanos et al. 2019), monitor tumor progression, and provide prog­ nostic information. Given that the human body cannot syn­ thesize methionine, it must be obtained through diet, leading to fluctuations in methionine availability within the glioma tumor microenvironment. Research has demonstrated that methionine-restricted diets can inhibit tumor growth and prolong the lifespan of laboratory animals (Ji et al. 2024). However, methionine levels in the microenvironment of brain gliomas are considerably lower than those in serum. This discrepancy raises an important question: how do brain glioma cells modulate their internal signal transduction net­ works to adapt to fluctuations in methionine levels within their microenvironment? This question remains a significant scientific challenge worthy of further investigation. The expression of genetic information from mRNA to protein involves a complex process that encompasses transcription, alternative splicing, RNA processing, and translation (Nam et al. 2021). Currently, the transcriptional regulation in response to amino acid levels is relatively well understood. The accumulation of uncharged tRNAs following amino acid deprivation activates GCN2, which phosphorylates eIF2α to suppress the ternary complex, thereby inhibiting global cap-dependent translation while paradoxically facilitating the cap-independent translation of mRNAs harboring uORFs (e.g., ATF4) or IRES elements (e.g., c-MYC). This activation induces the upregulation of genes associated with amino acid metabolism (Pathria and Ronai 2021). Furthermore, the smooth and efficient process­ ing of newly synthesized RNA is a key step in the transition from transcription to translation. The role of this process in the amino acid response, however, remains unclear and war­ rants further investigation. Current research employs a “competitive model” to elucidate the mechanisms of nascent RNA processing and degradation. The nuclear export receptor NXF1/NXT1 col­ laborates with the TREX complex to mediate RNA nuclear export, with Aly/REF export factor (ALYREF), a key com­ ponent of the TREX complex, functioning as a nuclear export adapter protein (Borden 2020; Fan et al. 2019; Kata­ hira 2012; Masuda et al. 2005). Conversely, the multi-sub­ unit exosome complex, which possesses both endonuclease and 3′−5′exonuclease activities, degrades structurally or quantitatively abnormal RNA (Andersen et al. 2013).

text: mediate RNA nuclear export, with Aly/REF export factor (ALYREF), a key com­ ponent of the TREX complex, functioning as a nuclear export adapter protein (Borden 2020; Fan et al. 2019; Kata­ hira 2012; Masuda et al. 2005). Conversely, the multi-sub­ unit exosome complex, which possesses both endonuclease and 3′−5′exonuclease activities, degrades structurally or quantitatively abnormal RNA (Andersen et al. 2013). RNA helicase MTR4 serves as an indispensable auxiliary factor within the exosome complex (Olsen and Johnson 2021), participating in RNA degradation by forming complexes with various proteins. The core of this competitive model lies in the competitive binding mechanism of the 5′ capbinding protein ARS2: as RNA matures, ALYREF and mRNA transport protein 4 (MTR4) compete for ARS2 bind­ ing, jointly determining the final fate of mRNA (Melko et al. 2020). When an mRNA effectively recruits ALYREF, it is able to exit the nucleus efficiently. Conversely, MTR4 may bind to ARS2 and recruit the exosome for degradation of the mRNA (Fan et al. 2017). In our previous work, we pre­ pared a low-methionine medium based on the approximate proportions of methionine found in cerebrospinal fluid and serum, subsequently generating methionine-tolerant cells. An earlier study demonstrated that MTR4 was degraded via ubiquitination in a methionine-starvation environment, thereby promoting the processing of methionine methyl­ transferase methionine adenosyltransferase 2 A (MAT2A) mRNA (Wang et al. 2021). In this study, we further inves­ tigate the role of MTR4 in the responses of glioma cells to fluctuations in methionine levels. In this study, we found that in a low methionine envi­ ronment, the methylation of MTR4 results in its ubiquitina­ tion and subsequent degradation. This process leads to the transcriptional upregulation of the transporter protein solute carrier family 1 member 5 (SLC1A5), which in turn pro­ motes intracellular methionine levels. Cell culture Human glioma cell lines U251, U87 and human embryonic kidney 293 T cells were obtained from the Type Culture Collection of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China). All cells were cultured in a humidified incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO₂ using DMEM medium supplemented with 10% FBS. The preparation method for the methioninefree medium is as follows: Dissolve 12.94 g of L-gluta­ mine-free DMEM high-glucose methionine-free powder, 3.7 g Na2CO3, and 0.584 g of L-glutamine in 1 L of dou­ ble-distilled water (Upadhyayula et al. 2023). By adding varying concentrations of methionine to this base medium, experimental media with different methionine levels can be prepared. Consequently, glioma cells U251 were cultured continuously for 20 days in a medium containing one-fourth of the normal methionine concentration (7.5 mg/L). This successfully established a tolerant cell line capable of stable proliferation in a low-methionine environment, designated U251-M. Gene transfection and RNA interference The Flag-MTR4wt, Flag-MTR4K397A, Flag-MTR4K417A, Flag-MTR4K436A and Flag-MTR4K852A plasmid were constructed by TSINGKE Biological Technology (Beijing, China). Glioma cells were seeded overnight in 6-well plates at a density of 3 × 105 cells, then the plasmid was transfected into cells with Lipofectamine®2000 Reagent (Invitrogen, USA). DNA was diluted to a final concentration of 1 µg plasmid DNA per 100 µL medium before supplementing 2 µL DNA Transfection Reagent. After a 15-minute incuba­ tion, the DNA complex was added to the cells in a dropwise manner. The transfected cells were harvested for further analysis after incubation for 48 h at 37 ℃. Cells were seeded in 6-well plates at a 40–60% conflu­ ence, transfected with siRNA (50 nM) with Lipofectamine RNAiMAX Reagent (Life Technologies, CA, USA) in OptiMEM medium (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’ protocol.

In a methionine-starvation environment, MTR4 undergoes methylation, which in turn affects its ubiquitination Cellular sensing of methionine is not only dependent on SAM, but the utilization of methionine is also reliant on SAM (Tassinari et al. 2024). SAM serves as a precursor for the methylation of biological macromolecules. Con­ sequently, we are particularly interested in the regula­ tory role of methionine metabolism in glioma concerning on protein methylation. Protein methylation is critical for both the structure and function of proteins, and it interacts with other post-translational modifications, such as phos­ phorylation and ubiquitination (Lee et al. 2017; Liu et al. 2020). However, does MTR4 undergo methylation, and is this modification regulated by methionine metabolism? To explore this, we conducted preliminary experiments using immunoprecipitation (IP) with an antibody specific for lysine methylation. We found that MTR4 indeed undergoes methylation, and its methylation levels were significantly upregulated when glioma cells were treated with lowmethionine medium (Fig. 3A). Given that low methionine conditions lead to a subsequent reduction in protein levels (Fig. 3B), we hypothesized that MTR4 methylation may be a prerequisite for its reduction. To test this hypothesis, gli­ oma cells were treated with JIB04, a broad-spectrum inhibi­ tor of protein demethylases. IP results showed that JIB04 treatment significantly increased MTR4 methylation levels while concurrently reducing its protein levels (Fig. 3C-D). When glioma cells were treated with different concentra­ tions of JIB04, MTR4 protein levels decreased in a dosedependent manner (Fig. 3E). To explore whether the protein reduction was caused by ubiquitination, a recovery experi­ ment was conducted using MG132. The results showed that the combined action of JIB04 and MG132 could restore the protein level reduction caused by JIB04 (Fig. 3F). More­ over, JIB04 treatment increased MTR4 ubiquitination lev­ els (Fig. 3G-H). In U251 glioma cell lines stably expressing MTR4, both methylation and ubiquitination of MTR4 were elevated under low-methionine conditions, with a similar trend observed following JIB04 treatment (Fig. 3I). These results preliminarily confirm our hypothesis that MTR4 methylation promotes its ubiquitination and degradation under methionine-starvation conditions. activity confers proliferative ability to low-methionine-tol­ erant cells. This phenomenon has already been applied in PET-CT imaging (Lilja et al. 1985; Yang et al. 2019), sug­ gesting that methionine could serve as an effective thera­ peutic target. Some researchers have proposed reducing the availability of methionine through methionine-restricted diets or other methods (Upadhyayula et al. 2023). However, methionine plays a role in linking the tumor microenviron­ ment with cellular metabolism, epigenetic regulation, and even mitosis (Li et al. 2023). As a result, methionine deple­ tion may lead to complex and potentially adverse effects, such as aneuploidy and abnormal expression of genes that drive tumor progression. Additionally, the methionine lev­ els in the glioma tumor microenvironment are already sig­ nificantly lower than those in serum, raising questions about the extent to which dietary methionine restriction could alter the methionine concentration in the tumor microenvi­ ronment.

title: MTR4 methylation-dependent degradation activates mTORC1 signaling to promote glioma cell survival under methionine starvation.
text: identified the histone lysine methyl­ transferase KMT2B and found that KMT2B can methylate MTR4. In mammalian cells, the serine/threonine kinase mTOR has been identified as a central factor in sensing methio­ nine and its derivatives (Villa et al. 2021). mTOR serves as the catalytic core of two multiprotein complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2, with cell growth primarily regulated by mTORC1 activity. Upon methionine intake, cells rapidly convert methionine to SAM, which binds to SAMTOR and interacts with metabolites to exert downstream effects (Jiang et al. 2023). Methionine depletion leads to a reduc­ tion in SAM levels, causing SAMTOR to associate with KICSTOR (a scaffold protein complex) and GATOR1 (a GTPase-activating protein complex), thereby inhibiting the mTORC1 signaling pathway and halting cell proliferation and cell cycle progression (Gu et al. 2017). In this study, we found that restored mTOR activity conferred prolifera­ tive ability to low-methionine-tolerant cells. Amino acid transporters play a critical role in amino acid sensing and mTORC1 activity regulation. SLC1A5 exhibited asymmet­ ric specificity for amino acids: Ala, Cys, Val, and Met were exclusively transported inward, while Gln, Ser, Asn, and Thr were transported bidirectionally (Pingitore et al. 2013). In this study, SLC1A5 promoted cell growth under lowmethionine conditions by maintaining methionine influx and sustaining mTORC1 activity. Conclusion In summary, this study describes the signaling feedback mechanisms in glioma cells under methionine starvation conditions. It includes the methylation of MTR4, which affects its ubiquitination, as well as the regulatory role of MTR4 in controlling SLC1A5-mediated methionine uptake under methionine starvation. This process helps maintain mTORC1 activity, thereby promoting cell growth and pro­ liferation (Fig. 6F). title: Integrating artificial intelligence into small molecule development for precision cancer immunomodulation therapy.
text: npj | drug discovery Perspective https://doi.org/10.1038/s44386-025-00029-y Integrating artiﬁcial intelligence into small molecule development for precision cancer immunomodulation therapy Check for updates Henry Sutanto1,2 & Deasy Fetarayani2,3 This perspective examines how artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) is transforming small-molecule development for precision cancer immunomodulation therapy. It outlines AI-driven approaches for de novo design, virtual screening, multi-parameter optimization, and ADMET prediction, targeting immune checkpoints, tumor microenvironment modulation, antigen presentation, and metabolic pathways. The article highlights patient stratiﬁcation, multi-omics integration, digital twin simulations, translational challenges, and future directions, underscoring AI’s potential to deliver effective, personalized immunomodulatory therapeutics. Cancer immunotherapy is a therapeutic modality that harnesses the body’s immune system to recognize and eliminate tumor cells. Unlike traditional therapies such as chemotherapy and radiation, which act directly on tumor cells, immunotherapy modulates immune checkpoints, cellular effectors, or cytokine signaling to restore or enhance antitumor immunity. Broadly, immunotherapy can be categorized into several classes: First, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), which target inhibitory receptors such as programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), programmed death-ligand 1 (PDL1), and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein 4 (CTLA-4) to relieve T cell exhaustion1,2; Second, adoptive cell therapies (ACT) such as chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy3; Third, cytokine therapies, which employ immune-stimulatory cytokines like interleukin (IL)-2 or interferon alpha (IFNα); Fourth, cancer vaccines and oncolytic viruses, designed to boost antigen-speciﬁc immunity (Fig. 1); as well as other types of immunotherapies, including bispeciﬁc antibodies (e.g., bispeciﬁc T-cell engagers or BiTEs), antibody-drug conjugates, and monoclonal antibodies that exert their effects through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC)4–7. Despite clinical successes, conventional immunotherapies face several limitations that constrain their broad applicability. First, immune resistance mechanisms, including upregulation of alternate checkpoints, loss of antigen presentation machinery, and recruitment of suppressive immune cells (e.g., regulatory T cells [Tregs], myeloid-derived suppressor cells), can attenuate responses to ICIs and CAR-T cells8,9. Second, inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity can lead to inconsistent efﬁcacy across patient populations and tumor types10. Third, immune-related adverse events, stemming from systemic activation of immune pathways, often necessitate treatmentdiscontinuationandcanaffectmultipleorgansystems11,12.Finally, biologics such as monoclonal antibodies and cell therapies often require intravenous administration, are costly to produce, and may have limited tissue penetration, particularly in poorly vascularized tumors13,14. These challenges have catalyzed growing interest in small-molecule immunomodulators as a complementary or alternative strategy. Unlike monoclonal antibodies, which are the current mainstay for blocking pathways like PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4, small molecules offer several unique pharmacological and practical advantages (Fig. 1).

text: often require intravenous administration, are costly to produce, and may have limited tissue penetration, particularly in poorly vascularized tumors13,14. These challenges have catalyzed growing interest in small-molecule immunomodulators as a complementary or alternative strategy. Unlike monoclonal antibodies, which are the current mainstay for blocking pathways like PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4, small molecules offer several unique pharmacological and practical advantages (Fig. 1). These include oral bioavailability, greater stability under physiological conditions, lower production costs, and improved tissue penetration, especially into solid tumors. Moreover, they are often chemically tunable, and capable of intracellular target engagement, allowing for access to non-surface immune regulators such as transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) signaling intermediates, or metabolic enzymes like arginase. Additionally, their shorter development timelines and amenability to combination therapies make them attractive for expanding the reach of immunotherapy15–17. One of the most actively pursued targets for small-molecule intervention is the indoleamine2,3-dioxygenase1(IDO1)enzyme,whichcatalyzestryptophan degradation and contributes to immune suppression within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Inhibitors of IDO1, such as epacadostat, have been developed to reverse this immunosuppressive effect and reinvigorate T-cell responses18. Another major focus has been the design of small molecules that directly inhibit the PD-1/PD-L1 interaction. Though structurally challenging due to the large, ﬂat binding interface, several promising compounds have been identiﬁed that disrupt PD-L1 dimerization or promote its degradation. For instance, PIK-93 is a small molecule that enhances PD-L1 ubiquitination and degradation, improving T-cell activationwhencombinedwithanti-PD-L1antibodies19.Likewise,naturally occurring compounds such as myricetin have been shown to downregulate PD-L1 and IDO1 expression via interference with the JAK-STAT-IRF1 axis20. In recent years, artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force in pharmaceutical research and development, with a particularly profound impact on drug discovery. Traditional drug discovery is characterized by lengthy timelines, high failure rates, and escalating costs— often exceeding a decade and billions of dollars to bring a single compound to market. Moreover, the introduction of the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Modernization Act 3.0 underscoresa paradigm shift in preclinical drug development by formally positioning human-relevant alternative models—such as organ-on-chip systems, computational modeling, and AI-driven in silico approaches—as viable substitutes for traditional animal testing, with the FDA required to establish qualiﬁcation pathwaysforsuchmethods22.Concurrently,theSocietyforImmunotherapy of Cancer’s strategic plan explicitly highlights the exploration and integration of AI technologies to accelerate therapeutic discovery of cancer immunotherapy23. Thus, AI technologies such as machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and natural language processing (NLP) are now being integrated across nearly every phase of the drug development pipeline, from target identiﬁcation to clinical trial optimization, offering dramatic improvements in speed, cost-efﬁciency, and predictive power24. Pharmaceutical companies and startups alike are increasingly adopting AI tools to streamline compound screening, predict pharmacokinetics, and model drug-target interactions (DTIs). For example, generative models can design novel drug-like molecules with desired properties, while reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms ﬁne-tune these compounds toward therapeutic goals. These methods not only improve hit-to-lead timelines but also reduce reliance on extensive in vitro and in vivo screening25. The use of AI has already led to the development of AI-designed molecules like DSP-1181 (a serotonin receptoragonist),whichentered clinicaltrialsinlessthana year— an unprecedented milestone in the industry26,27. Beyond process efﬁciency, AI is also a cornerstone technology in precision medicine—the tailoring of therapeutic strategies to individual patient characteristics28. Precision medicine depends on integrating diverse data modalities, including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, clinical records, and environmental exposures29. AI algorithms excel at discovering complex patterns across these high-dimensional datasets, enabling the identiﬁcation of novel biomarkers, stratiﬁcation of patient subgroups, and prediction of individual drug responses30,31. AI-powered platforms such as CODE-AE have demonstrated the ability to predict patient-speciﬁc responses to novel compounds, dramatically advancing the feasibility of personalized therapeutics32. It also explores AI’s role in patient stratiﬁcation, integration of multi-omics data, and development of personalized treatment strategies using digital twins, highlighting how these advances are enabling the rational design of individualized small-molecule immunomodulation therapies. Foundations of AI in drug discovery Overview of AI techniques ML, a foundational subﬁeld of AI, encompasses a broad set of algorithms that allow computers to learn from data and make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed. The image illustrates the role of immunotherapy in driving cancer remission, highlighting existing immunotherapeutic agents such as adoptive cell therapy, cytokine therapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and cancer vaccines. It also emphasizes the emerging potential of small molecule therapeutics—deﬁned as chemical compounds with molecular weights of 0.1–1 kDa—in cancer immunomodulation therapy. Small molecules offer distinct advantages including oral bioavailability, enhanced tissue penetration, intracellular target engagement, chemical tunability, and greater stability under physiological conditions. Their lower production costs and amenability to combination therapies position them as promising complementary or alternative approaches to conventional biologics in cancer treatment. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44386-025-00029-y Perspective npj Drug Discovery | (2025) 2:25 2 workﬂows across target identiﬁcation, compound screening, and lead optimization by offering high-throughput, data-driven modeling strategies. ML techniques are commonly categorized into supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and RL, each serving distinct purposes in pharmaceutical research (Table 1). Supervised learning is the most widely used ML paradigm in drug discovery. It requires labeled datasets, where the algorithm learns a function that maps inputs (e.g., molecular descriptors) to outputs (e.g., binding afﬁnity or toxicity). This approach underpins numerous tasks, including quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) modeling, toxicityprediction,and virtualscreening.Algorithmssuchassupport vector machines (SVMs), random forests, and deep neural networks have demonstrated success in predicting bioactivity and ADMET (i.e., absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity) properties33,34.

Meanwhile, unsupervised learning involves training models on unlabeled data, uncovering hidden structures or patterns such as chemical clustering, diversity analysis, or scaffold-based grouping. Techniques like k-means clustering, hierarchical clustering, and principal component analysis (PCA) are employed to identify novel compound classes, discover unknown relationships between molecular features, or reduce dimensionality in large chemical libraries35,36. Next, RL represents a third, more interactive category of ML. In RL, an agent learns to make a sequence of decisions by interacting with an environment and receiving feedback in the form of rewards or penalties. In drug discovery, RL is particularly valuable in de novo molecule generation, where the agent iteratively proposes molecular structures and is rewarded for generating drug-like, active, and synthetically accessible compounds37,38. Deep Q-learning and actor-critic methods have been successfully applied to design compounds with optimized binding proﬁles and ADMET characteristics39,40. DL, a subﬁeld of ML, has become a cornerstone of AI-driven drug discovery due to its capacity to model complex, non-linear relationships withinlarge,high-dimensionaldatasets(Table2).CentraltoDLareartiﬁcial neural networks (ANNs), which are layered architectures inspired by the brain’s neural connectivity. These include feedforward neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), all of which have found use in tasks ranging from compound classiﬁcation to bioactivity prediction41. In recent years, generative models such as variational autoencoders (VAEs) and generative adversarial networks (GANs) have been especially transformative for de novo molecular design. VAEs consist of encoder-decoder architectures that learn a compressed latent space of molecules, enabling the generation of novel structures with speciﬁc pharmacological properties42. VAEs have been successfully applied to generate chemically valid and synthetically accessible drug-like molecules with targeted properties, such as binding afﬁnity or solubility43. GANs, on the other hand, employ a competitive learning framework between two networks: a generator that creates candidate molecules and a discriminator that evaluates their validity. In drug discovery, GANs have been used to generate novel compounds with enhanced diversity and improved binding proﬁles. For example, studies have demonstrated GAN-based models that produce target-speciﬁc inhibitors by learning from known DTIs44.

NLP overcomes this bottleneck by using algorithms to extract entities (e.g., drugs, proteins, pathways) and relationships (e.g., drug–target, drug–disease) from these sources, providing structured insights that can accelerate hypothesis generation and compound prioritization50. In drug discovery pipelines, NLP is applied to mine pharmacological effects, side effects, drug-drug interactions, and efﬁcacy from literatureusingentityrecognition,semanticparsing,andrelationextraction. Tools leveraging transformer-based architectures, such as BERT and its biomedical variants (e.g., BioBERT), are capable of achieving state-of-theart performance in identifying DTIs and other biomedical relationships from complex sentence structures51–53. Patent documents are particularly valuable as they contain detailed descriptions of novel compounds, formulations, and therapeutic claims. NLP-enabled patent mining systems— such as those implemented in platforms like IBM Watson for Drug Discovery—use hybrid model- and rule-based techniques to extract chemically relevant data, enabling early competitive intelligence and intellectual property analysis54. Ultimately, the integration of NLP with DL techniques provides a scalable solution for real-time, automated knowledge extraction. This enhances the ability of AI systems to inform downstream processes such as molecular design, target selection, and patient stratiﬁcation. Data sources and preprocessing Omics data—encompassing genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics— offeracomprehensivesnapshotofcellularstatesandmolecularinteractions, enabling precise characterization of disease phenotypes and therapeutic targets. When integrated with AI, these high-throughput datasets empower predictive models that can accelerate biomarker discovery, drug repurposing, and personalized therapy development55. Genomics involves the sequencingandanalysisofDNAtoidentifymutations,structuralvariations, and copy number alterations linked to disease. AI tools such as CNNs and ensemble models can efﬁciently interpret these large genomic datasets to uncover disease-driving genes and potential drug targets56,57. Transcriptomics, which assesses RNA expression proﬁles, provides dynamic insight into gene regulation in response to disease or drug treatment. DL architectures such as autoencoders and transformers are particularly effective at modeling transcriptomic data to identify dysregulated pathways and stratify patients based on expression signatures58–60. Proteomics captures protein abundance, modiﬁcations, and interactions—critical determinants of functional biology. Integrating proteomic data with genomics and transcriptomics enables multi-layered insights into disease mechanisms. AI methods, especially graph neural networks (GNNs) and integrative models, can map these proteomic signatures to drug-target networks, improving the identiﬁcation of actionable targets and predictive biomarkers61,62.

Notably, this integration has already yielded high-accuracy predictions of candidate compounds for speciﬁc cancer subtypes, dramatically reducing the time and cost of traditional screening pipelines56,63. Next, HTS enables rapid assessment of the biological activity of hundreds of thousands to millions of chemical compounds against diseaserelevant targets64. These large-scale assays are critical for generating the bioactivity data needed to train and validate ML and DL models65. HTS platforms use robotics, miniaturized assays, and automated data acquisition to test compounds at a pace and scalethat is impossibletoachieve manually. With throughput rates exceeding 10,000 compounds per week, HTS dramaticallyaccelerates hit identiﬁcationwhile generatingdiverse, high-quality datasetsfor downstreamAI applications66,67. Chemical libraries usedin HTS are carefully designed collections of compounds, including both synthetic molecules and natural products. The diversity and size of these libraries critically inﬂuence the success of AI models, as they determine the representational breadth of chemical space sampled during screening. AIenhanced virtual screening (VS) approaches can signiﬁcantly improve the efﬁciency of HTS by preselecting compounds with high predicted activity, thereby reducing cost and increasing hit rates. For example, ChemPrint, a DL platform, integrated molecular embeddings and t-SNE clustering to navigate uncharted molecular space and achieve hit rates exceeding 40% in prospective studies targeting AXL and BRD4—far surpassing traditional HTS yields68. Speciﬁcally, in two prospective campaigns targeting AXL and BRD4, ChemPrint achieved hit rates of 41% (12 out of 29 hits) and 58% (7 out of 12 hits), respectively. The chemical hits were structurally novel, showing Tanimoto similarity of 0.4 (AXL campaign) and ~0.3 (BRD4 campaign) compared to both the training datasets and ChEMBL databases. Pairwise diversity scores of ChemPrint are 0.17 (AXL) and 0.11 (BRD4), demonstrating notable internal diversity among identiﬁed hits68. The integration of HTS with AI is also redeﬁning the scope and use of virtual chemical libraries, which can be exponentially larger than physical ones.

In vitro biochemical assays have long been a cornerstone of experimental pharmacology, providing precise, mechanistic insights into drug–target interactions. Unlike omics-based or HTS approaches, which often generate large, complex datasets requiring substantial normalization, in vitro assays typically yield well-deﬁned kinetic and thermodynamic parameters—such as half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50), inhibition constant (Kᵢ), or association rate constant (kon) / dissociation rate constant (koff)—that are directly interpretable and readily integrated into AI pipelines71. These datasets, obtained from enzymatic activity measurements, ligand-binding assays, or receptor activation studies, serve as high-quality, low-noise inputs for AI algorithms, particularly those focused on predictive modeling of structure–activity relationships (SAR) or drug–target afﬁnity72. Beyond enzymatic assays, biophysical methods such as surface plasmon resonance (SPR), isothermal titration calorimetry, and differential scanning ﬂuorimetry are increasingly recognized as valuable AI data sources. These techniques produce quantitative data on binding kinetics, thermodynamics, and protein stability, which can enhance the predictive capacity of AI models by capturing nuanced molecular recognition patterns73,74. For example, SPR-derived real-time association and dissociation curves can be transformed into kinetic descriptors that AI models leverage to distinguish between compounds with similar equilibrium afﬁnities but different pharmacokinetic behaviors. In vitro cellular assays, including reporter gene assays, electrophysiological measurements, and phenotypic microscopy-based screens, also contribute high-value data.

These datasets—often small but highly standardized— are valuable for training ML models that predict clinical pharmacokinetics and safety liabilities. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44386-025-00029-y Perspective npj Drug Discovery | (2025) 2:25 5 Model training and validation The process of training AI models in drug discovery is a multi-stage endeavor that balances computational rigor with the complexity of biochemical and pharmacological data (Fig. 2). A typical workﬂow begins with the curation and preprocessing of datasets, which may include molecular descriptors, bioassay results, or physicochemical proﬁles. Data preprocessing is crucial, as the inherent variability in experimental protocols can introduce bias and noise. Standardization of molecular representations— such as converting chemical structures into simpliﬁed molecular input line entry system (SMILES) strings, molecular graphs, or 3D conformers—is an early step, often followed by feature engineering to generate descriptors relevant to model objectives77. These engineered features serve as the inputs to AI algorithms, and their quality directly impacts model accuracy and generalizability. Model selection depends heavily on the task at hand— classiﬁcation models (e.g., predicting active vs. inactive compounds) commonly employ algorithms such as random forests, SVMs, or deep neural networks, while regression models (e.g., predicting IC50 or ADMET properties) often favor gradient boosting or graph convolutional networks (GCNs)78,79. Neural architectures, especially those adapted for cheminformatics—such as message-passing neural networks—can learn directly from molecular graphs, obviating some manual descriptor engineering and potentially capturing subtle SAR80.

Training involves iterative optimization of model parameters using algorithms like stochastic gradient descent or Adam, guided by a loss function that quantiﬁes prediction error81. In drug discovery, loss functions are often task-speciﬁc; for example, mean squared error (MSE) for afﬁnity prediction, cross-entropy for classiﬁcation, or custom multi-objective functions when balancing potency, selectivity, and ADMET properties simultaneously. Regularization techniques, such as dropout, weight decay, or early stopping, are applied to prevent overﬁtting —a signiﬁcant risk when working with small or biased biochemical datasets82. Evaluation and validation strategies are also integral to the training cycle. Cross-validation, particularly k-fold and scaffold-split approaches, are widely used to assess generalization performance. Finally, model retraining and continual learning strategies are increasingly applied as new experimental data becomes available. This dynamic updating is critical in drug discovery, where chemical space exploration is ongoing, and novel scaffolds, targets, and assay modalities emerge regularly. Active learning frameworks, in which the model selectively queries new compounds for experimental testing to improve its predictive boundaries, have shown particular promise in reducing experimental cost while maximizing predictive improvement83. As abovementioned, model validation is a critical step in the cycle, ensuring that predictive models are both accurate and generalizable to novel chemical entities. The choice of validation strategy must account for the unique challenges of molecular datasets, including structural redundancy, assay variability, and limited representation of chemical space. To address this, scaffold-based splitting—partitioning compounds based on Bemis–Murcko scaffolds—has become a gold standard for smallmolecule drug discovery, as it better simulates real-world scenarios in which a model encounters novel chemotypes85,86. Beyond dataset partitioning, cross-validation techniques provide a robust means of assessing performance stability. K-fold cross-validation, in which the dataset is divided into k subsets with iterative training and testing, is widely applied, though in drug discovery its design must avoid information leakage from highly similar molecules87. Time-split validation—separating training and test data based on the date of assay measurement—can model the temporal aspect of drug development pipelines, testing whether an AI system can predict future discoveries from historical data88. External validation, using datasets from independent experimental campaigns, is considered the highest standard for evaluating model generalizability. For instance, models trained on data from one biochemical assay may be validated against the same target’s activity measurements obtained from a different assay format or lab89,90. This can reveal overﬁtting to assay-speciﬁc artifacts and guide retraining with more diverse inputs. Evaluation metrics must also be carefully selected based on the task. For classiﬁcation tasks, metrics such as area under the ROC curve (AUC), precision–recall curves, and balanced accuracy are preferred over simple accuracy, as they better handle the class imbalance often present in bioactivity data. For regression tasks, root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and the coefﬁcient of determination (R²) are standard, with domain-speciﬁc thresholds guiding acceptable performance. Emerging best practices in AI validation also include applicability domain (AD) analysis, which assesses whether a given compound falls within the chemical space the model was trained on.

In combination with uncertainty quantiﬁcation methods, such as Bayesian neural networks or Monte Carlo dropout, AD analysis enables more transparent decisionmaking in AI-assisted drug design. Approaches for interpreting AI models Interpretability of AI models in drug discovery is increasingly recognized as essential for building trust, guiding medicinal chemistry decisions, and satisfying regulatory expectations. Black-box models, such as deep neural networks and ensemble methods, can achieve high predictive performance but often lack transparent decision-making pathways. To address this, a range of model interpretation approaches has been developed, enabling researchers to identify molecular features, structural motifs, or assay conditions that drive predictions92. Feature attribution methods are among the most widely used tools for interpretability. Techniques such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Modelagnostic Explanations (LIME) estimate the contribution of each input variable—such as molecular descriptors or graph nodes—to a given prediction93,94. These methods can highlight pharmacophoric features or toxicophores responsible for predicted potency or adverse effects, enabling more targeted lead optimization. In deep learning models for cheminformatics, attention mechanisms and gradient-based visualization methods, such as saliency maps and integrated gradients, are increasingly employed to pinpoint substructures most relevant to the output. For example, in GNNs, node-level attention scores can reveal speciﬁc atoms or bonds contributing to predicted bioactivity, providing interpretable chemical rationale alongside predictions95. Another important class of interpretability approaches involves surrogate modeling, where simpler, more transparent models (e.g., decision trees or linear regressions) are trained to approximate the behavior of a complex model within a deﬁned local chemical space. This allows researchers to explore interpretable decision boundaries without sacriﬁcing the predictive accuracy of the original model96. Beyond individual predictions, global interpretability techniques aim to understand model behavior across the entire dataset. In a drug discovery context, this can help elucidate SAR or identify assay biases embedded in the training data97.

AI-driven small molecule design workﬂows De novo molecular generation De novo molecular generation enables the creation of novel compounds with speciﬁc chemical and biological properties from scratch98,99. This approach is particularly powerful in the context of cancer immunotherapy, where the ability to rapidly generate and optimize ligands for targets such as PD-L1, IDO1, or STING is critical. SMILES-based RNNs have been widely used to model and generate molecules encoded in the SMILES format. These models learn the syntax of chemical structures and produce syntactically valid molecular strings, facilitating the generation of drug-like compounds. However, early SMILES-based RNNs often suffered from low molecular diversity and mode collapse, limiting their utility in exploring broad chemical spaces100. Advances such as bidirectional RNNs and curriculum learning have improved their capability to generate diverse and target-speciﬁc libraries101. To address the limitations of linear molecular representations, GNNs have gained prominence for de novo design. Unlike SMILES strings, GNNs operate directly on molecular graphs, allowing for more chemically intuitive learning (Table 2). These models capture the topology and connectivity of atoms and bonds, enabling generation and optimization of structurally valid and biologically relevant compounds. Conditional GNNs can be guided to produce molecules with desired pharmacological proﬁles by incorporating target-speciﬁc constraints or physicochemical properties during generation102. Next, RL has also become a crucial technique for optimizing generative models. In these frameworks, an AI agent iteratively constructs molecules and receives rewards based on predeﬁned criteria such as binding afﬁnity, drug-likeness, toxicity, or synthesizability. For example, the 3D-MolGNNRL system uses RL to build molecules atom-by-atom within a target binding pocket, optimizing for multiple objectives including activity and potency103. Similarly, memoryassisted RL approaches help increase scaffold diversity and reduce the issue of redundant outputs common in traditional RNN-based RL methods104. QSAR modeling, traditionally a statistical approach, has been transformed by ML into a powerful predictive framework. ML-enhanced QSAR uses molecular descriptors (e.g., physicochemical, topological, or 3D features) to model the relationship between a compound’s structure and its biological activity. For example, Wang et al. applied stepwise regression and multiple linear regression to derive robust QSAR models for predicting peptide– major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I binding afﬁnity based on amino acid physicochemical parameters105. Similarly, Liu et al. combined QSAR with Gaussian process regression and molecular docking to screen for natural IRF-7 inhibitors from a large natural product library, achieving micromolar binding afﬁnities in follow-up assays106. DL has further advanced VS through structure-based models capable of capturing spatial and chemical features from protein–ligand complexes. CNNs, especially in 3D formats, are used to extract interaction features from voxelized representations of protein-ligand binding sites. For instance, the L3D-PLS model by Huo et al. integrates a CNN module with partial least squares regression to predict binding afﬁnities from aligned ligands, outperforming traditional 3D-QSAR methods on small datasets107. Similarly, DeepAtom applies a lightweight 3D-CNN to learn atomic interaction features from protein-ligand structures and achieves high predictive accuracy onPDBbind datasets108.Recentadvancementsintransformer-basedmodels have introduced a new dimension to drug-target afﬁnity prediction. Models https://doi.org/10.1038/s44386-025-00029-y Perspective npj Drug Discovery | (2025) 2:25 7 like TF-DTA and TC-DTA integrate transformer encoders with CNNs to jointly model protein sequences and drug SMILES strings, achieving stateof-the-art performance in predicting binding afﬁnities109,110. These models can accurately capture long-range dependencies in biological sequences, enhancing generalization across novel protein targets and diverse chemical scaffolds. Together, ML-based QSAR modeling and DL-based structural prediction approaches represent a dual backbone for modern VS. Their synergy—combining ligand-based and structure-based perspectives— enables more accurate, efﬁcient identiﬁcation of candidate compounds. ADMET and pharmacokinetics prediction ADMET properties are critical determinants of a compound’s success as a drug. Historically, poor ADMET proﬁles have been responsible for the majority of clinical trial failures. AI offers powerful solutions by enabling in silico ADMET prediction, which allows researchers to evaluate pharmacokinetic and toxicity properties of drug candidates before initiating costly and time-intensive in vitro or in vivo experiments. Recent AI frameworks, such as ADMET-AI, utilize advanced ML models to perform rapid, largescale ADMET proﬁling across millions of compounds. This system integrates absorption and toxicity endpoints to assist in early decision-making and prioritization of candidates for experimental validation. ADMET-AI outperforms existing tools in speed and accuracy, processing over a million molecules in just a few hours and achieving top scores on benchmark datasets111. Likewise, DL platforms like Deep-PK use GNNs and graphbased molecular signatures to predict over 70 ADMET-related endpoints, demonstrating strong generalization across diverse chemical classes and offering interpretable predictions112. In addition to prediction, AI is increasingly used for multi-objective optimization, where candidate molecules are simultaneously reﬁned to meet multiple criteria, such as potency, bioavailability, metabolic stability, and low toxicity. For example, the Retro Drug Design framework optimizes de novo molecules to satisfy six distinct ADMET properties, generating kinase inhibitors with high novelty and experimental validation success rates113. Other integrated systems, such as those promoted by the Life Intelligence Consortium, aim to unify de novo generation models with ADMET predictors into end-to-end platforms that can autonomously propose and evaluate new small-molecule structures114. By automating and enhancing ADMET and pharmacokinetic evaluation, AI drastically reduces the cost and attrition rate in drug development. While monoclonal antibodies dominate the clinical landscape for checkpoint blockade, small molecules are emerging as promising alternatives or complements due to their ability to access intracellular targets, offer oral bioavailability, and reduce immunogenicity. For example, phenyl-pyrazolone derivatives have shown potent anti-PD-L1 activity by inducing PD-L1 dimerization and interfering with PD-1 binding, while also conferring antioxidant properties116. AI-assisted frameworks are also being employed to optimize PD-L1-binding small molecules, streamlining hit-to-lead timelines117. CTLA-4 isanotherclinicallyvalidated checkpoint forwhich small-molecule inhibitors are being developed using AI-powered discovery methods. Recent work has demonstrated that AI-based VS of millions of compounds can yield potent CTLA-4 binders that inhibit CTLA-4/CD80 interactions, with validated anti-tumor effects in both in vitro and in vivo models118. These studies illustrate how DL and structure-based screening can expand chemical space exploration beyond traditional pharmacophores. IDO1 inhibitors such as epacadostat have advanced to clinical trials, though early-phase failures have spurred efforts to reﬁne compound selectivity and patient stratiﬁcation18,119. VISTA represents another emerging checkpoint, particularly relevant in cancers resistant to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. High VISTA expression has been observed in immunosuppressive TME and is associated with poor immunotherapy response in cancers such as pancreatic adenocarcinoma125. Small molecules targeting VISTA are under preclinical and early clinical development, with oral dual inhibitors like CA-170 showing simultaneous inhibition of PD-L1 and VISTA, and demonstrating anti-tumor activity in early-phase trials126. To date, there is no AI-based technology harnessing VISTA in cancer immunotherapy. Nonetheless, AI potentially enables a new generation of small-molecule checkpoint inhibitors with improved speciﬁcity, novel mechanisms (e.g., dimerization, degradation), and rapid optimization pipelines. These developments hold promise for expanding immunotherapy efﬁcacy across previously refractory tumor types and patient populations. Tumor microenvironment modulation TME plays a critical role in immune evasion, progression, and therapy resistance in cancer. It is rich in immunosuppressive cytokines, regulatory immunecells,hypoxicstress,andmetabolicbyproductslikeadenosine,allof which contribute to impaired T cell activity. Among the most promising targets for small-molecule modulation within the TME are TGF-β pathway and adenosine A2A receptors (A2AR). AI-enabled drug discovery platforms are now being leveraged to identify and optimize small-molecule inhibitors targeting these pathways, enhancing the precision and efﬁcacy of immunotherapy strategies127–129.

AI-assisted efforts have contributed to the development of selective small-molecule TGF-β receptor I (TGFβR1) inhibitors like YL-13027, which demonstrated promising antitumor effects in early-phase clinical trials. In a phase I study, YL-13027 was well tolerated and induced a partial response in a triple-negative breast cancer patient, showing the potential for personalized application in genomically deﬁned tumors130. These advancements are supported by DL platforms that integrate genomic and transcriptomic features to predict TGF-β signaling activity and guide target engagement. A study introduces AI-HOPE-TGFbeta, a novel conversational AI platform that integrates clinical and genomic data to explore dysregulation of the TGF-β signaling pathway in colorectal cancer (CRC), with a focus on early-onset CRC (EOCRC) and Hispanic/Latino (H/L) populations, who face poorer outcomes. Built on the LLaMA 3 language model, the system translates natural language queries into automated bioinformatics workﬂows, enabling realtimeanalysessuchasmutationfrequencycomparison,survivalanalysis,and stratiﬁcation by race, MSI status, tumor stage, and treatment. The platform successfully replicated known ﬁndings—like the poor survival of SMAD4mutant EOCRC patients treated with FOLFOX—and uncovered new insights, including a potential enrichment of BMPR1A mutations in H/L populationsandMSI-speciﬁcsurvivalbeneﬁtsinSMAD4-mutatedpatients. It also demonstrated the ability to perform subgroup analyses by ethnicity, even with limited data. These results highlight the power of AI-HOPETGFbeta to democratize complex genomic analysis, enable disparityfocused precision oncology, and accelerate translational research in the TGF-β pathway127. Another study developed and validated a TGF-β risk score to assess immune microenvironment characteristics and predict immunotherapy efﬁcacy in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Using previously reported TGF-β–related genes and single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA), Wu et al. established an initial risk model, which was then optimized using the LASSO-COX algorithm for clinical applicability. The TGF-β risk score was found to correlate strongly with TME phenotypes—negatively associated with NK cell inﬁltration and positively linked to macrophages and ﬁbroblasts, indicating a “cold” immune landscape in high-risk patients. Importantly, patients with higher scores showed greater predicted responsiveness to immunotherapy, suggesting potential clinical utility in treatment stratiﬁcation129.

Simultaneously, the adenosinergic signaling axis, particularly via A2A and A2B adenosine receptors, has gained traction as a therapeutic target. Elevated extracellular adenosine in tumors suppresses immune responses via A2AR on T cells and natural killer cells. A recent study has produced M1069, a potent dual A2A/A2B receptor antagonist. M1069 outperformed A2A-selective inhibitors by rescuing IL-2 and IL-12 production in immune cells, suppressing pro-tumor cytokines like vascular endothelial growth factor, CXCL1, and CXCL5, and reducing tumor growth in CD73-high breast tumor models129. An in silico study further showcases the integration of generative chemical language models with structure-based drug design (SBDD) to enable de novo generation of small-molecule ligands directly from protein structures, without prior knowledge of ligand scaffolds. Using the Augmented Hill-Climb optimization algorithm, the framework efﬁciently balances multiple objectives, including protein-ligand complementarity, leading to the generation of chemically novel ligands for A2AR—many of whichare absent from commercial libraries. Experimental screening yielded an impressive 88% binding hit rate, with 50% showing functional activity, including three nanomolar ligands and two novel chemotypes. Structural validation through co-crystallization of the top binders revealed their binding modes, effectively closing the AI-driven SBDD loop131. Another study presents a multistage VS pipeline combining DL, pharmacophore modeling, and molecular docking to identify dual adenosine A1AR and A2AR antagonists. Screening over 1.17 million compounds from the ChemDiv library led to 19 candidate molecules, two of which—C8 and C9, featuring 1,2,4-triazole scaffolds—demonstrated nanomolar binding afﬁnities and potent antagonistic activity in both radioligand binding and cAMP functional assays. Molecular dynamics simulations further conﬁrmed stable and strong interactions between these compounds and both A1AR and A2AR132. Next, another study demonstrates the effectiveness of Deep Docking, a DL-driven VS workﬂow designed for ultra-large molecular libraries. Applied to the Enamine REAL library containing billions of compounds, the method enabled efﬁcient prioritization through four training iterations, followed by Glide docking, pharmacophore ﬁltering, and manual selection. Out of 39 candidates tested experimentally, two novel A2AR hits with unique scaffolds were identiﬁed133.

Antigen presentation and neoantigen pathways Effective cancer immunotherapy depends not only on T-cell activation but also on the efﬁcient presentation of tumor antigens through MHC molecules. However, many tumors downregulate components of the antigen processing and presentation machinery (APM), including transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP), tapasin, and MHC class I/II molecules, to evade immune detection. Enhancing these pathways through small molecules represents a promising strategy to restore tumor immunogenicity, particularly when integrated with AIdriven drug design to optimize molecular speciﬁcity and pharmacodynamics. One strategy involves restoring or enhancing MHC class I expression. Tumors often suppress MHC I through gene deletion, transcriptional inhibition, or degradation pathways. Recent work has identiﬁed heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) inhibitors as potent smallmolecule inducers of MHC-I surface expression. Using an in situ click chemistry–based derivatization strategy, Kelly et al. developed over 300 analogs that enhanced MHC-I expression and improved T cell activation, with compounds like CliMB-325 showing reduced toxicity and increased immunogenicity134. Small molecules have also been shown to target upstream regulators of MHC expression. Suppression of fatty acid synthase (FASN) has been linked to increased MHC class II expression via metabolic reprogramming. A recent study identiﬁed a panel of FASN inhibitors that selectively induced MHC-II on tumor cells, enhancing CD4+ T cell recruitment and suppressing tumor growth, thereby linking lipid metabolism to antigen presentation and immune activation135. Furthermore, IFNγ has long been recognized for its ability to enhance antigen presentation via upregulation of TAP, LMP2/7, and tapasin. While cytokine therapy is associated with systemic toxicity, small molecules that mimic IFNγ-induced transcriptional effects are under investigation. For instance, TAP1 and TAP2 expression, commonly downregulated in lung carcinomas, can be restored by agents like decitabine and histone deacetylase inhibitors, enhancing MHC-I expression and restoring CD8+ T cell recognition136. These advances are especially relevant in tumors with defects in neoantigen processing. TAP- and tapasin-deﬁcient cancers, such as small cell lung carcinoma, present signiﬁcant challenges to immunotherapy.

Metabolic reprogramming Tumor cells exploit metabolic pathways to establish an immunosuppressive microenvironment that inhibits effective anti-tumor immunity. Among these, arginase (ARG1/ARG2) and IDO1 are two of the most clinically relevant enzymes, both of which deplete key amino acids—L-arginine and tryptophan,respectively—therebyimpairingT-cellproliferation,activation, and effector function. AI-guided drug discovery has emerged as a transformative strategy in designing potent small-molecule inhibitors against these targets, optimizing them for both efﬁcacy and pharmacokinetic proﬁles121,124,138. Arginase inhibitors have shown great promise in reversing tumor-mediated immunosuppression. The dual ARG1/ARG2 inhibitor OATD-02 demonstrates both immunomodulatory and direct anti-tumor efﬁcacy in murine models of colorectal, kidney, and leukemia cancers. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44386-025-00029-y Perspective npj Drug Discovery | (2025) 2:25 10 Unlike earlier generation inhibitors, OATD-02 can effectively target intracellular ARG2, which has been strongly associated with poor prognosis and tumor aggressiveness. The molecule showed superior tumor regression and immune activation, particularly when combined with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, making it an ideal candidate for personalized immunotherapeutic regimens139. Similarly, CB-1158 (also known as INCB001158) is an orally bioavailable ARG1/2 inhibitor that has entered clinical trials. It enhances CD8+ T-cell inﬁltration and improves outcomes when used in combination with checkpoint blockade therapies. Preclinical studies conﬁrm its ability to elevate intratumoral arginine levels, reinvigorate suppressed T cells, and potentiate IFNγ signaling pathways, positioning it as a versatile agent in combination therapy strategies140. The tryptophan-kynurenine axis, regulated by IDO1 and TDO, is another immunosuppressive mechanism frequently upregulated in immune-resistant tumors. RG70099 is a dual IDO1/ TDO inhibitor that signiﬁcantly reduces kynurenine levels and restores T cell effector function. RG70099 exhibits potent dual enzyme inhibition and favorable pharmacokinetics, suggesting its utility in a broad spectrum of malignanciescharacterizedbyhighIDO1/TDOexpression141,142.AI-assisted VS and molecular dynamics simulations have also contributed to the development of novel IDO1/TDO inhibitors.

Precision oncology meets AI-driven molecule design Patient stratiﬁcation Patient stratiﬁcation enables the identiﬁcation of individuals most likely to respond to speciﬁc treatments based on their unique tumor and immune characteristics (Fig. 3). AI, particularly ML and DL, has proven transformative in this domain by integrating multi-omics data—genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and imaging—to derive predictive models for immunotherapeutic response. These models are now being extended to small-molecule immunotherapies, where identifying responsive subgroups isessentialforclinicalefﬁcacyandsafety.AI-drivenstratiﬁcationmodelsuse unsupervised clustering and supervised classiﬁcation to segment patients into molecular subtypes based on immune-genomic signatures. For instance, transcriptomic clustering using SVMs and k-means has enabled the deﬁnition of immune “hot” and “cold” tumor proﬁles, based on the abundance of immune cells, cytokine expression, and co-stimulatory molecules. A study by Duan et al. identiﬁed ﬁve costimulatory molecule genes (FAS, TNFRSF14, TNFRSF17, TNFRSF1B, and TNFSF13B) that distinguished lung squamous carcinoma patients into distinct immune subclasses, enhancing predictions of immunotherapy beneﬁt144. Moreover, AI has been instrumental in discovering predictive biomarkers of response to small-molecule immunotherapies, including metabolic regulators, checkpoint expression, and neoantigen presentation pathways. For example, multimodal ML models that integrate metabolic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data have identiﬁed cytokine and checkpoint expression proﬁles Fig. 3 | Applications of artiﬁcial intelligence in small molecule immunotherapy drug discovery. Central to the process, AI enables accelerated hit identiﬁcation, de novo molecular generation, and predictive modeling of immune activity. It also supports optimization of ADMET (i.e., absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity) proﬁles, target discovery via systems biology, and patient stratiﬁcation for precision targeting. AI further facilitates integration with highthroughput screening (HTS), biomarker and neoantigen prediction, and rapid iteration through reinforcement learning. Additionally, it enables federated learning for secure multi-institutional data collaboration, promoting innovation while preserving privacy. Collectively, these AI-driven approaches are transforming the immunotherapeutic landscape by expediting the discovery of efﬁcacious, safe, and personalized small molecule therapies.

Integration of multi-omics for personalized design By combining transcriptomic, proteomic, and mutational data, AI systems can generate comprehensive tumor-speciﬁc immunoproﬁles, which are critical for identifying actionable neoantigens for therapeutic intervention. AI models excel at deciphering the complexity of high-dimensional datasets by learning non-linear relationships between different omics layers147. For instance, DL architectures have been used to extract features from somatic mutations, gene expression, and proteomic HLA-peptide data to predict which mutations give rise to immunogenic peptides. A study by BulikSullivan et al. showed that integrating exome sequencing, RNA-seq, and HLA-bound peptide mass spectrometry data signiﬁcantly improved neoantigen prediction, with a DL model achieving a tenfold increase in positive predictive value compared to standard afﬁnity-based tools148. ML also plays a pivotal role in reﬁning tumor-speciﬁc neoantigen selection. Digital twins and simulation platforms Digital twin technologies are emerging as a transformative component in precision oncology, enabling real-time, patient-speciﬁc simulation of drug responses and optimization of therapeutic strategies. A digital twin is a dynamic, data-driven virtual representation of an individual patient that integrates clinical, molecular, imaging, and physiological data. These virtual models, powered by AI, enable in silico experimentation, where the outcomes of different dosing schedules, combination therapies, or moleculespeciﬁc interventions can be simulated before patient exposure. One of the most advanced platforms, multi-level parameterized automata (MLPA), integrates macroscopic electronic health records with microscopic genomic data to simulate tumor progression and pharmacological responses with high ﬁdelity. MLPA leverages stochastic cellular automata to predict patient-speciﬁc responses to various drug regimens, including smallmolecule immunotherapies, achieving over 90% predictive accuracy in preclinical settings. These simulations support the optimization of drug dosing and scheduling based on the tumor’s growth dynamics and immune interactions152. In parallel, the theranostic digital twin (TDT) framework is being applied to optimize radiopharmaceutical and immunotherapeutic interventions. By incorporating physiologically based pharmacokinetic models and real-time imaging, TDTs allow oncologists to simulate drug absorption, distribution, and efﬁcacy across different tissue compartments. This capability is particularly valuable in determining optimal doses and sequencing for combination regimens, such as checkpoint inhibitors paired with metabolic or cytokine-targeting small molecules153. Digital twins are also advancing in the context of clinical trial simulation and treatment failure prediction. For example, digital-twin-based virtual populations were constructed in a Phase I study of the bispeciﬁc antibody mosunetuzumab, enabling accurate simulation of dose–response relationships and identiﬁcation of response biomarkers across subtypes of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. These simulations informed adaptive dosing protocols and predicted which patient subgroups would beneﬁt most, reducing both risk and development costs154. The integration of large language models (LLMs) into digital twin frameworks,suchasDT-GPT,enablespredictivehealthtrajectorymodeling without requiring prior data imputation. These LLM-powered digital twins maintain strong accuracy even under data sparsity and allow simulation of novel variables, which is critical for exploring hypothetical therapeutic scenarios and off-label drug uses in real-time155. Applications in AI-assisted small-molecule immunomodulation therapy AI-designed IDO1 inhibitors IDO1 has become a prominent target in cancer immunotherapy due to its role in tryptophan metabolism and immune suppression within the TME. Recent advances in AI have signiﬁcantly accelerated the discovery and optimization of small-molecule IDO1 inhibitors by integrating computational modeling, ML, and DL pipelines into the drug design process. One compelling example is the development of IDO1Stack, a two-layer stacking ensemble ML model speciﬁcally designed for IDO1 inhibitor prediction. This system incorporated ﬁve base classiﬁers (e.g., random forest, SVM, XGBoost) using eight types of molecular ﬁngerprints and combined them using logistic regression as a meta-classiﬁer. The model achieved excellent predictive performance (AUC of 0.952 on test data and 0.918 on external validation), demonstrating its robustness for VS. Furthermore, model explainability was addressed via SHAP, which highlighted substructure contributions to activity predictions124. In another study, a 2D-QSAR approach was applied to a dataset of 39 triazole derivatives to predict IDO1 inhibitory activity. Linear regression models trained on physicochemical descriptors demonstrated strong predictive power (R²_test = 0.809), withall compounds falling within the model’s applicability domain. This study provided a reliable framework for designing structurally novel IDO1 inhibitors using relatively small datasets156. Complementary to ML models, structure-based AI pipelines have also facilitated the identiﬁcation of promising chemical scaffolds. Xu et al. employed a DL-based DTI prediction tool, DeePurpose, to guide the synthesis of 1,2,3-triazole-erlotinib derivatives. Docking studies and ADME proﬁling conﬁrmed high afﬁnity and drug-like properties of several candidates, including a lead compound with an IC₅₀ of 0.32 μM against IDO1 in HeLa cells121. Beyond in silico predictions, metabolite-based optimization strategies have been aided by AI to enhance stability and pharmacokinetics. For instance, Hopkins et al. used structural data and metabolic modeling to design IDO1 inhibitors with cyclopropyl-modiﬁed cores, improving bioavailability and reducing human predicted dose to as low as 9 mg once daily157. These case studies demonstrate how AI-driven pipelines—ranging from ensemble learning and QSAR to deep DTI prediction—can streamline the discovery and development of next-generation IDO1 inhibitors. Importantly, these platforms are not only predictive but also interpretable, providing insights into molecular determinants of activity that can guide iterative design cycles in immuno-oncology drug development.
