One of the most notable examples is Generative Tensorial Reinforcement Learning (GENTRL), a deep generative framework designed to rapidly identifynovelbioactive molecules158.GENTRL uses a combination of tensor decomposition, VAEs, and RL to optimize compounds for properties such as binding afﬁnity, drug-likeness, and synthetic accessibility. In a landmark study, GENTRL was used to identifypotent inhibitors of DDR1 kinase, with experimental validation achieved in just 21 days. Although DDR1 is not an immune checkpoint, this case highlighted GENTRL’s capacity to generalize across targets with well-deﬁned structures and paved the way for similar https://doi.org/10.1038/s44386-025-00029-y Perspective npj Drug Discovery | (2025) 2:25 12 applications in immuno-oncology159. The rapid lead generation and pharmacokinetic optimization capabilities make GENTRL an ideal platform for immune checkpoint modulation, where therapeutic windows are narrow and selectivity is paramount. Recent work has adapted this framework for immune targets such as PD-L1 and STK11-deﬁcient tumors. For example, researchers from Recursion Pharmaceuticals developed a HTS platform combining DL and RL to explore a uniﬁed chemical-genomic representation space. By embedding both gene knockouts via CRISPR and small molecule perturbations into the same latent space, they prioritized moleculescapableofsensitizingtumorstoICIs,especiallyinresistantphenotypes like STK11 mutations160. In parallel, ML-guided screening has been applied to identify PD-L1 dimerization inducers. One study used Random Forest classiﬁers trained on six 2D molecular ﬁngerprints to scan a database of ~16,000 bioactive compounds. Docking and biochemical validation narrowed the pool to two hits (CRT5 and P053), which exhibited IC₅₀ values of 22–34 μM in PD-1/PD-L1 HTRF binding assays—offering promising starting points for further RL-driven lead optimization161. The MOSES benchmarking platform, co-developed alongside GENTRL, has become a community standard for evaluating generative models in medicinal chemistry. It allows systematic assessment of validity, novelty, diversity, and synthesizability in generated compounds—crucial metrics for immune checkpoint drug development where functional diversity and selectivity are essential162.

Discovery of STING agonists The discovery of small-molecule agonists of stimulator of interferon genes (STING) has gained momentum in immuno-oncology due to STING’s central role in bridging innate and adaptive immunity through type I interferon signaling. Despite the early limitations of ﬁrst-generation cyclic dinucleotide agonists, recent advances—especially those involving AIassisted SBDD—have yielded potent, systemically deliverable STING agonists with optimized pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics. A standout case is the development of SB 11285, a nucleotide analog discovered through structure-guided design and validated using high-throughput reporter gene assays, qPCR, and caspase activation assays. SB 11285 demonstrated superior potency compared to the natural STING ligand 2’,3’-cGAMP, inducing IRF and NF-κB activation at nanomolar concentrations, and selective apoptosis in tumor cells but not PBMCs. This compound was shown to robustly induce immune signaling (e.g., RIG-I, ISG54, PD-L1) and antitumor activity in vitro, highlighting its promise as animmunomodulatorytherapeutic163.Inparallel,thediscoveryofMSA-2,a non-nucleotide small molecule STING agonist, exempliﬁes the integration of phenotypic screening and molecular modeling. MSA-2 binds STINGas a noncovalent dimer in a “closed-lid” conformation, favoring selective activation in the acidic TME. In murine models, oral MSA-2 induced potent interferon-β production, tumor regression, and synergized with anti–PD-1 therapy to generate durable antitumor immunity. The compound’s tumor selectivity and oral bioavailability marked a breakthrough in systemic STING agonist development164. Complementing these advances, AI also plays a pivotal role in predictive biomarker validation. A study by Lee et al. used [18F]FDG-PET imaging as a non-invasive pharmacodynamic biomarker for systemic STING agonists like diABZI. They demonstrated that [18F]FDG uptake in lymphoid organs correlated with CD69 and PD-L1 expression in T and B cells, effectively predicting treatment response in pancreatic cancer models165. AI-enabled models have also been used to design orally bioavailable STING agonists like ZSA-51, based on tricyclic benzo[4,5]thieno[2,3-c]pyrrole scaffolds. ZSA-51 exhibited nanomolar activation in THP1 cells and >30-fold increased potency over MSA-2, with enhanced lymphoid organ distribution and pharmacokinetics. Docking simulations validated its binding conformation, showcasing AI’s contribution to lead optimization166.

Collaborations between academia and industry The development of AI-driven small-molecule immunotherapies has been signiﬁcantly accelerated by strategic collaborations between academic institutions and AI-native biotechnology ﬁrms. Companies such as Insilico Medicine, Exscientia, and BenevolentAI exemplify the translational impact of such partnerships, leveraging DL, generative models, and biomedical data integration to redeﬁne immuno-oncology pipelines. Insilico Medicine has collaborated with pharmaceutical giants such as GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) to identify novel immunotherapeutic targets. GSK used Insilico’s AI platform, Pharma.AI, to explore previously uncharacterized disease pathways and immune-related molecular targets. This partnership marked a signiﬁcant move by big pharma into the AI drug discovery space, with GSK aiming to integrate Insilico’s capabilities into its broader immuno-oncology portfolio167. Evaluations of Pharma.AI have shown it consistently outperforms competing platforms in both usability and predictive accuracy, underscoring its value for immune target identiﬁcation168. Exscientia, another leader in AI-driven drug design, has forged multi-million dollar partnerships with Sanoﬁand Bristol Myers Squibb to design immune-related therapies using its Centaur Chemist™platform. This hybrid system integrates human domain expertise with DL models to optimize small molecules across multiple parameters simultaneously. Although some collaborations initially focused on metabolic and cardiovascular diseases, Exscientia has recently expanded into immunotherapy and inﬂammatory targets. These efforts include the development of AI-prioritized molecules for immunomodulatory enzymes and T cell checkpoints169. BenevolentAI combines biomedical knowledge graphs, literature mining, and ML to accelerate immunotherapy target identiﬁcation. The company has collaborated with major pharmaceutical organizations to uncover new mechanisms and targets in diseases with immune involvement, including autoimmune conditionsand solidtumors.For example,BenevolentAI’s work with GSK and others involves integrating omics datasets with real-world evidence to prioritize targets amenable to small-molecule modulation, including PDL1 and IDO1. Challenges and limitations Data quality and availability High-quality, curated data is the foundational input for AI models in drug discovery. However, despite the abundance of biological and chemical data generated from omics studies, HTS, and clinical trials, major data curation challenges continue to impede the performance and generalizability of AI models. The three primary obstacles are data quality, algorithmic bias, and data scarcity. Data quality issues arise from errors in labeling, missing metadata, inconsistent formatting, or the use of outdated experimental protocols. Such inconsistencies can propagate noise in training datasets, leadingtooverﬁtting,misclassiﬁcation,orunreliablepredictions.AImodels, particularlyDLsystems,aresensitivetosuchnoiseduetotheirhighcapacity for memorization. One downstream risk of poor data quality is the occurrenceofdata hallucinationduringhypothesisvalidation,whereanAImodel generates predictions or mechanistic explanations that appear biologically plausible but are not actually supported by empirical evidence170. In drug discovery, this can result in high-conﬁdence yet spurious drug–target associations, misleading mechanistic pathways, or overestimated compound efﬁcacy, ultimately wasting experimental resources and reducing trust in the model’s outputs. Suchhallucinations often arise from overﬁtting to biased or noisy datasets, insufﬁcient orthogonal validation, or the use of synthetic training data without adequate cross-checks. This concern is especially pronounced in pharmacokinetic and toxicity prediction, where small deviations in data can result in large errors in model outputs171. Algorithmic bias is another critical concern, often stemming from unbalanced datasets that overrepresent speciﬁc molecular scaffolds, targets, or patient populations. Models trained on biased data are less likely to generalize to novel chemical spaces or underrepresented disease subtypes. For https://doi.org/10.1038/s44386-025-00029-y Perspective npj Drug Discovery | (2025) 2:25 13 instance, one study demonstrated that cross-domain bias in materials and drug discovery signiﬁcantly reduced prediction reliability when models were applied to datasets outside their training distribution172. Data scarcity, particularly for rare diseases, novel targets, or ﬁrst-in-class compounds, presents a signiﬁcant barrier to developing robust AI models. Many datasets lack sufﬁcient labeled examples to train deepnetworks effectively, leading to performance degradation. Strategies such as transfer learning, one-shot learning, and federated learning have emerged as potential solutions to this issue. These techniques leverage prior knowledge or distributed datasets to improve model performance in data-poor settings173. Addressing these challenges is essential for realizing the full potential of AI in precision oncology and small-molecule drug design.

AI models used for de novo drug design or structurebasedVS(e.g.,moleculardocking,CNNs,transformers)dependonaccurate 3D structures of target proteins. This severely limits the application of AI tools in identifying selective small-molecule modulators for these targets176. Efforts like AlphaFold have provided computationally predicted protein structures, yet these models may lack accuracy in ﬂexible binding pockets or dynamic protein–protein interfaces common in immune checkpoints. Furthermore, predicted structures often omit key posttranslational modiﬁcations or allosteric conformations that are critical for immunomodulation177. Together, these data-related limitations create signiﬁcant barriers to the widespread deployment and scalability of AI for immunotherapy drug design. Model interpretability and trust One of the most persistent challenges in deploying AI in drug discovery— especially for immuno-oncology—is the “black-box” nature of DL models, which makes them difﬁcult to interpret and trust in clinical and regulatory contexts. These models often achieve high accuracy by capturing complex, non-linearrelationshipsacrossmassive,high-dimensionaldatasets,butthey do so at the expense of transparency. This opacity presents a signiﬁcant barrier to adoption in ﬁelds like drug development, where regulatory bodies and clinicians demand clear justiﬁcations for predictions related to patient safety and therapeutic efﬁcacy. The need for interpretability has catalyzed the emergence of Explainable AI (XAI) techniques. XAI aims to elucidate how AI models arrive at speciﬁc decisions, enabling both domain experts and regulatorstoassesstheirvalidity.Popularpost-hocinterpretabilitytools include SHAP and LIME, which have been increasingly used in AI-driven drug discovery pipelines. These methods quantify the contribution of each input feature (e.g., molecular substructure or genomic mutation) to a prediction, thereby providing mechanistic insight into drug–target relationships and toxicity risks178. In regulatory terms, explainability is becoming essential. Drug regulatory agencies, including the United States FDA and EuropeanMedicinesAgency(EMA),aredevelopingframeworkstoevaluate AI-based medical tools and expect a degree of interpretability that supports auditing and reproducibility. Transparent models—particularly those incorporating hybrid explanation frameworks combining saliency maps, decision trees, and feature attribution—have been proposed as a middle ground that balances model performance with regulatory clarity179. Moreover, the integration of XAI is shown to improve model usability by domain experts, such as medicinal chemists and immunologists. Interpretable models facilitate downstream decisions like compound prioritization, offtarget assessment, and biomarker validation, which are critical for earlyphase immunotherapeutic design92. Nevertheless, challenges remain. There is often a trade-off between interpretability and performance, and no universal XAI method ﬁts all drug discovery contexts. In many cases, modelspeciﬁc tuning is required to ensure that interpretability does not compromise generalization or introduce bias through oversimpliﬁcation. Additionally,explainingdecisionsinvolvinghigh-dimensional,multi-omics inputs—such as those used for immunogenomic stratiﬁcation—remains an active area of research. Federated learning and secure data sharing As AI-driven immunotherapy advances toward personalization, the need for secure, privacy-preserving collaborative learning across institutions becomes paramount. Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a critical technology to enable multi-institutional collaboration in AI-based drug discovery and precision oncology without sharing sensitive patient data. FL allows models to be trained locally on institutional datasets and only shares model parameters or gradients—not raw data—ensuring compliance with data protection laws like GDPR and HIPAA. A landmark example of FL at scale is the MELLODDY project, a collaboration among 10 pharmaceutical companies, academic labs, and tech partners to build a secure federated model for drug discovery. Utilizing encrypted gradient sharing and decentralized access control within a Kubernetes-based cloud architecture, MELLODDY enabled joint model training across proprietary compound librarieswithoutcompromisingconﬁdentiality.Theplatformdemonstrated scalability and generated actionable insights for pharmacological modeling across hundreds of terabytes of data188,189. For more targeted applications in cancerimmunotherapy,federatedQSARmodelingplatformslikeFL-QSAR have proven capable of matching centralized training performance while maintaining data privacy. Using horizontal FL, the platform enabled predictive modeling of structure-activity relationships across siloed datasets with comparable accuracy to pooled training, showcasing its potential to unify immunotherapy discovery efforts across institutions with different compound libraries190. Nevertheless, challenges remain, particularly when participating institutions have non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data—a common issue in real-world biomedical applications. Solutions include global model stabilization via selective data sharing or incorporating small representative datasets to harmonize distributions. A recent framework showed that such techniques improved generalization in federated drug discovery without violating privacy constraints191. Ethical concerns around algorithmic bias, auditability, and trust in federated environments are also under active investigation. Secure multiparty computation, differential privacy, and blockchain-based audit trails are being layered onto FL architectures to provide transparent model evolution and prevent data leakage or reverse engineering of sensitive patient features192. Role of quantum computing in AI for drug design Quantumcomputing(QC)ispoisedtorevolutionizeAI-drivendrugdesign, particularly by transforming molecular simulation and optimization processes that underpin small-molecule discovery. Traditional computational drug discovery methods struggle with the combinatorial explosion of conformational space and the complex quantum behavior of molecular interactions. Quantum computing, through algorithms like the Variational Quantum Eigensolver and Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm, offers a fundamentally new computational paradigm that can model electronic structures and reaction pathways with exponentially greater precision than classical methods. In drug design, quantum computing’s strength lies in its ability to solve the Schrödinger equation for complex molecules with high ﬁdelity. For example, quantum-enhanced simulations can accurately compute drug–target binding energies, optimize reaction energetics, and map protein-ligand conformations that are computationally intractable with classical systems. When integrated with AI, such hybrid approaches signiﬁcantly accelerate hit-to-lead optimization. Recent studies have demonstrated that quantum-assisted ML models outperform classical analogs in simulating protein folding and predicting pharmacokinetics for structurally novel compounds193. Quantum computing is particularly synergistic with generative AI platforms for de novo molecular design. In one review, Pyrkov et al. outlined how quantum simulations embedded within generative models can explore chemical space more effectively by resolving electron correlation in small molecules and reﬁning SAR for difﬁcult targets like immune checkpoints and G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs)194. Such quantum-AI hybrids can simulate hundreds of molecular structures in parallel, generating binding-afﬁnity proﬁles with precision unattainable by classical physics-based scoring functions alone. Moreover, quantum-enhanced neural networks and quantum kernel methods are emerging as tools to predict complex pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic behaviors from multi-omics data. These models, still in early development, have been shown to accelerate optimization cycles and improve the predictive accuracy of toxicity and metabolism outcomes, key parameters for immunomodulatory compounds195. While the potential is vast,currentlimitationsincludetheimmaturityofquantumhardware,noise in intermediate-scale devices (NISQ), and challenges in integrating quantum pipelines with real-world biological datasets. However, platforms like ChemiQ and other quantum chemistry simulators are already being used to test low-energy conformations of biologically relevant compounds, laying the groundwork for future scalable applications196. Expanding targets beyond traditional checkpoints Despitethesuccessofcheckpoint inhibitorslike PD-1,PD-L1,and CTLA-4, many patients either fail to respond or eventually relapse, highlighting the urgent need to discover and target novel immunoregulatory pathways. AIdriven systems biology is emerging as a powerful approach to uncover such targets by integrating high-dimensional multi-omics, protein–protein interaction (PPI) networks, and patient-derived datasets. A recent study by Augustine et al. used graph-based ML to model ~12,000 genes and 99,000 PPIs across diverse immune subsets derived from single-cell RNA-seq data. Their integrative pipeline incorporated bulk transcriptomics, immunopeptidomics, SNP-phenotype associations, and CRISPR screens to prioritize immune-oncology targets. This method identiﬁed novel immunotherapy targets related to macrophage polarization and antigen presentation pathways, which are now undergoing experimental validation https://doi.org/10.1038/s44386-025-00029-y Perspective npj Drug Discovery | (2025) 2:25 15 in organoid-immune co-cultures197. Parallel discoveries have pointed to the importance of alternative immune checkpoints (AICs), including B7-H3 (CD276), B7-H4, VISTA, and HHLA2, particularly in tumors resistant to standard checkpoint blockade. These molecules are often expressed on cancer stemcells and contribute to therapyevasionand immune escape. AIpowered clustering and immune deconvolution models have shown that these AICs co-express with stemness markers and are enriched in immunosuppressive microenvironments, suggesting a role in driving both resistance and tumor progression9. Moreover, AI-enhanced systems immunology approaches are uncovering novel regulatory axes within the TME. Studies showed checkpoints such as TIGIT, LAG-3, and TIM-3, as well as less conventional regulators including galectins and adenosine receptors, inﬂuence immune inﬁltration and T-cell exhaustion in speciﬁc tumor contexts4. Many of these emerging targets are already in early-phase trials and are being paired with AI-driven patient stratiﬁcation strategies. Importantly, these discoveries are being accelerated by the integration of causal inference models, which help distinguish correlative from functionally relevant pathways. This enables the identiﬁcation of master regulatory nodes—genes or proteins that control multiple downstream immune-suppressive networks and thus serve as high-leverage therapeutic targets. Conclusion AI is fundamentally reshaping the landscape of small-molecule drug design for cancer immunomodulation therapy by accelerating target discovery, molecule optimization, and personalized treatment development. This perspective article has highlighted how AI technologies—ranging from generative models and RL to multi-omics integration and digital twins—are convergingtoenabletherationaldesignofimmunomodulatorycompounds withunprecedentedprecision.Inparticular,theapplicationofAIindenovo molecular generation, ADMET prediction, patient stratiﬁcation, and the identiﬁcation of novel immune pathways is bridging critical translational gaps in precision oncology.

As high-throughput automation and secure collaborative infrastructures mature, AI-driven systems will likely become integral to realtime, patient-speciﬁc immunomodulation therapy development. Ultimately, the integration of AI with systems biology and immuno-oncology holds the transformative potential to deliver personalized, durable, and accessible cancer treatments across diverse patient populations. title: Age-related auditory nerve deficits propagate central gain throughout the auditory system: Associations with cortical microstructure and speech recognition.
text: Age-related auditory nerve deficits propagate central gain throughout the auditory system: Associations with cortical microstructure and speech recognition Emily M. Fabrizio-Stovera,*, James W. Diasb, Carolyn M. McClaskeyb, Kelly C. Harrisb aMedical University of South Carolina, Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, USA bMedical University of South Carolina, Department of Otolaryngology – Head and Neck Surgery, USA Abstract There is growing evidence that perceptual difficulties associated with age-related hearing loss are not solely due to cochlear damage and are exacerbated by central nervous system changes. We examined electrophysiological (EEG) responses to clicks and diffusion kurtosis imaging in 49 older (29 female) and 26 younger (20 female) adults to determine the extent to which auditory nerve (AN) deficits in older adults contributed to functional and structural changes throughout the auditory system. Older adults exhibited smaller AN responses, similar brainstem responses, and larger auditory cortex (AC) responses, demonstrating progressive “central gain.” Audiometric thresholds were not predictive of EEG measures. Reduced AN function predicted deficits in cortical microstructure (lower AC fractional anisotropy) in older adults, consistent with microstructure degeneration. These lower fractional anisotropy values in the AC of older adults also predicted larger AC responses and more central gain. Older adults exhibited significantly lower AC fractional anisotropy and kurtosis fractional anisotropy coupled with higher mean and radial diffusivity compared to younger adults. AC fractional anisotropy, radial diffusivity, axial diffusivity, and mean diffusivity were all significant predictors of speech-in-noise (SIN) recognition in older adults. The results suggest that reduced afferent input in older adults not only results in functional changes throughout the auditory system consistent with progressive gain but also contributes to deficits in AC structure beyond those explained by age alone, contributing to SIN recognition deficits. Keywords Auditory Central Gain; Aging; Human; Myelin Integrity; Speech-in-noise 1. Introduction Older adults with and without hearing loss often experience difficulties recognizing speech, particularly in challenging listening environments (Dubno et al., 1984; Başkent et al., 2014; Goossens et al., 2017; Holder et al., 2018; Kocabay et al., 2022). Many studies of aging and speech recognition focus on characterizing the auditory periphery (Zeng et al., 2005; Hoben et al., 2017; Bramhall and McMillan, 2024). Although age-related hearing loss and, even more so, auditory nerve (AN) deficits (Makary et al., 2011; Dias et al., 2024), are two of the most common conditions of aging, little is known regarding how the central auditory system adapts to this progressive decline in auditory input. Our prior research (Harris et al., 2022; Rumschlag et al., 2022) and others (Salvi et al., 2017; Johannesen and Lopez-Poveda, 2021; Hutchison et al., 2023) suggests that in older adults, the loss of afferent input contributes to hyperexcitability, or “central gain”, in the auditory system that may be maladaptive to speech-in-noise (SIN) recognition. Specifically, central gain refers to the adaptive increase in neural response amplitudes within central auditory pathways that occurs in response to reduced peripheral input.

title: Age-related auditory nerve deficits propagate central gain throughout the auditory system: Associations with cortical microstructure and speech recognition.
text: Johannesen and Lopez-Poveda, 2021; Hutchison et al., 2023) suggests that in older adults, the loss of afferent input contributes to hyperexcitability, or “central gain”, in the auditory system that may be maladaptive to speech-in-noise (SIN) recognition. Specifically, central gain refers to the adaptive increase in neural response amplitudes within central auditory pathways that occurs in response to reduced peripheral input. It is still unknown if central gain in the AC is generated locally, or reflects amplified responses propagated from subcortical structures. Age-related central gain has been observed at both the level of the auditory brainstem and cortex (Harris et al., 2022, Overton and Recanzone, 2016; Dobri and Ross, 2021; Xue et al., 2023; Rumschlag et al., 2022). Animal studies have shown that deficits in inhibitory neurotransmission at the brainstem contribute to central gain (Palombi et al., 2001; Keine et al., 2016; Ono and Ito, 2024) and our prior work has confirmed a similar effect in humans (Rumschlag et al., 2022). Results from cortical studies also suggest an important role of inhibitory loss in cortical central gain (Harris et al., 2022; Resnik and Polley, 2021; Cisneros-Franco et al., 2018). Heterogeneous effects are reported following transient auditory deprivation in younger adults, with central gain occurring in the brainstem (Maslin et al., 2013; Brotherton et al., 2017), the auditory cortex (AC) (Graterón et al., 2022), or both (Hutchison et al., 2023). However, plasticity associated with chronic conditions, like age-related deafferentation, may not be well modeled by such transient manipulations (Seybold et al., 2012). Here, we expand on our prior work by examining how age-related AN deficits predict changes in brainstem activity and cortical activity source-constrained to the AC. We predicted that gain effects arise at both the brainstem and AC, and would result in progressive amplification of the evoked response from AN to brainstem to AC. Deficits in peripheral input are thought to engage homeostatic plasticity mechanisms that reduce GABAergic expression in the central auditory system. We have previously shown Fabrizio-Stover et al. In addition to GABA, more recent evidence suggests that a loss of myelin may contribute to hyperexcitability (Borges et al., 2023).

In addition to GABA, more recent evidence suggests that a loss of myelin may contribute to hyperexcitability (Borges et al., 2023). Myelin faciliates saltatory conduction and in addition to its role in hyperexcitability, myelin integrity is essential for the efficient and accurate encoding of complex stimuli, like speech, especially in difficult listening environments (Zeng et al., 2005; Long et al., 2018; Harris et al., 2021). Aging is associated with myelin degeneration (Rawji et al., 2023) and a hallmark of age-related hearing loss is deficits in auditory temporal processing consistent with myelin degeneration (Strouse et al., 1998; Gallun et al., 2014; Ozmeral et al., 2016). To examine the extent to which afferent loss predicted structural deficits in the AC, we computed metrics of microstructural integrity from diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI) that are closely associated with myelin. Age effects on cortical diffusion metrics are well established (Zhao et al., 2015; Gray et al., 2020; Schilling et al., 2023) and, although mixed, there is some evidence to suggest that hearing loss may be associated with changes in cortical diffusion metrics (Tarabichi et al., 2018; Husain et al., 2011; McEvoy et al., 2023; but see Profant et al., 2014). However, the role of afferent loss on diffusion metrics reflecting myelin integrity and central gain, and the role of these factors in SIN recognition, remain largely unknown in older adults. This is the first study to use a within-subject design to characterize the spatial pattern of central gain from the AN to the brainstem and AC in older adults. We also examined how age and decreased afferent input predict diffusion metrics associated with cortical microstructure as a proxy measure of myelin integrity in the central auditory system. We tested the overarching hypothesis that age-related loss of afferent input predicts microstructural degeneration in the AC, contributing in part to central gain and poorer SIN recognition. Understanding how a loss of afferent input with age may affect AC microstructure and, in turn, how AC microstructure may affect SIN recognition, can shed light on new therapeutic targets to improve the speech recognition of older adults. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Participants Forty-nine older adults [Age: 55–82 years, mean age: 66, SD= 7.870, 29 female] and 26 younger adults [Age: 18–30 years, mean age: 24, SD= 2.942, 20 female] were recruited from the Charleston, South Carolina, community. All participants were native English speakers and had a Mini-Mental Status Examination score of at least 27. Participants with a history of head trauma, seizures, conductive hearing loss or otologic disease, self-reported central nervous system disorders, or an inability to safely undergo magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were excluded. 50 participants overlapped with those in our previous publication (20 young, 30 older) (Harris et al., 2022). Younger participants had pure tone audiometric thresholds ≤ 25 dB HL from 0.25 kHz to 8.0 kHz. Older participants were included if their thresholds were ≤ 65 dB HL from.25 to 4.0 kHz. No participants had asymmetries between their ears in excess of 15 dB HL. Participant audiograms are shown in Figure 1. A pure-tone average (PTA) was calculated for each participant, representing the average hearing thresholds in the test (right) ear from 0.5 kHz to 4.0 kHz. PTAs in older Fabrizio-Stover et al. PTA was used to examine the potential effects of hearing level on AN function, cortical microstructure, and SIN recognition. Participants provided written informed consent before participating in this study approved by the Medical University of South Carolina. 2.2. Electrophysiological measures of AN, brainstem, and cortical function To assess central gain, we examined the amplitude of the AN compound action potential (CAP) N1 response, auditory brainstem response (ABR) wave V, and cortical P1-N1 response evoked to a 100 dB pSPL click stimulus. To evaluate cortical activity in the AC and visual cortex (serving as a control region), we used a distributed source model to estimate P1-N1 amplitudes within these regions of interest (ROI) as described below. 2.3.

To evaluate cortical activity in the AC and visual cortex (serving as a control region), we used a distributed source model to estimate P1-N1 amplitudes within these regions of interest (ROI) as described below. 2.3. AN and ABR acquisition and analysis CAPs were collected as part of several ongoing studies. Subsets of these CAP data have been reported elsewhere (Dias et al., 2024; Harris et al., 2021; McClaskey et al., 2018; Rumschlag et al., 2022), although their associations with ABR wave V and the cortical functional and structural characteristics described below are reported here for the first time. The CAP N1 and ABR wave V were elicited using 100 μs rectangular pulses (clicks) presented at a rate of 11.1/s with alternating polarity at 100 dB pSPL. Two runs were recorded at each stimulus intensity, with 1100 trials each (550 of each polarity). Stimuli were presented through an ER3C electrically-shielded insert earphone (Etymotic Technologies, IL, USA). CAP N1 responses were recorded using a tympanic membrane electrode (Sanibel, Denmark) in the test (right) ear, an inverting electrode placed on the contralateral (left) mastoid, and a low forehead grounding electrode. ABR wave V was simultaneously recorded using a high forehead active electrode, an inverting mastoid electrode (on the right mastoid), and a low forehead grounding electrode. All recordings were collected at a sampling rate of 20 kHz using a custom TDT (Tucker Davis Technologies, FL, USA) headstage connected to the bipolar channels of a Neuroscan SynAmpsRT amplifier in AC mode with 2010x gain (Compumedics, Canberra, Australia). Testing was done in an acoustically and electrically shielded room. Participants reclined in a chair and were encouraged to rest quietly for the duration of testing. Participants were allowed to sleep during CAP/ABR recording sessions. Continuous neural activity was analyzed off-line in MATLAB (MathWorks, Natick, MA) using the toolboxes EEGlab (Delorme and Makeig, 2004) and ERPLab (Lopez-Calderon and Luck, 2014). Continuous EEG signals were bandpass filtered between 0.150 kHz and 3.0 kHz. Stimulus triggers were delivered by TDT RPvdsEx and were shifted to account for the 1 ms delay introduced by the earphones and the 0.6 ms delay of the TDT digital-to-analog convertor.

Epoched responses for the remaining trials were averaged. Cortical response acquisition Cortical EEGs were recorded from a 64-channel Neuroscan QuickCap (international 10– 20 system) connected to a SynAmps RT 64-channel Amplifier. Vertical electro-oculogram activity was recorded using bipolar electrodes placed above and below the left eye. A Krios digital scanner (NDI, Ontario, Canada) was acquired midway through data collection. Therefore, QuickCap electrodes were digitally mapped to the participant’s scalp for a subset of participants (n = 31). Of the 27 younger adults, 10 had mapped electrodes (7 female). Of the 48 older adults, 21 (12 female) had mapped electrodes. In participants missing the digitized map, a 64-channel Neuroscan QuickCap default electrode map, from the ICBM152 data set, was used. During EEG recordings, participants were allowed to recline in the same chair and room used for CAP and ABR recording. Participants were not allowed to sleep during cortical recordings and were instead instructed to read. Neural activity was recorded to a 100 μs 100 dB pSPL alternating polarity click with a 2000 ms inter-stimulus interval (20 ms jitter). This is the same stimulus used for CAP and ABR acquisition, but presented at a slower rate. Participants completed two sessions of 200 trials and the continuous EEG data were then processed offline using EEGLab and ERPLab. The recorded EEG data were down sampled to 0.5 kHz, bandpass filtered from 1 to 30 Hz, re-referenced to the average of all electrodes, and corrected for ocular artifacts using independent components analysis. Individual trials were then segmented into epochs around the click onset (−100 ms to +500 ms) and baseline corrected (−100–0 ms). Any epochs contaminated by peak-to-peak deflections in excess of 100 μV were rejected using an automatic artifact rejection algorithm. 2.5. Source-constrained EEG analyses Source currents of the event related potentials were estimated using a cortical source estimation procedure in Brainstorm (Tadel et al., 2011). FreeSurfer (Fischl, 2012) was used to segment the T1 weighted image from each participant and create their individual boundary element model (BEM). Next, the MRI from each participant was co-registered with their respective EEG electrode map.

Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript were co-registered using the Brainstorm 64-channel Neuroscan QuickCap default electrode maps from the ICBM152 data set. Co-registration was performed using the nasion, left auricular point, right auricular point, anterior fissure, posterior fissure, and inter-hemispheric point as fiducials. The forward model was computed using the Symmetric BEM with OpenMEEG software with adaptive integration (Gramfort et al., 2010). Conductivities of the scalp, skull, and brain were set as 1, 0.0125, and 1, respectively. The noise covariance matrix for each participant was calculated from the pre-stimulus baseline. Source estimation was performed using the dynamic Statistical Parametric Mapping approach (Dale et al., 2000) with loose constraints (0.2), where minimum norm imaging was performed and then scaled with respect to the noise covariance, resulting in a map of z-scores. To localize responses to the left auditory and visual cortices, scouts of both regions were defined from the S_temporal_transverse_L and G_cuneus_L areas of the Destrieux atlas (Destrieux et al., 2010), which closely overlap AC and visual cortex, respectively. The final sourceconstrained EEG waveform for each region consisted of the averaged value from all vertex points within the scout. Source-constrained event related potential waveforms were analyzed using a custom MATLAB script. The approximate latencies of the first prominent negative peak (C1/N50), first prominent positive peak (P1), second prominent negative peak (N1), and second prominent positive peak (P2) were visually identified and recorded. These latencies were used to set the detection windows for the exact locations of the P1 and N1 peaks. P1 was defined as the maximum positive peak between C1/N50 and N1, and N1 was defined as the maximum negative peak between P1 and P2.

Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript DKI data was processed using PyDesigner to compute diffusion parameters (Dhiman et al., 2021). Standard preprocessing was performed, consisting of Marchenko-Pastur principal component denoising, Gibbs ringing correction, eddy current correction, Echo Planar Imaging distortion correction, removal of non-brain tissue, gaussian smoothing, and Rician noise bias correction. Diffusion maps of computed fractional anisotropy (FA), kurtosis FA, mean diffusivity (MD), axial diffusivity (AD), and radial diffusivity (RD) were used for this study. Both DKI and diffusion tensor imaging metrics were used in this study to best capture the microstructural characteristics of the AC and whole brain, as recommended by previous studies of such diffusion metrics (Canales-Rodriguez et al., 2014; Pasternak et al., 2018) FA values are generally thought to reflect the integrity of structures affecting water diffusion such as axonal membranes that affect the anisotropy, or directionality, of diffusion in cortical tissue (Van Hecke et al., 2016). Although FA can be computed in non-myelinated tissues, FA values are widely interpreted as reflecting general white matter integrity (Assaf and Pasternak, 2008). As white matter myelination decreases, FA values decline (Horsfield et al., 1998; Hüppi et al., 1998). Kurtosis FA values are a measure of anisotropy of diffusion kurtosis, or how directionally variable the tissue’s complexity is, and is thought to reflect tissue heterogeneity (Glenn et al., 2015). RD values, reflecting diffusivity perpendicular to the main fiber direction, are also thought to be associated with myelin integrity (Song et al., 2002), but can be affected by factors such as crossing fibers or edema (Winklewski et al., 2018). AD values reflect diffusion parallel to fiber tracts, so that reduced AD may reflect axonal injury or less of coherent axonal organization (Salat, 2014). MD values are an average of RD and AD, reflecting overall diffusivity, regardless of direction, and are therefore highest in regions with no barriers to diffusion (Basser and Pierpaoli, 1996). Higher FA and kurtosis FA with lower MD and RD are associated with more microstructural integrity. Average FA, kurtosis FA, MD, and RD values were extracted from an ROI corresponding to the primary AC (TE 1.0 from the Julich Brain Atlas, Amunts et al., 2020) using the DSI studio software package (http://dsi-studio.labsolver.org). This area has a high degree of overlap with the area used for computed source-constrained event related potentials for AC (see above).

Due to the limited field of view of the DKI scans, brainstem diffusion measures were not available for many of our participants, limiting our structural analyses to the cortex. 2.7. SIN recognition We measured SIN recognition using the Quick Speech-in-Noise Test (QuickSIN; Etymotic Technologies) (Killion et al., 2004). QuickSIN data were collected from all participants. The QuickSIN test consists of five lists of six low-probability sentences, each with five keywords per sentence, totaling 30 keywords in each list. Sentences were presented in a four-talker babble. Sentences were presented binaurally using TDH-39 headphones using a combination of an Onkyo Compact Disk Player (Onkyo, Osaka, Japan) and an Interacoustics AA222 Audio Traveler (Interacoustics, Middelfart, Denmark). For each list, the six sentences are presented in a progressively decreasing signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) from 25 to 0 dB in 5 dB steps, with sentences presented at 70 dB HL and the background noise level varying. Then, we summed the number of correctly identified keywords to arrive at a total correct score out of a possible 30. QuickSIN performance is reported as SNR loss, calculated as 25.5 minus the total keywords correct (Killion et al., 2004, Etymotic Research). General linear modeling and generalized linear mixed-effects modeling were performed using the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015). 2.9. Pattern of central gain through the levels of the auditory pathway We hypothesized that age-related loss of afferent auditory activity contributes to central gain, with gain occurring at the brainstem and further amplified at the cortex. To test this, we examined gain using a multivariate approach that tested for age group differences in AN (CAP N1), brainstem (ABR wave V), and source-constrained AC activity (P1-N1). We used source-constrained visual cortex activity (P1-N1) as a cortical control. We hypothesized that age-related deficits in AN activity would predict a recovery of response amplitudes – the absence of an age-group difference – at the auditory brainstem and an amplified response at the AC in older adults relative to responses from younger adults. To test this pattern of central gain through the auditory system, we used a general linear model approach. Consistent with our hypothesis, we predicted that older adults, compared to younger adults, would have smaller AN responses (CAP N1 amplitudes), similar responses at the auditory brainstem (ABR wave V amplitudes), and larger responses in AC (AC P1-N1 amplitudes). To determine the extent to which the relationships we observed with the AC are specific to the AC, we also examined relationships with responses measured in the visual cortex (see “Source-constrained EEG analysis pipeline”). The units of measure for source-constrained event related potentials are arbitrary; this is a byproduct of source reconstruction. Response amplitudes can also vary systematically from one level of the auditory system to another. As such, for these analyses testing the pattern of gain, amplitudes were z-scored at each level of the auditory pathway (CAP N1, ABR wave V, and source-constrained P1-N1) and visual cortex (source-constrained P1-N1) across age groups. CAP N1 amplitudes were z-scored after being converted to absolute values so that larger (more negative) responses would correspond to positive z-scores. By z-scoring response amplitudes in this way, we can compare age-group differences in response amplitude at different levels of the auditory pathway.

If a diffusion metric was found to be a significant predictor of AC P1-N1, then the whole brain average of the specific metric was incorporated into the model as a control to test the degree to which the observed relationship is specific to AC. Building upon these analyses, we used linear regression models to test the degree to which AC diffusion metrics were significant predictors of the magnitude of cortical gain in older adults. AC gain in older adults was quantified using the same method described in Harris et al. (2022). In short, CAP N1 amplitudes predict cortical P1-N1 amplitudes in younger adults. The parameters of the linear model derived from this relationship in younger adults were used to predict the expected cortical response in each older adult, based on their CAP N1 amplitude, using the predict.lm function from the R package “stats” (R Core Team, 2021). To determine if AC gain was evident in our older adults, we used a paired-samples t-test to test whether observed auditory cortical responses were larger than those predicted from the CAP N1 amplitude. To quantify the AC gain in each participant, the predicted auditory cortical response was subtracted from the observed auditory cortical response (Harris et al., 2022). Our definition of AC gain is dependent on the linear relationship between CAP N1 amplitudes and P1-N1 amplitudes in younger adults. Therefore, as we cannot assess gain in the younger adults, they were not included in this analysis. 2.12. Central gain propagates through the auditory pathway An LMER model examining the extent to which age-group and level (AN, brainstem, cortex) of the auditory pathway predict response amplitudes showed a significant interaction between age group and level (Table 1). Response amplitudes were normalized using the zscoring method outline in the methods. Although averaged audiometric thresholds (averaged from 0.25 kHz to 8.0 kHz) were significantly higher in older adults than younger adults [p < 0.001], thresholds were not a significant predictor of response amplitude across levels of the auditory system and visual cortex [β= −0.107, t = 0.098, p = 0.616]. These results are broadly consistent with models of central gain and age-related central nervous system degeneration. Although AN response amplitudes predict AC FA across age groups, AC FA only predicts cortical response amplitudes in older adults. This may be due to age-related degeneration in the AC coupled with central gain that occurs in response to reduced afferent auditory input. We quantified central gain in older adults as the difference between the observed AC P1-N1 amplitudes and the AC P1-N1 amplitudes predicted from the AN response (using parameters for the relationship between CAP N1 and AC P1-N1 measured in younger adults). This metric of central gain represents the degree to which AC response amplitudes are larger than would be expected from afferent input (Harris et al., 2022). We used this metric of central gain to test our hypothesis that lower FA in the AC, which predicted larger cortical response amplitudes (see above), also predicts more AC gain in older adults. As we have previously shown, older adults exhibited significant central gain, such that observed AC P1-N1 responses were significantly larger than those predicted from their AN response (CAP N1) amplitudes [p < 0.001]. Our linear model found that lower AC FA predicted a greater degree of gain in the AC of older adults [β= −0.402, t = −2.596, p = 0.014]. Conversely, AC kurtosis FA, as well as MD, AD, and RD, were not predictors of AC gain [kurtosis FA: β= −0.395, t = −1.3, p = 0.202. MD: β= 0.079, t = 0.460, p = 0.627. Discussion The underlying mechanisms and spatial patterning of age-related auditory central gain and the contribution to SIN recognition are not well understood. Evidence from human and animal models shows that a loss of afferent auditory input results in compensatory central gain and structural changes in multiple regions of the auditory system, including the brainstem and cortex (Chambers et al., 2016; Harris et al., 2022; Rumschlag et al., 2022; Hutchison et al., 2023). In this study, we demonstrated that 1) older adults exhibit a spatial pattern of progressive central gain through the levels of the auditory system, with evidence for gain at the auditory brainstem and additional gain at the AC; 2) in older adults, reduced afferent auditory input predicted lower AC white matter integrity (lower AC FA); 3) AC FA deficits predicted larger auditory-evoked responses and more central gain in the AC of older adults; and 4) reduced AC microstructural integrity (lower AC FA, higher AC RD, AD & MD) is associated with poorer SIN recognition in older adults. 4.1. Central gain in the brainstem and cortex Our results expand on previous studies showing age-related central gain in both the auditory brainstem (Grose et al., 2019; Parthasarathy et al., 2019; Johannesen and Lopez-Poveda, 2021; Rumschlag et al., 2022) and AC (Alain et al., 2022; Harris et al., 2022). Findings from mice have shown that cochlear denervation results in relatively more central gain in the AC compared to the inferior colliculus (Chambers et al., 2016).

Findings from mice have shown that cochlear denervation results in relatively more central gain in the AC compared to the inferior colliculus (Chambers et al., 2016). Translating these results to older adults, we demonstrated that the magnitude of central gain, when compared to younger adults, is larger in the AC than in the brainstem (Figure 8). Although older adults did not show significantly larger brainstem responses in comparison to younger adults, this lack of difference demonstrates gain: if older adults did not exhibit gain, then their brainstem responses should be significantly lower than in younger adults, similar to the significantly smaller AN responses observed in older adults compared to younger adults. This is the first study to show that central gain progressively increases through the levels of the human auditory system, with amplification of responses at the brainstem followed by further amplification at the AC. Although the mechanisms underlying central gain are not Fabrizio-Stover et al. Page 13 Neurobiol Aging. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2026 June 25. Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript fully known, work from animal models and our current study have linked gain to myelin degeneration or hypomyelination in the AC (Borges et al., 2023). Similarly, our prior work and others have linked central gain to reduced inhibition in the brainstem and AC (Keine et al., 2016; Salvi et al., 2017; Harris et al., 2022). Further studies are needed to better understand how altered signaling and central gain in the lower levels of the auditory system (e.g., inferior colliculus) might interact with changes at the cortex to exacerbate gain at higher levels of the auditory system. We found no predictive effect of audiometric thresholds on suprathreshold performance. These findings are consistent with the results of other studies (from our laboratory and others) that show little or no correlation between audiometric thresholds and suprathreshold measures of ABR wave V amplitude (Delano et al., 2020; Maass et al., 2024; Rumschlag et al., 2022), ABR I/V ratio (Delano et a., 2020), or amplitude of neural activity measured using EEG (Sauve et al., 2022; Harris et al., 2022). Visual cortex responses were also not significantly different between younger and older adults. 4.2.

Visual cortex responses were also not significantly different between younger and older adults. 4.2. Use of source space for source-constrained EEGs For this analysis, we chose to use a source estimation approach to study event related potentials generated from specific brain regions as opposed to dipole-based approaches that use sensor space. Source-based approaches are advantageous for investigating plasticity in aged adults, as changes in the underlying cortical architecture likely affects the regions contributing to a given event related potential. Using source-space not only allows for more accurate localization and better temporal resolution of brain activity when compared to sensor space, but also provides excellent test-retest reliability. Dipole fitting procedures often involve using generic brain templates, while our analysis used individual head models for the EEG forward solution, allowing for better alignment of sources within a participant. While the use of source space was selected to examine plastic activity in the AC, interpretations of these data should consider the influence of model-based assumptions. 4.3. AN activity and AC microstructural complexity Our results support the notion that reduced afferent input can result in altered cortical microstructure, consistent with myelin integrity deficits, in the central auditory system. Myelin is integral for ensuring the synchronous neural responses needed for generation of the CAP. Degeneration of peripheral myelin is known to negatively affect AN responses in human and animal models (Panganiban et al., 2022; Chiappa et al., 1980; Marangos, 1996). For the current investigation we used diffusion metrics that are hypothesized to reflect the microstructural integrity of underlying tissue (Beaulieu, 2002; Pasternak et al., 2018), including myelin (Assaf and Pasternak, 2008; Song et al., 2005; Winklewski et al., 2018). Smaller FA and kurtosis FA coupled with larger RD, AD, and MD values are generally interpreted as disruptions in tissue microstructure. In this study, we found that only AC FA was associated with reduced AN activity.

Smaller FA and kurtosis FA coupled with larger RD, AD, and MD values are generally interpreted as disruptions in tissue microstructure. In this study, we found that only AC FA was associated with reduced AN activity. In humans, hearing loss has been shown to relate to FA, MD, AD, and RD in the inferior colliculus and AC (Husain et al., 2011 (FA, MD); Profant et al., 2014 (FA, AD, MD); Ma et al., 2016 (FA, MD, RD); Lin et al., 2008 (FA, MD, RD)), although these relationships are Fabrizio-Stover et al. Page 14 Neurobiol Aging. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2026 June 25. Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript inconsistent across studies and interactions with age were often not considered (Tarabichi et al., 2018). While MD indicates the rate of water diffusion though tissue and can serve as a metric of tissue integrity, anisotropy measures (FA and kurtosis FA) reflect the consistency with which fluid moves and RD reflect the degree of fluid movement perpendicular to neural fibers. Both FA and RD have been shown to be altered after demyelination, as demyelination removes barriers to perpendicular diffusion (RD) and reduces anisotropy (FA) (Assaf and Pasternak, 2008; Schmierer et al., 2007; Song et al., 2002, 2005). However, FA may be more sensitive to early or subtle white matter changes like changes in axonal coherence (CanalesRodriguez et al., 2014). Furthermore, changes in kurtosis FA metrics may only become evident when more complex, heterogeneous tissue alterations occur (Hansen and Jespersen, 2016; Canales-Rodriguez et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2016). Our finding that deficits in afferent auditory activity may contribute to lower AC FA in older adults suggests that simpler, directional microstructural changes, rather than complex architectural reorganization, occurs in the AC in response to afferent auditory loss. 4.4. Potential role of myelin in central gain Our finding that AC FA is a significant predictor of central gain is consistent with evidence from animal models that hypomyelination in the auditory system may result in hyperexcitation (Borges et al., 2023). Our results also complement our previous work finding a link between AC gain and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) (Harris et al., 2022).

title: Age-related auditory nerve deficits propagate central gain throughout the auditory system: Associations with cortical microstructure and speech recognition.
text: role of myelin in central gain Our finding that AC FA is a significant predictor of central gain is consistent with evidence from animal models that hypomyelination in the auditory system may result in hyperexcitation (Borges et al., 2023). Our results also complement our previous work finding a link between AC gain and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) (Harris et al., 2022). Together, these findings suggest that age-related changes in cortical microstructure and GABA, perhaps a result of age-related AN deficits, can account for the central gain observed in older adults. GABA can directly affect cortical myelin, such that modulation of GABA can increase the population of mature oligodendrocytes and improve myelination (Zonouzi et al., 2015; Shaw et al., 2019), and FA measures (Cisneros-Mejorado et al., 2020, 2024) in animal models. However, only a single study thus far has examined the relationship between GABA and diffusion metrics of white matter integrity (FA), and only in younger adults (Ziminski et al., 2023). More work is needed to understand the link between GABA and myelin, and how age-related changes in these biological factors can contribute to central gain and speech recognition deficits. 4.5. Associations with SIN As we stated earlier, myelin integrity is essential for the efficient and accurate encoding of complex stimuli, like speech (Zeng et al., 2005). Previous research has shown the importance of white matter tracts in speech recognition (Shekari and Nozari, 2023), including SIN recognition in older adults (Perron et al., 2021). Despite older adults exhibiting greater difficulties perceiving SIN, studies on the effect of age AC microstructural integrity on diffusion metrics in the auditory system are mixed, with some showing a significant reduction in microstructural integrity with age (Husain et al., 2011 (FA and MD); Ma et al., 2016 (FA, MD, RD); Profant et al., 2014 (AD)) while others show no effect of age (Profant et al., 2014 (FA, MD); Koops et al., 2021 (FA and MD)). Our current results support previous findings in which preserved micro-structural integrity contributes to better SIN recognition in older adults. Fabrizio-Stover et al. Page 15 Neurobiol Aging. Myelin as a potential therapeutic target for SIN difficulties Understanding the relationships between afferent loss, central gain, myelin integrity, and speech recognition could lead to new targets for intervention. Our results show that AC microstructural integrity predicts SIN recognition in older adults. Myelin can change throughout the lifespan in response to experience (Osso and Hughes, 2024). Social isolation (Liu et al., 2016) or acute hearing loss (Kurioka et al., 2021) can result in myelin deficits, while learning can increase oligodendrogenesis and myelination (de de Villers-Sidani et al., 2010; Hughes et al., 2018; Bacmeister et al., 2020). Evidence from human models also suggests a connection between learning and white matter modulation (Scholz et al., 2009). Although the exact mechanisms by which myelin integrity influences SIN recognition are relatively unknown, the ability of myelin to dynamically change throughout the lifespan, coupled with our findings that AN function may modulate AC microstructure, suggests a potential novel target to treat age-related deficits in SIN recognition. 4.7. Potential limitations The current study used diffusion imaging to assess white matter integrity. DKI metrics for white matter microstructure (FA) are associated with myelin, but can be influenced by other factors (e.g., fiber dispersion, inflammation) (Beaulieu, 2002; Takahashi et al., 2002; Jones et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2021). Novel techniques for imaging myelin, including myelin water imaging, may improve our understanding of the mechanisms contributing to cortical degeneration and central gain observed in the current study. Another limitation is that, due to field of view constraints, we were not able to examine the relationship between brainstem white matter microstructure and central gain. Future studies that examine myelin throughout the auditory system are needed to address these remaining knowledge gaps. 5. Summary and conclusions Our results demonstrate that older adults exhibit progressive central gain at the level of the auditory brainstem and cortex. In older adults, reduced afferent auditory input predicted reduced AC white matter integrity, which in turn predicted AC gain. Deficits in microstructural integrity predict poorer SIN recognition in older adults.

Summary and conclusions Our results demonstrate that older adults exhibit progressive central gain at the level of the auditory brainstem and cortex. In older adults, reduced afferent auditory input predicted reduced AC white matter integrity, which in turn predicted AC gain. Deficits in microstructural integrity predict poorer SIN recognition in older adults. Together, these results suggest that loss of afferent auditory input in older adults triggers maladaptive plasticity in the auditory system, resulting in progressive central gain and altered cortical microstructure that may contribute to poorer SIN recognition. Several gaps in knowledge remain and future studies using myelin-specific metrics are needed to further our understanding of the relationship between auditory afferent loss, central gain, and AC structural integrity. title: Evaluating Unimodal and Multimodal Tracking Strategies for the Reconstruction of Language-related White Matter Tracts.
text: RESEARCH https://doi.org/10.1007/s00062-025-01601-9 Clinical Neuroradiology (2026) 36:485–497 Evaluating Unimodal and Multimodal Tracking Strategies for the Reconstruction of Language-related White Matter Tracts Lydia Marleen Schilling1 · Anna-Lena Ciesla1 · Julia My Van Kube1 · Peter Dechent2 · Christian Heiner Riedel1 · Nicole E. Neef1 Received: 5 September 2025 / Accepted: 1 December 2025 / Published online: 10 December 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Purpose Accurate reconstruction of language-related white matter pathways is essential for preoperative planning in brain surgery. While functional (f) MRI activation is often used to guide diffusion (d)MRI tractography, advanced automated protocols rely instead on subcortical anatomical priors. In this study, we evaluate the robustness of anatomically informed protocols without fMRI and compare them with fMRI-guided approaches. Methods Twenty healthy adults (aged 18–32) underwent fMRI during a language task and dMRI on a 3T MRI scanner. Six language-associated ﬁber bundles were reconstructed with XTRACT using unimodal and multimodal protocols. Reconstruction similarity was assessed using cross-correlations within-subjects, within-cohort, and across-cohorts. Normalized streamline counts served as a proxy for connectivity, and t-tests were used to quantify differences between tracking protocols. Results Protocols using anatomically informed subcortical seed and target masks, as well as their combination with functional masks, yielded higher agreement and greater normalized streamline counts than the fMRI-only protocol. The combined approach showed an additional advantage for reconstructing parieto-temporal white matter tracts. Conclusions These comparisons underscore how protocol choice shapes the reconstruction of language pathways and highlight the need to evaluate these tractography strategies in clinical cohorts. Keywords Diffusion MRI · Functional MRI · White matter tracts · Language · Preoperative mapping  Nicole E.

In language-sensitive regions, functional (f)MRI often guides tractography to reﬁne functional anatomy [1–4]. However, language fMRI is time-consuming, task-dependent, and requires patient compliance [5–7]. Minimizing its use could make preoperative neuroradiologic assessment more efﬁcient and consistent. This study tests whether a previously published automated tractography protocol without fMRIguided seed and target masks [8] performs comparably to, or better than, conventional fMRI-informed approaches for the purpose of language mapping. From a clinical perspective, maximizing tumor resection is associated with improved outcomes in both low[9] and high-grade gliomas [10, 11], though it must be carefully balanced against the risk of prospective cognitive deﬁcits [12, 13]. Tractography has become a cornerstone of this onco-functional balance [14], enabling patient-speciﬁc mapping of white matter tracts [15] and overcoming the anatomical constraints of traditional cadaveric dissection [16–18].

title: Evaluating Unimodal and Multimodal Tracking Strategies for the Reconstruction of Language-related White Matter Tracts.
text: perspective, maximizing tumor resection is associated with improved outcomes in both low[9] and high-grade gliomas [10, 11], though it must be carefully balanced against the risk of prospective cognitive deﬁcits [12, 13]. Tractography has become a cornerstone of this onco-functional balance [14], enabling patient-speciﬁc mapping of white matter tracts [15] and overcoming the anatomical constraints of traditional cadaveric dissection [16–18]. It informs surgical planning by identifying critical white matter pathways involved in motor, sensory, cognitive, speech and language functions [19, 20]. Tractography helps in delineating safe surgical corridors, deﬁning resection boundaries, and guiding surgical trajectories [21, 22], while also supporting intraoperative functional mapping through direct electrical stimulation or neurophysiological monitoring [23–25]. Beyond tumor surgery, tractography also contributes to other neurosurgical applications. For example, it helps characterize connectivity patterns associated with clinically effective electrode placements in patients with Parkinson’s disease undergoing subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation [26], and assists in optimizing the placement of stereo-EEG electrodes for epilepsy diagnostics using intracranial EEG [27]. White matter tracts are now increasingly recognized as essential not only for functional preservation but also for facilitating post-surgical neuroplasticity, particularly in multifunctional brain regions [28–30]. dMRI tractography plays a central role in guiding clinical decision-making across various neurological domains. fMRI is commonly used to localize eloquent cortex for surgical planning, with recent guidelines outlining best clinical practices [7, 31]. The arcuate fasciculus, a key language pathway linking frontal, parietal, and temporal regions, including Broca’s and Wernicke’s areas, is often reconstructed using dMRI tractography seeded from fMRIidentiﬁed language areas [1, 32–34]. However, both fMRI language mapping and dMRI tractography are resource-intensive. Language fMRI depends on patient compliance and is time-consuming, while tractography requires specialized expertise and is highly sensitive to user-deﬁned parameters [35]. Additionally, commercial software varies in quality and often lacks robust algorithms to account for pathological tissue, limiting reliability in clinical use [36]. These limitations highlight the need for standardized, robust, and accessible tractography methods, whether guided by fMRI or not, to support broader clinical integration. To overcome the limitations of conventional tractography workﬂows, recent efforts have focused on automated and standardized approaches. One automated pipeline for reconstructing language-related tracts, based on atlasderived anatomical criteria and clinical diffusion protocols, has shown strong agreement with expert segmentations and alignment with task-based fMRI [34]. Similarly, XTRACT, a publicly available tool integrated into FSL (https://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/docs/#/), provides robust and reproducible tractography protocols for the adult human brain [8].

text: recent efforts have focused on automated and standardized approaches. One automated pipeline for reconstructing language-related tracts, based on atlasderived anatomical criteria and clinical diffusion protocols, has shown strong agreement with expert segmentations and alignment with task-based fMRI [34]. Similarly, XTRACT, a publicly available tool integrated into FSL (https://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/docs/#/), provides robust and reproducible tractography protocols for the adult human brain [8]. The tool offers robust extraction of white matter tracts using data from large-scale datasets such as the Human Connectome Project and UK Biobank. These developments mark important progress toward reliable and clinically scalable tractography. The aim of this study was to compare two standardized tractography protocols for reconstructing languagerelated white matter tracts: a unimodal approach using only diffusion MRI, and a multimodal approach guided by functional MRI. For the unimodal method, we applied the standard XTRACT protocol, which places seed and target masks within white matter structures [8]. For the multimodal method, we used anatomically constrained, fMRIderived seed masks placed in cortical regions. We also evaluated a combined approach that integrates XTRACTdeﬁned subcortical masks with fMRI-guided cortical seed masks. We focused on six major language structures: the frontal aslant tract (FAT), arcuate fasciculus (AF), superior longitudinal fascicules III (SLF3), middle longitudinal fasciculus (MdLF), inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF), and uncinate fasciculus (UF) [8, 37]. The FAT connects the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) with medial frontal regions and is primarily implicated in speech initiation and verbal ﬂuency K Evaluating Unimodal and Multimodal Tracking Strategies for the Reconstruction of Language-related White Matter Tracts 487 [38, 39]. The AF and SLF3 form the dorsal language pathway [40–42], linking frontal parietal and temporal regions to support sound-to-articulation mapping [43], complex syntax processing [44], and semantic [45]. The MdLF, ILF, and UF form the ventral pathway [40, 41], which has been associated in particular with semantic processing and language comprehension [43, 46], though it supports other functions such as episodic memory, associative learning, and social and emotional functioning [47, 48] as well. Language fMRI activation maps were obtained using a word decision task that contrasted the processing of compound words with the processing of non-lexical, rhyming pseudowords. The compound> rhyme contrast highlights regions involved in semantic processing by comparing meaningful stimuli (compound words) with phonologically similar but meaningless ones. Conversely, the rhyme> compound contrast identiﬁes regions involved in phonological processing and articulatory mapping, as it emphasizes sound-based decision-making in the absence of semantic content.

Methods Participants Twenty healthy volunteers (10 females; age 18–32 years, mean 24 years) participated. Exclusion criteria included MRI contraindications, neurological or psychiatric disorders, chronic diseases requiring medication, drug abuse, and current pregnancy or breastfeeding. All were native German speakers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision. All were right-handed (Edinburgh Inventory [53]; laterality quotient 70–100). The study was approved by the Ethics committee of the University Medical Center Göttingen and was in accordance with the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants gave written informed consent and obtained an expense allowance for taking part in this study. K 488 L. Schilling et al. Diffusion-weighted MRI was performed using a spinecho EPI sequence with the following imaging parameters: voxel size 2× 2× 2mm3, TE= 82ms, TR= 7.5s, FoV= 104× 104, 64 axial slices covering the whole brain, no interslice gap. Diffusion-weighted MRI data were acquired for 64 diffusion-encoding gradient directions with a b-value of 1000s/mm2. In addition, one anatomical reference image without diffusion-weighting (b-value= 0s/mm2) was obtained for ofﬂine motion correction. The dMRI acquisition was accelerated using partial Fourier imaging (factor 6/8) and parallel imaging (GRAPPA) with an acceleration factor of 2. Fat saturation was applied using a spectral saturation pulse. The dMRI sequence took 8min 32s. To correct for susceptibility-induced distortions, an additional spin-echo EPI image without diffusion-weighting and with reversed phase-encoding direction was acquired for ﬁeld unwarping using the topup method [55]. Preprocessing T1WI were segmented using FastSurfer [56]. Functional data were analyzed with FSL v6.0 using the FEAT pipeline [57, 58]. Preprocessing included motion correction, 5mm FWHM spatial smoothing, high-pass ﬁltering (cutoff= 90s), co-registration to the anatomical image, and normalization to the MNI152 T1 template. First-level models included the four conditions convolved with the hemodynamic response function, with temporal derivatives as nuisance regressors. Two contrasts were computed: compound> nonword rhyme and nonword rhyme> compound. Second-level analysis averaged these contrasts across the four runs. The resulting maps were used to examine cortical correlates of language processing (Fig. 1c); other conditions pertain to a separate study. Statistical inference used a cluster-forming threshold of Z> 3.1 and a family-wise error-corrected extent threshold of p< 0.05 [59]. Diffusion data were ﬁrst denoised and corrected for Gibbs ringing artifacts using the dwidenoise and mrdegibbs commands in the MRtrix package (https://github.com/ MRtrix3/mrtrix3, [60]). Further preprocessing was carried out with the FMRIB Software Library (FSL, http://www. fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl), including correction for susceptibilityinduced distortions, eddy currents, and head motion using topup and eddy. Brain extraction was then performed, and standard DTI contrast maps were computed. All processed datasets were visually inspected to ensure the absence of artifacts from acquisition or preprocessing.

All protocols include the midline sagittal plane as an exclusion mask to restrict tracking to the ipsilateral hemisphere. As implemented in XTRACT (FSL version 6.0.7.16), two seeding strategies were applied: (a) standard single-region of interest (ROI) seeding for FAT, SLF3, AF, and UF; and (b) a reverse-seeding approach, where seed and target masks were swapped and resulting path distributions combined for MdLF and ILF (https://git.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/xtract). All masks were warped to each subject’s native space, and the resulting tractography outputs were resampled back into standard space. All protocols used default probtrackx2 parameters: a curvature threshold of± 80°, maximum 2000 streamline steps, 1% subsidiary ﬁber volume threshold, randomized seeding in regions of crossing ﬁbers, loopchecking, and no minimum length constraint. Step sizes of 0.5mm and 0.2mm were used. The tract distributions were then normalized based on the total number of valid streamlines, i.e., those not rejected by the inclusion or exclusion masks. Anatomical masks were derived from two sources. In the following, full labels and their corresponding abbreviations are provided here for reference. First, from an fMRIguided partitioning of the cortex [51, 52], we included the inferior frontal gyrus encompassing pars opercularis and pars triangularis (IFG), the inferior frontal gyrus pars orbitalis (IFGorb), the anterior temporal region (AntTemp), and the posterior temporal region (PostTemp). Second, we included additional regions based on morphometric partitions from the Harvard-Oxford Cortical Structural Atlas as implemented in FSL, including the inferior frontal gyrus pars opercularis (IFGop), superior frontal gyrus (SFG), the precentral gyrus (pCG), supplementary motor area (SMA), the anterior and posterior divisions of the supramarginal gyrus (aSMG, pSMG), angular gyrus (AG), superior temporal gyrus (STG), and the temporal pole (TP). For each tract, these masks were used to constrain seed and target regions as follows. The seed region for the FAT was constrained by the SFG and SMA, and the target region by the IFG. For the AF, the seed region was constrained by the IFG and the target by PostTemp. The seed region for the SLF3 was constrained by the pCG and IFGop, with targets in the aSMG and pSMG. For the MdLF, the seed mask included STG and AG, while the target was constrained to the TP. The ILF was tracked using a PostTemp seed and AntTemp target. Lastly, the UF was seeded in the AntTemp and targeted to the IFG and IFGorb. Tractspeciﬁc individual cortical masks were stored within a dedicated protocol folder, and speciﬁed via the –p option of the xtract function. The analyses were performed using the default parameters, as outlined in the preceding description of the Xtract protocol.
