Another possible stochastic variable is the presumed variable penetrance of CRISPR-mediated mutations, or other intrinsic factors known to be inﬂuential in cell reprogramming efﬁcacy, such as cell-cycle stage or duration (Smith et al., 2010). We identiﬁed another potential source of stochastic variability that might have contributed to a low incidence of colony formation. As seen in Figure 6A, most wildtype OP6 cells, as well as knockdown cells, expressed very low levels of the Sox2 protein, a critical factor for establishing and maintaining pluripotency (Schaefer and Lengerke, 2020). However, we observed rare wildtype and knockdown OP6 cells with elevated Sox2 expression that approximated levels evident within colonies (Fig. 6A and B). We wondered whether rare Sox2 outlier cells might enable colony formation. We induced Sox2 over-expression in OP6 cells and observed colony formation with this treatment alone (Fig. 6C). When combining Sox2 over-expression with CRISPR-mediated EHMT2 perturbation, colony formation was *3.5 times enhanced relative to either treatment alone (Fig. 6C). These data, along with data already discussed, suggest that OP6 colony formation was enabled by three conditions: mitotic activity (i.e., T-antigen expression, Fig. 3B), elevated expression of the Sox2 transcription factor, and reduction of chromatin barriers through EHMT2 perturbation. Discussion We utilized CRISPR to knock down EHMT2 protein in olfactory-derived OP cells, and observed cell transformation based on several phenotypic markers, including cell morphology, growth properties, and gene expression status. One important question is whether this transformation was attributed speciﬁcally to EHMT2 perturbation. We reported targeted disruptive mutations in the EHMT2 gene, and that EHMT2 protein expression correspondingly decreased, and therefore, it seems unlikely that the observed phenotypes were due to a CRISPR off-target effect.

Finally, we note that immortalization via large T-antigen expression was necessary but not sufﬁcient to cause transformation—colony formation does not occur without its expression, yet neither does it occur in wildtype OP cell lines (nor in the GD25 cell line) that are likewise immortalized (Fig. 3B). We propose that mitotic activity permitted EMHT2 perturbation to be effective —that is, progression through the cell cycle would be necessary to lose H3K9 methylation (Ma et al., 2015) and cell-cycle progression is generally a necessity for cell state change (Souﬁand Dalton, 2016). A second question concerns the rarity of colony formation. We note that under optimized protocols, ESC colony formation (iPSC) is also quite inefﬁcient (Rao and Malik, 2012). We suggested three possible reasons for the low incidence of colony formation here involving stochastic attributes. First, we suggest that colony formation may require a rare partnership between a wildtype and knockdown cell, as suggested by the fact that colonies only form in mixed primary transfected cultures, but not within homogeneous EHMT2 knockdown cultures. Second, sox2 over-expression experiments suggest that colony formation depends on, or is enhanced by, elevated Sox2 levels, which are rare in wildtype OP cells. In vivo, stochastic Sox2 expression within the OSN lineage might constitute a bet-hedging strategy for reallocation of cellular resources within a regenerative regime.

In vivo, stochastic Sox2 expression within the OSN lineage might constitute a bet-hedging strategy for reallocation of cellular resources within a regenerative regime. Dedifferentiation within the OE has previously been observed, and was enhanced by chromatin perturbation and compromised in a Sox2-depleted background (Lin et al., 2017). Third, transcriptional adaptation (TA) may limit transformation frequency following EHMT2 knockdown. TA involves the degradation of mutant or CRISPR-targeted mRNA and compensatory upregulation of homologous or functionally related transcripts (Sztal and Stainier, 2020). In this context, TA may partially restore G9a-dependent chromatin regulation through upregulation of paralogs such as G9a-like protein (Collins and Cheng, 2010). This buffering likely preserves epigenetic stability in most cells, restricting colony formation to rare instances where compensation fails. A model for colony formation A third question we raise concerns the apparent cellular heterogeneity observed within colonies. As noted above, some of this heterogeneity might be attributed to a colonyforming partnership. We observed colony subpopulations with different cell morphologies and divergent gene expression proﬁles, including EHMT2 expression, that would be consistent with this idea. We speculate that EHMT2 knockdown in one cell may enable reactivation of ESC genes that might signal a partner wildtype cell to silence neural genes (requiring EHMT2 function). For example, the C3 colony subpopulation might have derived from a knockdown cell that subsequently upregulated TGFB1 to signal a nearby wildtype C5-like cell to dedifferentiate and upregulate stem markers, resulting in a more stem-like C4 cell. Perhaps consistent with this model, we note that an RNA-seq trajectory analysis suggested transitions from C5 (most OP6-like) to C4 (most stem-like). The most important question of our study pertains to whether some of the cells within colonies had indeed reprogrammed toward a pluripotent stem cell. title: Transcriptomic Signatures in TP53 Positive and Negative Tumor Samples in NSCLC.
text:  Gene Therapy ,11 . BBC ,11 . DBC ,8#!* =!*& . C      1875-5631/26 2026 Bentham Science Publishers 1 Miao Xie1, Baoguang Liu2, Ziyi Chen1, Tongtong Cao1 and Xiaoyan Zhang1,* 1College of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Henan University of Chinese Medicine, Zhengzhou, Henan, China; 2Department of Chinese Medical Sciences, Henan University of Chinese Medicine, Zhengzhou, Henan, China Abstract: Introduction: Lung cancer, specifically non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. TP53, a crucial tumor suppressor gene, is often mutated in various cancers, including lung cancer. This study focuses on the differences in transcriptomic profiles between TP53-mutated (TP53+) and TP53-wildtype (TP53-) NSCLC tumor samples, aiming to develop a gene signature that can predict overall survival and immune response, particularly in the context of immunotherapy. It aims to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) associated with TP53 status in non-small cell lung cancer and develop a gene signature that can predict overall survival and immune response. Methods: Gene expression profiles from TP53-positive and TP53-negative NSCLC tumor samples were analyzed. Data were sourced from the GEO database (GSE8569, n = 69) and the TCGA database (n = 1026). Differential expression analysis was conducted to identify DEGs, which were further analyzed using LASSO regression to develop a prognostic gene signature. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was performed to validate the expression of selected genes. Results: A total of 535 DEGs (168 up-regulated, 367 down-regulated) were identified in TP53+ samples. Further analysis with TCGA data narrowed this down to 29 genes, from which 12 were identified as prognostic features using LASSO analysis. This 12-gene signature effectively stratified patients into low- and high-risk groups for overall survival. Differences in immune cell infiltration and immune pathway activity were significant between these groups, indicating the potential of the gene signature to predict immune response. Among the genes analyzed, BMP2, LPXN, IER3, ANLN, TNNT1, OGT, KRT8, BARX2, PRC1, and SNX30 showed statistically significant differences in qPCR results. Discussion: The 12-gene signature demonstrates robust predictive capability for survival outcomes and immune response patterns in NSCLC patients, suggesting its potential clinical utility in precision oncology. The observed correlation between TP53 mutation status and immune microenvironment alterations provides valuable insights into the mechanistic basis of immunotherapy resistance and response. Conclusion: This study identifies a TP53-associated transcriptomic signature that is significantly associated with overall survival in lung cancer patients.

Moreover, the majority of lung cancer cases are diagnosed at an advanced stage, when the prospects for curative treatment are significantly diminished [6]. This late-stage diagnosis is partly attributed to the subtle and non-specific nature of early symptoms, as well as the limitations in current screening and diagnostic methodologies [7]. The risk factors for lung cancer are well documented, with tobacco smoking being the most prominent [8]. However, a significant proportion of cases occur in nonsmokers, implicating a range of other etiological factors, including environmental and occupational exposures, genetic predispositions, and lifestyle elements [9]. Therefore, the multifactorial nature of lung cancer etiology underscores the need for a comprehensive understanding of its risk factors and pathogenesis to devise effective prevention and early detection strategies. In the face of these challenges, the past few decades have witnessed remarkable advancements in the field of lung cancer research and treatment. Currently, lung cancer patients receive surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted therapy as treatments [10]. Among them, the advent of targeted therapy and immunotherapy has revolutionized the therapeutic landscape, offering new hope to patients, especially those with advanced disease [11]. These advancements have been propelled by a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying lung cancer, including the pivotal role of genetic alterations. In particular, mutations in the TP53 gene, which plays a critical role in cellular processes such as DNA repair, apoptosis, and cell cycle regulation, have been identified in a significant proportion of lung cancer cases [12, 13]. The TP53 pathway's involvement in tumorigenesis and cancer progression makes it a critical target for therapeutic intervention and a valuable biomarker for disease prognostication and treatment response prediction [14-16]. In addition to its oncogenic role, TP53 expression levels also have significant implications for therapeutic outcomes. Studies have shown that TP53 mutations and altered expression influence the sensitivity of tumors to various treatment strategies, including chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. For instance, TP53 mutations have been associated with resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, as the loss of TP53 function impairs the DNA damage response and apoptotic pathways [17, 18]. Furthermore, the expression of TP53 has been shown to impact the immune microenvironment, influencing the effectiveness of immunotherapy [19].

Furthermore, the expression of TP53 has been shown to impact the immune microenvironment, influencing the effectiveness of immunotherapy [19]. In this context, understanding TP53 expression levels in tumors is crucial for predicting treatment response and guiding the selection of appropriate therapeutic approaches. Given the substantial burden of lung cancer and the central role of genetic and molecular factors in its pathogenesis and treatment response, there is a pressing need for continued research into the development of novel diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic strategies [20]. In this context, the exploration of TP53-associated transcriptomic signatures represents a promising frontier. Such signatures have the potential to refine the prognostication of lung cancer outcomes and predict responses to emerging treatment modalities, including immunotherapies. 2. METHODS 2.1. Data Source The gene expression profiles used for the identification of TP53-associated genes in NSCLC were obtained from the publicly available GEO dataset (https://www.ncbi.nlm. nih.gov/geo/; GSE8569, n = 69), which contains microarray-based transcriptomic data derived from surgically resected lung tumor tissues. A total of 69 NSCLC tumor samples with high-quality RNA were selected, including 41 TP53-mutant (TP53+) and 28 TP53-wildtype (TP53−) cases. These tissue samples were provided by the CNIO Tumor Bank Network in collaboration with multiple Spanish hospitals. Pathological classification was performed independently by two certified pathologists according to the 2004 WHO classification [21]. The RNA sequencing data and the corresponding clinical data of lung cancer samples were deposited in the TCGA database (https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/). All data related to the study were gathered from the TCGA and GEO databases. The acquisition and application of data were conducted following TCGA and GEO publication guidelines and data access policies. Duplicate genes were assigned the average expression value in this study. The expression data were normalized by log2(value+1) transformation [22]. A549 and H1299 cells were provided by the Nanjing University of Chinese Medicine (Nanjing, China). 2.2. Definition of TP53 Mutation Status To distinguish between TP53-mutant (TP53+) and TP53-wildtype (TP53−) samples, we adopted the classification criteria provided in the original GSE8569 study. Specifically, TP53 mutation status was determined by sequencing exons 5–8 of the TP53 gene, which represent the most frequently mutated regions in non-small cell lung cancer.

Definition of TP53 Mutation Status To distinguish between TP53-mutant (TP53+) and TP53-wildtype (TP53−) samples, we adopted the classification criteria provided in the original GSE8569 study. Specifically, TP53 mutation status was determined by sequencing exons 5–8 of the TP53 gene, which represent the most frequently mutated regions in non-small cell lung cancer. The mutation screening was conducted using PCR amplification and direct automatic sequencing following standard protocols, as described in the original dataset references [21]. Samples with any non-synonymous mutation in these exons were classified as TP53-mutant (TP53+), while those without such mutations were classified as TP53-wildtype (TP53−). 2.3. Screening of TP53-associated Genes in Lung Cancer A total of 69 NSCLC tumor samples (NTP53+ = 41, NTP53= 28) were analyzed to screen TP53-associated differentially expressed genes in lung cancer. The R package “limma” was utilized to ascertain TP53-associated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between TP53+ and TP53- groups. The threshold was set as a p-value < 0.05 and | log2 fold change (FC)| > 0.5 [23]. 2.4. Functional Analyses of TP53-associated Differentially Expressed Genes The R packages “clusterProfiler” and “org.Hs.eg.db” were utilized to perform the gene and Encyclopedia of Genome (KEGG) pathway and gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis. The threshold was set as a p-value < 0.05. The R packages “ggplot2”, “igraph” and “ggraph” were utilized to visualize the results. We used the Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interaction Genes (STRING, https://www.stringTranscriptomic Signatures in TP53 Positive and Negative Tumor Samples in NSCLC e15665232357300 Current Gene Therapy, 2026, Vol. 26, No. 5 3 db.org/) to explore the potential interaction between two different genes with a confidence value ≥ 0.4 (intermediate) [24]. The protein-protein networks were visualized using the R packages “igraph” and “ggraph”. 2.5. Screening of Differentially Expressed Genes and Prognostic Genes in Lung Cancer from TCGA A total of 1041 lung cancer tumor samples and 108 paracancerous samples from TCGA database were analyzed to screen differentially expressed genes and prognostic genes in lung cancer from TCGA. The R package DESeq2 was utilized to ascertain differentially expressed genes, and the R package “survival” was utilized to ascertain prognostic genes using the Cox proportional hazards method [25]. The high-risk group and low-risk groups of lung cancer were divided by 1-50 and 51-100. The threshold was set as a pvalue < 0.05. 2.6.

The high-risk group and low-risk groups of lung cancer were divided by 1-50 and 51-100. The threshold was set as a pvalue < 0.05. 2.6. Construction of Transcriptomic Signature for Survival Prognostication Our study took the intersection of the TP53-associated genes, differentially expressed genes, and prognostic genes as the potential genes for the transcriptomic signature for survival prognostication. The R package “glmnet” was utilized to obtain valuable genes with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) analysis. The LASSO algorithm addresses collinearity and overfitting by excluding genes that may have high correlations with other genes [26]. The key genes were then analyzed by univariate and multivariate Cox models. Finally, a prognostic risk score model was built through multivariate Cox regression [27]. The risk score values of patients were calculated by the expression levels and correlation coefficients of their transcriptomic signatures. The nomogram, according to the multivariate Cox regression analysis results, was developed using the R package “rms”. The ROC curves and survival analysis were utilized to evaluate the predictive value of the transcriptomic signature between low- and high-risk score groups [28]. 2.7. The Immune Landscape of the Transcriptomic Signature Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) was utilized to apply genetic markers to each cancer sample based on immune cell populations and immune pathways, for quantifying the infiltration score of 16 immune cells and the activity of 13 immune-related pathways, using the R package “gsva” [29]. The immune landscape of high- and low-expression-level groups of a single gene from the transcriptomic signature was investigated. Additionally, the immune landscape of high- and low-risk groups of transcriptomic signatures was also investigated by ssGSEA, estimate and CIBERSORT methods. 2.8. The Expression Level of Target Genes Through qPCR A549 cells were cultured in complete medium (RPMI1640 supplemented with 10% FBS and 100 U/mL penicillin-streptomycin). H1299 cells were cultured in complete medium (DMEM/F12 supplemented with 10% FBS and 100 U/mL penicillin-streptomycin). All cells were incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2 for 24 hours. A549 cells have been characterized to express wild-type p53, while H1299 cells are reported to be p53-null (p53.free.fr/Database/Cancer_cell_ lines/HB_cell_lines.html). Total RNA was extracted from the samples using an RNA isolation kit, as per the manufacturer's instructions.

DISCUSSION The study first presents an analysis of TP53-associated differentially expressed genes in lung cancer, culminating in the construction of a transcriptomic signature with significant prognostic value. TP53, a gene frequently mutated in various forms of cancer, plays a pivotal role in cell cycle regulation and apoptosis [30]. In lung cancer, the status of TP53 is a critical determinant of the tumor's behavior and patient outcome [31]. By integrating data from public databases such as GEO and TCGA, this work not only identifies a set of DEGs linked to TP53 status but also correlates these with patient survival and the potential response to immunotherapy. Through a series of analyses, including differential expression analysis, pathway enrichment, and proteinprotein interaction networks, followed by LASSO and Cox regression modeling, our study develops a reliable 12-gene prognostic signature. This signature not only stratifies lung cancer patients into distinct risk categories but also provides insight into the underlying immune response, offering dual utility in both prognostication and therapeutic guidance. In this study, we identified a 12-gene transcriptomic signature associated with TP53 status that provides prognostic insights for NSCLC patients. The link between this signature and clinical outcomes, particularly overall survival, is evident from the Kaplan–Meier survival analysis, which demonstrated a significant difference in survival between patients stratified into low- and high-risk groups based on their transcriptomic risk scores. The 12-gene signature comprises HMGA1, ANLN, BARX2, BMP2, EREG, IER3, KRT8, LPXN, PRC1, TNNT1, OGT, and SNX30, representing diverse biological processes and molecular pathways implicated in lung cancer pathogenesis. Each gene has been independently associated with cancer-related processes in previous studies, strengthening the biological validity of our signature. These genes are involved in critical cellular processes that are frequently dysregulated upon TP53 mutation, providing mechanistic insights into how TP53 status influences lung cancer progression and immune response. HMGA1 (High-mobility group AT-hook 1) functions as a chromatin architectural factor that exhibits altered expression patterns in TP53mutant tumors [32, 33]. In NSCLC, HMGA1 promotes metastasis through pathways that are normally suppressed by wild-type TP53, representing a critical downstream effector of TP53 dysfunction [34, 35]. ANLN (Anillin actin-binding protein), essential for cytokinesis and cell cycle progression, shows elevated expression in TP53-mutant tumors due to loss of TP53-mediated cell cycle checkpoint controls [3638].

In NSCLC, HMGA1 promotes metastasis through pathways that are normally suppressed by wild-type TP53, representing a critical downstream effector of TP53 dysfunction [34, 35]. ANLN (Anillin actin-binding protein), essential for cytokinesis and cell cycle progression, shows elevated expression in TP53-mutant tumors due to loss of TP53-mediated cell cycle checkpoint controls [3638]. This TP53-dependent dysregulation of ANLN contributes to chromosomal instability and accelerated tumor growth in NSCLC [39, 40]. BARX2 (BarH-like homeobox 2) exhibits altered regulation in the context of TP53 mutation, affecting cellular adhesion and cytoskeletal organization [41, 42]. In NSCLC, BARX2 suppresses tumor progression through inhibition of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway, a function that may be compromised in TP53-mutant tumors [43-45]. BMP2 (Bone Morphogenetic Protein 2), a member of the TGF-β superfamily [46], shows differential expression between TP53-mutant and wild-type tumors, influencing the tumor microenvironment and immune cell recruitment [47-51]. In NSCLC, BMP2 overexpression correlates with advanced disease and metastasis, particularly in TP53mutant contexts [52, 53]. EREG (Epiregulin), an EGF family member, exhibits altered expression in TP53-mutant tumors, affecting epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and immune evasion mechanisms [54, 55]. In NSCLC, EREG contributes to therapeutic resistance [56-58], a hallmark of TP53-mutant tumors. PRC1 (Protein Regulator of Cytokinesis 1), involved in cell division regulation, shows dysregulated expression in the absence of functional TP53 [59, 60]. KRT8 (Keratin 8) expression patterns differ between TP53-mutant and wild-type tumors, affecting epithelial integrity and immune cell interactions [63-65]. In NSCLC, KRT8 enhances TGF-β signaling and promotes EMT [66], processes that are modulated by TP53 status [67]. TNNT1 (Troponin T1) shows differential expression based on TP53 status and influences cellular migration patterns that affect immune cell infiltration [68-70]. IER3 (Immediate Early Response 3) participates in TP53-dependent stress response pathways [71, 72], with altered function in lung tumors contributing to sustained ERK activation [73]. LPXN (Leupaxin) mediates cell adhesion processes that are disrupted in TP53-mutant tumors, affecting tumor-immune cell interactions [74-77]. OGT (O-GlcNAc transferase) catalyzes modifications that influence TP53 function and stability [78], while SNX30 (Sorting Nexin 30) participates in trafficking pathways that are remodeled in the context of TP53 mutation [79].

Our analyses revealed significant associations between this TP53-associated gene signature and immune cell infiltration patterns, with the high-risk group exhibiting distinct immune profiles. These findings establish a direct link between TP53 mutational status, transcriptional dysregulation, and alterations in the tumor immune microenvironment, offering valuable insights for immunotherapy stratification in NSCLC patients. Furthermore, TP53 mutations have been shown to impair the expression of key genes involved in antigen presentation (e.g., MHC class I molecules) and immune surveillance, thereby contributing to immune escape [80, 81]. For instance, loss of TP53 function is associated with reduced interferon signaling and impaired recruitment of cytotoxic T cells, which are critical for effective antitumor immunity [82, 83]. Several genes in our 12-gene signature, including HMGA1, KRT8, and EREG, have been implicated in modulating immune checkpoints, epithelial– mesenchymal transition (EMT), and cytokine secretion, all of which influence the tumor immune microenvironment and potentially attenuate responses to immunotherapy [8488]. The high-risk group, characterized by upregulation of these genes also displayed lower levels of activated CD8+ T cells and higher infiltration of immunosuppressive cells such as Tregs and M2 macrophages, suggesting a more immune-evasive phenotype. These observations provide a plausible biological explanation for the poorer therapeutic outcomes often observed in TP53-mutant NSCLC patients and underscore the importance of integrating TP53 mutational status and immune gene signatures when designing personalized immunotherapeutic strategies. Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the prognostic gene signature was developed and validated using retrospective datasets (GEO and TCGA), and no independent clinical cohort was included for external validation. Second, although we explored immune cell infiltration based on transcriptomic data, functional validation of the immune-modulatory roles of the identified genes is still lacking. Third, the in vitro qPCR validation was limited to two lung cancer cell lines (A549 and H1299), which may not fully capture the heterogeneity of NSCLC in patients. Additionally, the prognostic signature was derived primarily from TP53 mutation status, which may not account for other genomic or epigenetic alterations influencing patient prognosis.

Moreover, functional experiments are needed to elucidate the biological mechanisms by which these genes influence tumor progression and the immune microenvironment. Integrating multi-omics data and investigating the response to specific immunotherapies in TP53-stratified patients may further enhance the clinical utility of this signature. CONCLUSION In summary, this study systematically identified TP53associated differentially expressed genes in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) using an integrated analysis of GEO and TCGA datasets. Through LASSO regression and Cox proportional hazards modeling, we developed a robust 12gene transcriptomic signature that effectively stratifies lung cancer patients into distinct prognostic groups. This signature not only demonstrated predictive value for overall survival but also revealed significant associations with immune cell infiltration and immune pathway activity, suggesting its potential as a biomarker for both prognosis and immune landscape assessment. Moreover, qPCR validation in TP53+ (A549) and TP53− (H1299) lung cancer cell lines confirmed the differential expression of key genes within the signature, supporting its biological relevance. However, this study is limited by the lack of prospective clinical validation and functional experiments. Future research should focus on validating the signature in larger, independent cohorts and elucidating the mechanistic roles of these genes in tumor progression and immune regulation. Overall, our findings provide valuable insights into the transcriptomic alterations associated with TP53 mutation status in lung cancer and offer a promising gene signature for risk stratification and future immunotherapy guidance. title: Exploring Molecular Pathways in Metastasis of Breast Cancer Cells to the Brain: Insights from Gene Expression Analysis and Cellular Origins.
text: © 2023 Journal of Microscopy and Ultrastructure | Published by Wolters Kluwer - Medknow 115 Abstract Original Article Introduction Breast cancer (BC) is the second‑most common reason of cancer death among women.[1,2] BC initiates due to abnormal alterations of cell growth leading to tumor development. According to recent statistics from the World Health Organization, BC is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in women globally, with an estimated 2.3 million new cases diagnosed in 2020 alone. It is also the leading cause of cancer‑related deaths among women, accounting for approximately 685,000 deaths in the same year.[3] In 2018, recent estimations have reported approximately 2.1 million cancer patients all over the world. BC makes up around 21.8% of all cancer occurrences in Saudi women. BC is considered the ninth leading cause of death in women in Saudi Arabia,[4] and has been reported as the second‑most frequently occurring cancer.[5] The number of BC estimations will increase proportionally to community growth and age in Saudi Arabia over the coming years.[6] The current treatment options for BC include a combination of surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and hormone therapy. The choice of treatment depends on various factors, such as the stage of cancer, hormone receptor status, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) status, and individual patient characteristics.[7] Introduction: Breast cancer (BC) metastasis to the brain poses a significant challenge in improving outcomes for BC patients. This study aimed to identify the biological mechanisms and associated genes involved in BC cell metastasis to the brain. Materials and Methods: Genome‑wide gene expression profiles (GSE42568 and GSE43837) generated on a microarray platform were obtained from the GEO database. GSE42568 included 104 BC and 17 normal breast biopsies, while GSE43837 comprised 19 human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)‑positive human BCs with brain metastases and 19 HER2‑positive nonmetastatic primary BCs. Differential gene expression and protein interaction analysis were performed to identify significant gene clusters associated with BC metastasis to the brain. Results: Two significant clusters of genes were identified in BC. The first cluster included genes such as EEF1A1, RPL8, RPS3A, RPN2, PSMD2, RPL18, RPL7, and RPS3. The second cluster included genes such as ASPN, COL6A3, COL3A1, LUM, VCAM1, FASLG, GBP1, CXCL9, DAXX, H3F3A, H3F3B, and KMT2D. The Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genome pathway analysis revealed the significance of genes in the second cluster in pericentric heterochromatin assembly, telomeric heterochromatin assembly, and collagen type III trimer.

Many receptors and the associated signaling pathways are considered prominent elements that impact BC development.[9] In addition, numerous oncogenes and anti‑oncogenes are implicated.[10] Gene expression alteration can be effectively investigated by microarray data analysis, which is a highly sensitive and high throughput approach. Consequently, the expansion of microarray analysis will enhance the understanding of BC diagnosis and treatment.[11] Inherited mutations are responsible for around 5%–10% of all cases of BC. The most frequent causative genes are BRCA1 and BRCA2,[12] which increase the probability of hereditary BC.[13] The possibility of BC progression escalates up to 55%–65% in women carrying a mutated BRCA1. Moreover, the BC risk increases to 45% if BRCA2 is mutated.[14] Mutations in some genes such as STK11, TP53, ATM, PTEN, CDH1, CHEK2, and PALB2 are associated with the development of BC.[15] Nongenetic risk factors may initiate BC development, including family history, race/ethnicity, breast lesion, radiation exposure, hormones, overweight/obesity, and lack of physical activity.[16] BM is one of most frequently occurring adult brain tumors,[17] affecting >25% of cancer patients. In the later stage of the disease, 10%–15% of patients with BC develop BM.[18] The estimation of BM incidence ranges from 7 to 14/100,000.[19] Studies have shown that BC metastasis to the brain involves complex interactions between cancer cells and the brain microenvironment. Factors such as angiogenesis, immune response, signaling pathways, and specific genes have been implicated in this process.[20,21] Oncogenes involved in BC to BM cascade can be classified into three types: initiation, progression, and virulence. Initiation genes include CDH2, TWIST, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). CDH2 and TWIST enhance detachment, whereas MMPs cause degeneration of the extracellular matrix (ECM). VEGF plays a role in angiogenesis, and PTGS2 and MMP‑1 are involved in tumor progression. The PTGS2 and MMP‑1 are implicated in the colonization of metastases by the extravasation of tumor cells. The virulence genes include interleukin 6 and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) α, which support cell survival during circulation and promote growth in the distant microenvironment.

Identifying the genes associated with BC metastasis, particularly to the brain, is crucial as it can provide valuable insights into the underlying biological mechanisms driving cancer cell spread. This knowledge may potentially lead to the development of targeted therapies or interventions aimed at preventing or treating metastasis, ultimately improving patient outcomes and reducing the burden of metastatic BC.[24] Therefore, the aim of this study was to identify common genes in breast/ metastatic brain cancer datasets involved in BC metastasis to the brain using microarray analysis. Enrichment analysis is used to determine the annotations for the common and exclusive genes of both datasets. The‑protein‑protein interactions (PPI) network analysis is applied to the common genes in both datasets and exclusive genes of metastatic brain cancer. Cluster identification is used to determine the common genes in both datasets and of metastatic brain cancer. Therefore, gene ontology (GO) analysis of the gene clusters is important. Materials and Methods Data source For the current research, two gene expression profiles (GSE42568 and GSE43837) were chosen and retrieved from the GEO database. The GSE42568 dataset utilized the GPL570 Affymetrix Human Genome U133 Plus 2.0 Array and included 104 BC samples and 17 normal breast biopsies. The platform for GSE43837 is the GPL1352 Affymetrix Human X3P Array. The expression profile was obtained by the analysis of 19 HER2‑positive human BCs with brain metastases and 19 HER2‑positive nonmetastatic primary human BCs. Preprocessing of data and analysis of differentially expressed genes The R affy package was utilized for analyzing the data, employing the Robust Multi‑array average algorithm.

The common DEGs between the two datasets were obtained through the Venn package in R. Gene ontology enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes GO analysis and DEGs functional enrichment analysis were conducted. The analyses were conducted for the common genes between GSE42568 and GSE43837 datasets, unique BM and BC genes, and the modules of combined common and unique metastases genes. The immunofluorescence protein expression data for each query gene were analyzed using the Protein Atlas web‑based tool. The tool provides information on the expression levels of each gene in different tissue types, including normal and cancerous tissues. A scoring system was used to measure expression levels, ranging from 0 (indicating no expression) to 5 (indicating high expression). Results Identification of differentially expressed genes We analyzed a total of 1262 DEGs from the GSE42568 database, consisting of 486 upregulated genes and 776 downregulated genes. In addition, we examined 77 DEGs from the GSE43837 database, comprising 26 upregulated genes and 51 downregulated genes. Overall, 15 common genes overlapped between the GSE42568 and GSE43837 databases [Figures 1 and 2]. Protein–protein interactions network analysis After analyzing a total of 1339 genes from both the BC and BM datasets, we examined 15 common DEGs using the DEGs PPI network complex [Figure 2]. The analysis revealed a network of 15 nodes and eight edges [Tables 1-3 and Figure 3a]. The 62 unique BM genes examined through the DEGs PPI network complex showed 59 nodes and 64 edges [Figure 3b]. The 77 common genes were examined in a combined PPI network complex, which revealed 74 nodes and 104 edges [Figure 3c]. We used Cytoscape to generate the PPI network and performed module analysis using the MCODE plug‑in. Two significant clusters, labeled clusters 1 and 2, were extracted from the PPI network [Figure 4a and b]. Cluster 1 contained eight genes, namely, EEF1A1, PSMD2, RPL7, RPL8, RPL18, RPS3, RPS3A, and RPN2, whereas Cluster 2 consisted of 12 genes, namely, ASPN, COL3A1, VCAM, H3F3B, GBP1, H3F3A, CXCL9, KMT2D, FASLG, DAXX, LUM, and COL6A3. Cluster analysis through gene ontology function plus Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes enrichment pathways There are three classes of DEGs based on GO analysis, including biological, cellular components, and molecular pathways. For cluster 1, GO functions included GO: 1900022, GO: 1905051, and GO: 0032358. The GO: 1900022 regulates d‑erythro‑sphingosine kinase activity, whereas the GO: 1905051 maintains regulation of the cellular base excision repair process.

Discussion BC is one of the main causes of mortality in women, with brain metastasis (BM) representing a major risk factor for poor prognosis.[25-27] Despite significant research efforts, the underlying mechanisms of BC metastasis to the brain remain poorly understood.[25] Progression to BM may result from angiogenesis, immunity, signaling kinase, and genes such as COX2 and ST6GALNAC5. In recent studies, long noncoding RNA was also associated with metastatic BC to the brain.[28-32] A previous study identified five DEGs, namely, MMP2, MMP11, VCAM1, CXCL12, and MME, implicated in primary brain cancer and BC metastasis to the brain. These genes play essential roles in metastases processes.[33] In this study, VCAM1, a gene that is expressed in cytokine‑activated endothelium and encodes a cell surface sialoglycoprotein, was found in cluster 1. VCAM1 protein regulates adhesion between leukocytes and endothelial cells and contributes significantly to signal transduction. It has been associated with atherosclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis progression, and three alternative splice variants have been reported, which encode several isoforms. VCAM1 contributes to leukocyte circulation from blood to tissue during the inflammatory response and may be expressed abnormally in multiple types of cancers. It includes BC, melanomas, and gastric cancer.[34] Thus, VCAM1 may contribute to the progression of BC and BM. The modified proteasome has a particular role as an immunoproteasome. The immunoproteasome refers to the preparation process of class I major histocompatibility complex peptides. The immunoproteasome also contributes to the TNF signaling pathway. PSMD2 demonstrates ubiquitous expression in the brain (RPKM 40.8). RPL8, RPL7, RPS3A, RPS3 RPL18, and RPN2 are ribosomal proteins identified in our study, and they may have a role in brain metastases, with PSMD2, because they are involved in the regulation of SLIT and ROBO expressions. ASPN encodes a cartilage extracellular protein, which belongs to the leucine‑rich proteoglycan family, and contributes to chondrogenesis regulation. In cartilage, it acts as a suppressor for transforming growth factor‑beta 1.[38] It connects calcium and collagen to promote collagen mineralization. ASPN polymorphism is associated with osteoarthritis susceptibility through the aspartic acid repeat domain and is also associated with intervertebral disc disease. Several transcript variants are initiated as a consequence of alternative splicing of ASPN. The FASLG gene encodes a transmembrane protein that is essential for inducing apoptosis initiated by binding to FAS. The FAS/FASLG signaling pathway has a basic role in immune system regulation as it regulates activation‑induced cell death which occurs in T‑cells. It also initiates cytotoxic T‑lymphocyte‑induced cell death. In addition, FASLG has been implicated in the progression of several cancers and may be correlated with brain metastases from BC. H3‑3A and H3‑3B genes control the nucleosome composition of the chromosomal fiber. These genes comprise introns, and their mRNA is polyadenylated, unlike that of most histone genes. The encoded protein is a replication‑independent element of the histone H3 group. As histone modification indicates epigenetic mechanisms, H3‑3A and H3‑3B genes might have a potential association with BC and the development of BM. title: Discovery of N-[2-(4-methylquinolin-2-yl)phenyl]acetamidine as a new potent nitric oxide synthase inhibitor against glioma progression.
text: Vol.:(0123456789) Molecular Diversity (2026) 30:6977–6984 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11030-025-11309-0 ORIGINAL ARTICLE Discovery of N‑[2‑(4‑methylquinolin‑2‑yl)phenyl]acetamidine as a new potent nitric oxide synthase inhibitor against glioma progression Marialucia Gallorini1 · Rosa Amoroso1 · Amelia Cataldi1 · Cristina Maccallini1 Received: 2 April 2025 / Accepted: 23 July 2025 / Published online: 5 August 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract Gliomas are aggressive brain tumors with limited treatment options, often leading to poor patient outcomes despite surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. Current therapies, such as temozolomide and radiation, provide only temporary control, as gliomas frequently develop resistance. Therefore, there is an urgent need for new therapeutics to improve survival and quality of life for patients. In the present study, we explore the hypothesis that the dual inhibition of both the neuronal and inducible nitric oxide synthases could represent a promising therapeutic approach, being these two enzymes often dysregulated in gliomas. To this end, the new quinoline-based compound 3 was synthetized by a simple, innovative and solvent-free procedure. The molecule was a potent dual inhibitor and demonstrated significant antitumor activity against glioma, both as a monotherapy and in combination with temozolomide. Graphical abstract The new quinoline-based compound 3 was synthetized by a simple, innovative and solvent-free procedure. The molecule was a potent dual nitric oxide synthase inhibitor and demonstrated significant antitumor activity against glioma, both as a monotherapy and in combination with temozolomide. Keywords Anticancer · Drug discovery · Dual inhibitors · Glioma · Hybridization · Nitric oxide synthase · Synthesis Introduction Gliomas are a group of primary brain tumors that originate from glial cells, which provide support and protection for neurons in the central nervous system (CNS). Gliomas represent the most common type of primary brain tumor, accounting for approximately 30% of all brain tumors and around * Cristina Maccallini cristina.maccallini@unich.it 1 Department of Pharmacy, University “G. d’Annunzio” of Chieti-Pescara, Chieti, Italy 6978 Molecular Diversity (2026) 30:6977–6984 80% of malignant brain tumors [1]. There are different types of gliomas, such as astrocytoma, oligodendrogliomas, and ependymomas, and each type can be further categorized by grade, reflecting the tumor's aggressiveness: low-grade (Grade I and II, according to the World Health Organization (WHO)) tumors tend to grow slowly and may not be immediately life-threatening, while high-grade (WHO Grade III and IV) tumors, such as glioblastoma multiforme, are highly malignant and associated with poor prognosis due to their rapid growth and invasive nature [2].

title: Discovery of N-[2-(4-methylquinolin-2-yl)phenyl]acetamidine as a new potent nitric oxide synthase inhibitor against glioma progression.
text: further categorized by grade, reflecting the tumor's aggressiveness: low-grade (Grade I and II, according to the World Health Organization (WHO)) tumors tend to grow slowly and may not be immediately life-threatening, while high-grade (WHO Grade III and IV) tumors, such as glioblastoma multiforme, are highly malignant and associated with poor prognosis due to their rapid growth and invasive nature [2]. Chronic inflammation is a significant contributor to glioma growth, since it facilitates tumor promotion and neo-vascularization, which are critical for its survival and expansion [3, 4]. Glioma cells can modulate immune responses, leading to an immunosuppressive microenvironment that facilitates tumor growth. The inducible isoform of nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is often overexpressed in gliomas. This enzyme is deputed to the biosynthesis of nitric oxide (NO) and it is typically induced in response to inflammatory stimuli such as cytokines and microbial products to produce large amounts of NO. This is a free radical molecule endowed with multiple physiopathological functions. In the innate immune response, it can help to eliminate pathogens, but excessive NO production can lead to tissue damage and contribute to inflammatory diseases. This dualism is observed also in gliomas, where NO can induce apoptosis at low concentrations, but may also support tumor cell survival and resistance to treatments like chemotherapy and radiotherapy under certain inflammatory conditions [5]. The implications of iNOS in cancer biology are quite complex, and they do not rely only on NO concentration, but also on tumoral microenvironment and on cellular context, as reviewed elsewhere [6, 7]. Consequently, the inhibition of iNOS has garnered significant attention as a potential therapeutic strategy for gliomas. Previous in vitro studies have demonstrated that compounds such as ­NG -monomethyl–L–arginine (L-NMMA), CM544, FAB1020, and 1400W can reduce NO levels, inhibit glioma cells proliferation, and enhance the effectiveness of standard treatments like temozolomide (TMZ) [8]. Besides iNOS, there are two constitutive isoforms, i.e., the neuronal NOS (nNOS) and the endothelial NOS (eNOS). The eNOS-derived NO is a key regulator of vascular tone, promoting relaxation of smooth muscle cells in blood vessels, thereby facilitating increased blood flow and reducing blood pressure. The nNOS is involved in neurotransmission within the central nervous system, influencing synaptic plasticity and neuronal communication [9]. It has been reported that the expression of nNOS is significantly increased in gliomas, correlating with both histological grade and the proliferative potential of the tumors [10].

text: smooth muscle cells in blood vessels, thereby facilitating increased blood flow and reducing blood pressure. The nNOS is involved in neurotransmission within the central nervous system, influencing synaptic plasticity and neuronal communication [9]. It has been reported that the expression of nNOS is significantly increased in gliomas, correlating with both histological grade and the proliferative potential of the tumors [10]. Moreover, a recent study has reported that the treatment of a U87-MG glioma cell line with the iNOS inhibitor N6-(1-iminoethyl)-L-lysine (L-NIL), or 7-Nitroindazole (7-NI), an nNOS inhibitor, led to a reduction of clonogenic proliferation and nitrosative stress [11]. Based on the involvement of both iNOS and nNOS in glioma biology, in the present work we have hypothesized that a dual inhibitor targeting both enzymes could serve as a more effective therapeutic strategy than agents inhibiting either iNOS or nNOS alone. This strategy indeed, previously allowed to identify new compounds efficacious in models of neuropathic pain and inflammation. [12, 13]. To target both the nNOS/iNOS isoforms while preserving the physiological activity of eNOS, we hybridized the quinoline scaffold, previously shown to be effective in nNOS inhibition [14], with the acetamidine moiety, a key pharmacophore found in several potent iNOS inhibitors [15–17] (Fig. 1). Here we describe the synthesis of a molecule related to the general structure I (compound 3) by a simple, innovative and solvent-free procedure and its biological evaluation as a promising anti-glioma agent. Results and discussion Chemistry To obtain compound 3, a multicomponent solvent-free synthesis approach was used (Scheme 1), in which 2 equivalents of the 2-aminoacetophenone were reacted with 1 equivalent of ethyl acetimidate hydrochloride. The reaction proceeded in both ethanol and solvent-free conditions, although the last gave the best yield (see Table S1). In particular, we hypothesized that the ethyl acetimidate hydrochloride catalyzed a Friedländer-type reaction between the 2-aminoacetophenone molecules giving 3, according to Scheme 2. The initial reaction between the ethyl acetimidate with 2-aminoacetophenone gives an intermediate I that can react with a second molecule of 2-aminoacetophenone following mechanism A or B. Encouraged by the promising preliminary data, further preclinical investigation of 3 in a glioma model were performed. Assessment of cell viability and cytotoxicity in normal rat astrocytes (CTX) and C6 rat glioma cells To assess the biological effect of 3, increasing concentrations of the compound were administered on two rat cell lines, namely CTX and C6. CTX TNA2 is an astrocyte, type I cell line that was isolated from the cortex of 1-dayold rats, and it is widely used as a cell model for neurological studies [20]. The ­Ca2+-dependent NO-synthesizing enzymes eNOS and nNOS are constitutively expressed in astrocytes, whereas the expression of iNOS is typically assumed to be induced by cytokines and other agents during the immune response, and its activity does not depend on an increment in ­[Ca2+]i [21]. Activated astrocytes can contribute to the development of gliomas, where the iNOS has been demonstrated to be overexpressed [8]. Against this background, the rat CTX TNA2 and the C6 rat glioma cell lines were used to assess the biological activity of compound 3 in terms of cell viability and cytotoxicity occurrence (Fig. 2). Increasing concentrations of 3 were administered on both the cell lines for 24, 48 and 72 h. After the exposure to 3, viability percentages related to CTX decrease time-dependently and dose-dependently (Fig. 2a). After 24 h of exposure, this trend starts at 75 µM, whereas after 48 and 72 h, cell viability is lower than 60% already at 25 µM. When C6 rat glioma cells are exposed to 3 (Fig. 2b), percentages of cell viability dramatically fall to values lower than 40% starting from 75 µM at 24 h, and the significant decrease is even amplified after 48 and 72 h (percentages lower than 20%).

TMZ was administered at 500 µM, as already reported [22]. Unexpectedly, percentages of cell viability in the presence of TMZ + 3 are higher than the ones in the presence of 3 alone. It has been widely demonstrated that glioma cells activated several mechanisms involved in TMZ-resistance, contributing to unbeneficial clinical outcomes [23]. Some works report a function of neuronal nitric oxide synthase enzyme in temozolomide-induced damage of astrocytic tumor cells [24], it might be plausible to speculate that, by acting also on the inducible isoform, compound 3 is more efficient if used alone in vitro. Conclusions In conclusion, by the hybridization of different pharmacophores, a new dual nNOS/iNOS inhibitor was obtained. Compound 3 is highly accessible by means of a facile and eco-friendly synthesis and demonstrated significant antitumor activity against glioma, both as a monotherapy and in combination with TMZ. Compared to the selective iNOS inhibitors already known for their anti-glioma activity [8, 23], 3 offers a potential therapeutic advantage due to its dualism, making it effective also against gliomas with high nNOS expression. Moreover, its antiproliferative and cytotoxic effects, along with selectivity for tumor cells and a potential to improve TMZ efficacy, suggest that 3 could be considered in future therapeutic research. On the other side, to progress this scaffold toward therapeutic application, some issues remain to be addressed in future studies, such as the deeper understanding of the key molecular features driving selectivity and potency of 3, as well as its efficacy and safety in further glioma models. title: Roles of the NFI/CTF gene family in transcription and development: update 2025.
text: Roles of the NFI/CTF gene family in transcription and development: update 2025 Richard M. Gronostajski1,* 1Department of Biochemistry and Program in Genetics, Genomics and Bioinformatics, Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, University at Buffalo, Buffalo, NY, USA. Abstract This review is an update of the review entitled “Roles of the NFI/CTF gene family in transcription and development” published in Gene in 2000 (referred to hereafter as the 2000 Gene review). That review began with the sentence “The Nuclear Factor I (NFI) family of site-specific DNA-binding proteins (also known as CTF or CAAT box transcription factor) functions both in viral DNA replication and in the regulation of gene expression.”, which is as valid now as it was then. The subsequent focus of NFI research has been on the role of individual or multiple family members in gene expression during development, in various adult organ systems, and the effect of NFI mutations in human syndromes. Here we will cover post-2000 studies with an emphasis on the role of NFI genes in brain, skin, blood, skeletal muscle, and retinal development; recent studies on the effect of hemizygosity of NFI genes in human development; the role of NFI genes in cancer; and the recently described 3D structure of the NFIX DNA-binding domain. Keywords nuclear factor I; nuclear factor one; development; transcription; gliogenesis; retina 1. Introduction As described in detail in the 2000 Gene review [1], the NFI gene family was discovered as a required protein for the replication of Adenovirus type 2 and two years later identified as a site-specific DNA-binding transcription factor (TF) involved in the regulation of gene expression. We refer the reader to that review for information on the discovery of binding sites for NFI and the early characterization of NFI binding specificity, affinity, and homoand heterodimerization of NFI family members. In addition, the 2000 review gives a detailed description of the structure of the NFI gene family in mammals and the single NFI genes in Drosophila and Caenorhabditus elegans [1]. Only minor additions have been found since then, primarily the discovery of additional alternative promoter regions with alternate 1st exons and numerous alternatively spliced isoforms of the four mammalian genes NFIA, This article is an open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). * rgron@buffalo.edu . There has been explosive growth in the number of papers published on the NFI gene family since 2000 (Figure 1), and this review will focus almost solely on work performed since then. To summarize some of the most exciting discoveries regarding the NFI genes since the 2000 review: the use of knockout and/or conditional knockout alleles of the mouse NFI genes have shown how these genes are required for the development of multiple organ systems including brain, retina, muscle, liver, kidney, skin, lung, salivary gland and the hematopoietic and immune systems. Significant progress has also been made on the discovery of proteins with which NFI proteins interact to perform their functions. The role of NFI genes in various cancers has also been studied, as has the role of mutations in NFI genes in a number of rare genetic syndromes. A very large number of proteins have been shown to directly interact with various NFI family members in vivo. Finally, the structure of the NFIX DNA-binding domain has been determined, which may allow the development of therapeutics to treat diseases or syndromes in which NFI genes play a role. These and other findings are described in detail below. 2. Results 2.1. Use of germline knockout (KO) mice to study NFI gene function While there was considerable circumstantial evidence that NFI proteins function in the regulation of developmental genes discussed in the 2000 Gene review [1], it was through the use of germline and conditional knockout (KO) mice that essential roles for specific NFI gene products have been determined. All of the germline and conditional deletions generated to date are deletions or disruptions of the 2nd exon of the NFI genes, which encode the bulk of the DNA-binding domain.

All of the germline and conditional deletions generated to date are deletions or disruptions of the 2nd exon of the NFI genes, which encode the bulk of the DNA-binding domain. The remainder of this section will describe the initial phenotypes seen in germline knockouts of the Nfia, Nfib, Nfic, and Nfix genes, in that order. The first NFI gene to be disrupted was the mouse Nfia gene, whose homozygous germline disruption resulted in hydrocephalus, agenesis of the corpus callosum, aberrant hippocampus development, reduced GFAP expression, and significant perinatal lethality [2]. In addition, far fewer than expected heterozygous Nfia-disrupted mice survived to adulthood, indicating some degree of haploinsufficiency for Nfia. These findings will be discussed further in Sections 2.3 and 2.6 on “NFI genes in brain and spinal cord development” and “NFI genes in human syndromes, diseases and evolution”, respectively. Nfib was the second NFI gene subjected to germline disruption by two groups, and homozygous germline loss of Nfib resulted in early perinatal lethality due to lung immaturity [3, 4]. In addition to the lethal lung defect, loss of Nfib resulted in fetal loss of the basilar pons, aberrant hippocampus development, reduced GFAP expression, and callosal agenesis [4, 5], and the latter three phenotypes were also seen in germline Nfia-knockout mice [2]. This was an early indication that Nfia and Nfib might share important functions in brain development. These data will be discussed further in Section 2.3 “NFI genes in brain and spinal cord development”. Gronostajski Page 2 Acad Biol. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2026 October 06. Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Disruption of Nfic demonstrated that it is essential for normal tooth development in mice [6]. Homozygous loss of Nfic resulted in complete loss of molar tooth roots and aberrant incisor development due to defects in odontoblast development [7-9]. Nfic expression in tooth root formation appears due to a Smad4-Shh-Nfic signaling cascade required for root development [10]. Nfic was the first gene discovered whose disruption specifically affects tooth root development. These tooth defects cause postnatal lethality unless the mice are reared on a high-high-fat diet to allow nutrition sufficient for survival.

Nfic was the first gene discovered whose disruption specifically affects tooth root development. These tooth defects cause postnatal lethality unless the mice are reared on a high-high-fat diet to allow nutrition sufficient for survival. Subsequent studies showed that Nfic is also required for normal bone development and adipocyte and osteoblast differentiation [11, 12], likely due to regulation of Fgf [13] and Wnt signaling [12]. Nfic also regulates the proliferation in dental epithelial, pulp, and bone marrow stem cells [14] and ameloblast differentiation [15]. Nfic appears to be a target of miR-184 since downregulation of this microRNA promotes osseous differentiation of periodontal ligament stem cells by upregulation of Nfic [16]. In addition, the compound suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid enhances odontoblast differentiation at least in part through increasing the expression of Nfic [17]. Some of these findings are reviewed here [18]. Lastly, Nfic has been linked to the regulation of wound healing through the TGF-β1 pathway [19]. The first homozygous disruption of Nfix was postnatally lethal, with mice exhibiting hydrocephalus and partial agenesis of the corpus callosum [20]. In addition, spinal and bone ossification defects were seen [20]. A second germline KO of Nfix was generated from a conditional Nfix KO allele and found to have a similar but not identical phenotype [21]. In these animals, homozygous Nfix disruption resulted in delayed eyelid and ear opening and reduced weight gain, the latter of which could be partially alleviated with a soft dough diet [21]. Because these homozygous Nfix KO mice survived for a few weeks postnatally, their brains could be examined and were shown to be significantly larger than their WT littermates. This will be discussed further in Section 2.6 “NFI genes in human syndromes, diseases and evolution”. In addition, callosal and hippocampal dysgenesis and a reduced cerebellum were seen along with expansion of the cingulate cortex and excessive proliferation of Dcx+ cells in the lateral ventricles. Nfix expression was detected throughout telencephalon and hippocampus development from E12 to adult [21].

The cause of the differences in phenotype seen in the two KO mouse models is unclear, but could be due to differences in genetic backgrounds of the animals or due to differences in the KO allele, the first of which was a lacZ replacement of the second exon, while the second was a Cre-mediated deletion of the second exon. The first Nfix KO allele is no longer available (personal communication), while the second is now commercially available (JAX Strain #040481) and has been used for the studies discussed below. 2.2. Deletion of the single NFI gene in C. elegans While there are four NFI family members in all examined mammals, there is only a single NFI gene in the nematode C. elegans (nfi-1) and in Drosophila [1]. Since NFI genes have been found in all the examined multicellular organisms but not in bacteria, yeast, or archaea [22], one question to be addressed was whether NFI genes are essential for multicellular development. Somewhat surprisingly, deletion of the DNA-binding domain of nfi-1 resulted in relatively normal worm development but with locomotion defects, an egg-laying defect, a reduced adult life-span, and reduced pharyngeal pumping rate [23]. The egg-laying defect Gronostajski Page 3 Acad Biol. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2026 October 06. Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript was seen most strongly in homozygous KO worms but was also present in heterozygous nfi-1−/+ worms, revealing an unusual haploinsufficiency in C. elegans. The pharyngeal pumping defect appears to be cell autonomous and connected in some way with the shortened lifespan in that rescue of both phenotypes can be seen in KO worms expressing nfi-1 from the pharyngeal muscle-specific myo-2 promoter [24]. The egg-laying and motility defects are not rescued in myo-2::nfi-1 worms. Thus, an NFI gene is not required for DNA replication or nearly normal development of C. elegans.

The egg-laying and motility defects are not rescued in myo-2::nfi-1 worms. Thus, an NFI gene is not required for DNA replication or nearly normal development of C. elegans. The strong relationship between the worm nfi-1 gene and the mammalian NFI genes was confirmed by demonstrating that the worm NFI-1 protein bound to the same consensus sequence as the mammalian NFI proteins [25]. Recently a chemical screen has been performed in nfi-1-deficient worms to identify possible therapeutic agents for Malan syndrome [26], an overgrowth condition [27] due to a mutation in a single copy of the human NFIX gene. This will be discussed further in Section 2.6 “NFI genes in human syndromes, diseases and evolution”. The nfi-1 deficient worms are available from the Caenorhabditis Genetics Center (https://cgc.umn.edu). 2.3. NFI genes in brain and spinal cord development Nfia: Brain and spinal cord development is the area in which there have the greatest number of publications on the role of NFI genes. As described in Section 2.1, germline deletion of Nfia has dramatic effects on brain development [2], and many studies have extended these findings to determine the mechanisms leading to these defects. Homozygous disruption of Nfia was shown to disrupt the development of multiple glial structures during brain development, including the glial wedge, glial sling, and indusium griseum glia [28]. A frequently cited finding showed that Nfia controls the onset of gliogenesis in the chick and mouse spinal cord and is both necessary and sufficient for Glutamate-Aspartate Transporter protein induction in the developing ventricular zone (VZ) [29]. Nfia is also essential for the continued inhibition of neurogenesis in VZ progenitor cells [29], thus regulating the process known as the “gliogenic switch”. These findings indicated that Nfia was a master regulatory gene for gliogenesis in multiple regions of the brain and spinal cord. Subsequent studies showed that Nfia is expressed in many regions of the developing brain, including the prenatal deep cortical layers, subplate, and ventricular zone, and a large proportion of postnatal laterally projecting neurons [30]. These Nfia expression data, along with the mouse brain expression data for Nfib and Nfix, were subject to a review in 2009 [31].

text: and spinal cord. Subsequent studies showed that Nfia is expressed in many regions of the developing brain, including the prenatal deep cortical layers, subplate, and ventricular zone, and a large proportion of postnatal laterally projecting neurons [30]. These Nfia expression data, along with the mouse brain expression data for Nfib and Nfix, were subject to a review in 2009 [31]. Multiple lines of evidence indicate that Nfia is essential for normal gliogenesis, likely downstream of the Notch signaling pathway [32]. Nfia appears to bind to and promote the demethylation and activation of the Gfap gene in differentiating astrocytes [32], and binding sites of NFI proteins are also present in a number of other astrocytic genes, including S100b, aquaporin4, and clusterin [32]. In contrast, Nfia appears to function as a repressor of L1 gene expression in neuroblastoma cells [33], indicating that NFIA can function as either an activator or repressor of gene expression depending on the gene and cellular context. This concept is further supported by the finding that Nfia can repress expression of Hes1 and thus downregulate the Notch signaling pathway in telencephalic progenitor cells [34]. The pathways through which Nfia induces gliogenesis are under active investigation. Sox9 and Nfia form a complex and coregulate the expression of a specific set of genes induced during gliogenesis [35]. Lhx2 overexpression can override the activation of gliogenesis Gronostajski Page 4 Acad Biol. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2026 October 06. Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript by both Notch signaling and Nfia overexpression, suggesting that Lhx2 can antagonize Nfia activity in an as yet unknown manner [36]. Pax6 overexpression can also override Nfia-induced astrogenesis in the developing hippocampus, suggesting that it acts similarly to Lhx2 [37]. Neural stem cell models have proven useful in addressing Nfia function in astrogenesis. Nfia was shown to be a potent inducer of astrogenesis in mouse ESCderived astrogenic neural progenitor cells (aNPCs) [38]. Here Nfia is bound to promoters and enhancers of multiple astrocytic genes and is associated with H3K27ac enrichment at these sites. Depletion of Nfia from early astrocytes in this model led to changes in astrocyte shape and a reduction in expression of Gfap, Aldh1I1, Aldoc, and Aqp4, along with an increase in neurogenic genes [38]. Nfia cooperates with Atf3 in binding to at least 47 promoter/enhancer sites during gliogenesis and increases chromatin accessibility as measured by ATAC-seq [38].

Depletion of Nfia from early astrocytes in this model led to changes in astrocyte shape and a reduction in expression of Gfap, Aldh1I1, Aldoc, and Aqp4, along with an increase in neurogenic genes [38]. Nfia cooperates with Atf3 in binding to at least 47 promoter/enhancer sites during gliogenesis and increases chromatin accessibility as measured by ATAC-seq [38]. NFIA also induces gliogenesis in human long-term embryonic stem cell-derived neural stem cells, which spontaneously do not undergo the gliogenic switch [39]. This allows the production of large numbers of human astrocytes for future studies. Surprisingly, NFIA promotion of gliogenesis was most potent with a transient 5-10 day transgenic induction period followed by downregulation of NFI. Longterm induction of NFIA suppressed astrocytic differentiation. Transient NFIA induction also resulted in a lengthening of the G1 phase of the cell cycle, similar to what is seen during normal gliogenesis [39]. This suggests that continuous expression of NFIA might suppress gliogenesis by leading to G1 cell cycle arrest. TGFβ1-treatment of the neurogenic NSCs induced both NFIA expression and gliogenesis, but much less effectively than transgenic NFIA overexpression [39]. The potency of NFI genes for gliogenesis was shown most dramatically by the demonstration that a combination of NFIA, NFIB, and SOX9 induction was sufficient to reprogram mouse fibroblasts into astrocytes [40]. This direct trans-differentiation eliminates the need for embryonic or induced pluripotent stem cells, and if applicable to human cells, could be a source for patient-specific astrocytes. Along with its role in astrocyte development, loss of Nfia in adult mouse brains causes defects in astrocyte-mediated synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus, resulting in defects in learning and memory [41]. In addition to its role in gliogenesis, Nfia plays other roles in brain development. Conditional deletion of Nfia with a Wnt1-Cre allele eliminated the expression of Nfia in the dorsal root ganglion and resulted in a deficit in pinprick-responsiveness in the mice [42]; thus, Nfia appears necessary for the development of Npy2r-transient A-fiber nociceptor neurons. Germline disruption of Nfia greatly reduced cerebellar granule neuron (CGN) dendrite formation and the migration of cells from the cerebellum external granule layer [43]. Also, the expression of the cerebellar granule cell marker Gabra6 was decreased ~4 fold in Nfia KO mice [44]. Indeed, transcriptome analysis of germline Nfia KO brains indicated that there was a general delay in the maturation of neurons and oligodendrocytes [45].

Also, the expression of the cerebellar granule cell marker Gabra6 was decreased ~4 fold in Nfia KO mice [44]. Indeed, transcriptome analysis of germline Nfia KO brains indicated that there was a general delay in the maturation of neurons and oligodendrocytes [45]. In addition, Nfia appears to provide a protective role in neurons as Nfia−/− neurons are extremely sensitized to NMDA-induced excitotoxicity [46]. Nfia also inhibits the Sox10 induction of oligodendrocyte differentiation by forming a complex with Sox10 and preventing its function [47]. This inhibition of oligodendrocyte differentiation indicates a role for NFIA in suppression of oligodendrocyte maturation after white matter injury in hypoxia or multiple sclerosis [48]. With the availability of conditional Nfia KO alleles Gronostajski Page 5 Acad Biol. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2026 October 06. Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript (JAX Strains #032281 and #040481), it is expected that the role of Nfia in neurons, oligodendrocytes, and other cell types in the brain will be examined in more detail in the future. Nfib: The sharing of some brain phenotypes between germline Nfia KO and Nfib KO mice (see Section 2.1) indicated that both genes were important in brain development. Further studies on the Nfib germline KO mice showed that a subpopulation of glia from the hippocampal ammonic neuroepithelium is lost, resulting in severe morphological defects [49]. Nfib−/− brains have an increased number of proliferating cells in the cortical ventricular zone and increased levels of Ezh2 expression [50], and Nfib can bind to the promoter region of Ezh2 and repress its expression. Another mechanism by which Nfib may function is through forming a transcriptional regulatory network in adult neural progenitors with Sox11 and Pou3f4 to promote a neural fate [51]. There is a severe reduction in mature glial cells at the midline of the brains of Nfib−/− mice with no changes in proliferation or cell death, indicating a severe defect in astrocyte differentiation [52]. It seems likely that the callosal agenesis or dysgenesis seen in these mice is due to these glial defects, as callosal axons do not appear to express Nfib. In addition to callosal defects, other forebrain commissures are aberrant in Nfib−/− brains [52]. Nfib−/− mice also exhibit a defect in EphrinB1 expression in the cerebellum [43], a phenotype shared with Nfia−/− mice.

text: seems likely that the callosal agenesis or dysgenesis seen in these mice is due to these glial defects, as callosal axons do not appear to express Nfib. In addition to callosal defects, other forebrain commissures are aberrant in Nfib−/− brains [52]. Nfib−/− mice also exhibit a defect in EphrinB1 expression in the cerebellum [43], a phenotype shared with Nfia−/− mice. As mentioned above, Nfib can cooperate with Nfia and Sox9 to directly convert fibroblasts to astrocytes, further suggesting an important role in gliogenesis [40]. One surprising finding is that Drosha targets Nfib in hippocampal neural stem cells and promotes neurogenesis, indicating that Nfib in these cells promotes oligodendrogenesis [53]. Nfib is also essential for the normal generation of corticofugal neurons throughout cortical development [54]. The availability of a conditional Nfib KO allele (JAX Strain #040481) will allow more detailed analysis of Nfib function in the brain. Nfic: While no brain defects were detected in germline homozygous Nfic KO mice [6], we describe in Section 2.6 “NFI genes in human syndromes, diseases and evolution” that Nfic may play a role in human brain development. Nfix: The expansion of the cingulate cortex and reduction in cerebellum size in germline Nfix KO brains indicated a significant role in brain development [21]. Nfix is expressed in the progenitor cells in the external granule layer of the cerebellum, and loss of Nfix delays the postnatal development of the cerebellar granule neurons, Purkinje cells, and Bergmann glia [55] along with an early postnatal decrease in proliferation in the granule cell layer. This identification of a role for Nfix in cerebellar granule neuron development is consistent with findings that expression of a dominant-repressor NFI-engrailed transgene in CGNs represses GABRA6 expression [44]. In the forebrain, Nfix is expressed in ventricular zone progenitor cells of the neocortex and hippocampus and appears to repress the expression of Bobby Sox (Bbx) in these cells, as deletion of Nfix increases Bbx expression [56]. This repression may be related to the finding that Nfix regulates neural progenitor differentiation in the developing hippocampus [57]. Homozygous deletion of Nfix alters the balance between self-renewal and differentiation of hippocampal neural progenitor cells, resulting in extended progenitor proliferation, distortion of the hippocampus, and decreased glial marker Gronostajski Page 6 Acad Biol. Author manuscript; available in PMC 2026 October 06. Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript expression [57]. Nfix appears to interact with an alternatively spliced isoform of Lef1 to promote the quiescence of hippocampal NSCs [58]. Use of a conditional Nfix knockout allele showed that while loss of Nfix does not influence the survival of adult hippocampal neural stem cells, Nfix is required for the normal maturation and survival of neuroblasts derived from the stem cells [59]. These defects in hippocampal neuroblasts and neurons were associated with a deficit in learning tests in the adult mice [59]. Surprisingly, even heterozygous loss of Nfix is sufficient to induce abnormal hippocampus development and cause specific learning and memory deficits in adult mice [60]. These findings will be addressed further in Section 2.6 “NFI genes in human syndromes, diseases and evolution”. Some of these studies have been reviewed earlier [61]. Along with hippocampus defects, homozygous loss of Nfix causes major cortical defects. Nfix−/− mice show increased levels of proliferation in the subventricular zone (SVZ) of the lateral ventricles with more Pax6-expressing progenitor cells [62]. Increased proliferation within the SVZ may be due to a role of Nfix in regulating neural stem cell quiescence [63]. In addition, the migration of neuroblasts through the rostral migratory stream (RMS) is reduced, and gliogenesis within the RMS is delayed in Nfix−/− brains [62], leading to a smaller olfactory bulb. The defect in neuroblast migration occurs when Nfix is deleted from either adult neural stem cells in the SVZ or from migrating neuroblasts and appears related to aberrant neuroblast branching and increased expression of Npr2 in Nfix−/− neuroblasts [64]. Creb5 may promote the proliferation of SVZ neural stem cells through binding to the Nfix promoter and activation of its expression [65]. Surprisingly, deletion of Nfix in either adult hippocampal neural stem cells [59] or in cultured neural stem cells [66] causes a bias of differentiations towards the oligodendrocyte lineage, indicating that Nfix may normally repress oligodendrogenesis during gliogenesis. Finally, the hydrocephalus seen in Nfix−/− brains appears due at least in part to aberrant ependymal cell development [67].
