Overview and patient characteristics The dataset for this study included 83 consecutive patients with aggressive myocarditis from Fuwai Hospital who had undergone heart transplantation. The selection pipeline is illustrated in Graphical abstract. First, cardiac WSIs were obtained from patients with aggressive myocarditis, covering six speciﬁc locations as previously reported [ 29 ]. Next, deep learning-based pathology features were generated to classify aggressive myocarditis patients into diﬀerent phenotypic groups. Finally, RNA-seq and WES data were used to elucidate the underlying mechanisms underlying the diﬀerent phenotypes. The mean age of onset of the patients was 36.2 ± 14.59 years, with 61.4% of these patients being male ( n = 51). Additionally, 27.7% of patients had a documented history of infection prior to the onset of myocarditis, and more than half of the patients presented with ventricular arrhythmias, including premature ventricular contractions and ventricular tachycardia. The clinical characteristics of the cohort, along with integrated pathologic diagnoses, are summarized in Table S2. 3.2. A novel pathological classiﬁcation of aggressive myocarditis and comparison of clinical characteristics among phenogroups Our weakly-supervised deep learning model classiﬁed 83 patients with aggressive myocarditis into three stable phenogroups, each associated with diﬀerent clinical characteristics ( Table 1 ). Phenogroup 1 (PG1; n = 28; 34%) had the youngest age of onset (30.79 ± 14.11; p = 0.049) and the highest proportion of family history of myocarditis ( n = 9, 32%; p = 0.036). Furthermore, this group exhibited the lowest left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF, 26.86% ± 8.13%, p = 0.031), with all individuals receiving diuretic treatment ( n = 28, 100%; p = 0.038). Phenogroup 2 (PG2; n = 25; 30%) presented the highest diastolic blood pressure (71.54 ± 6.95 mmHg; p = 0.017), the highest total protein levels (70.82 ± 7.87 g/L; p = 0.026), the highest albumin levels (44.90 ± 3.76 g/L; p = 0.018), and the highest LVEF (33.61% ± 11.15%; p = 0.031).

Association of phenotypic groups with diﬀerent outcomes Given that our deep learning model classiﬁed patients into three phenogroups with distinct prognoses, we examined the survival diﬀerences across these groups ( Fig. 2 ). Survival time was deﬁned as the duration from the onset of symptoms to HTx. Among the phenogroups, PG3 has the shortest survival time from symptom onset to HTx, while PG1 exhibited the longest survival time (Median survival time: PG1, 8.1 years; PG2, 5.3 years; PG3, 2.02 years, p < 0.001). PG1 and PG2 had similar early survival rates (Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon test, p = 0.1414), but PG1 showed better late survival (Log-Rank test, p = 0.0409, Fig. 2a ). Previous reports have suggested that sex plays a role in the outcome of acute myocarditis, suggesting a higher risk of death or heart transplantation in women [ 30 ]. However, in our study, female patients with aggressive myocarditis had a similar risk of heart transplantation compared to male patients (Median survival: Male, 5.2 years; Female, 3.1 years, p = 0.1225, Fig. 2b ). Viral infection is known to be the most common etiology of myocarditis [ 31 ], and the presence of viral genomes has been identiﬁed as a univariate predictor of poor prognosis [ 32 ]. Consistent with these ﬁndings, a history of proviral infection signiﬁcantly impacted patient prognosis, particularly in the early stages (Median survival: proviral infection history positive, 1.15 years; proviral infection history negative, 5.18 years; p < 0.01, Fig. 2c ).

Extraction of extremal tiles associated with prognosis to identify regions of interest Another important aspect of the pathologic classiﬁcation process was its interpretability. The attention scoring module we employed allowed us to assign scores to each tile for a given patient, with higher values indicating a poor prognosis and lower values indicating a favorable prognosis ( Fig. 3a ). This scoring system can serve as a valuable tool for pathologists to identify speciﬁc areas of interest that are relevant to the survival of each patient. We aggregated scores from all 498 slides into a single distribution and then isolated those associated with high and low survival rates ( Fig. 3b ). RNA sequencing of cardiac samples to unravel underlying pathophysiology To further understand the cardiac pathophysiological diﬀerences between the phenogroups, we conducted genome-wide transcriptome analysis through RNA sequencing of cardiac samples from a sub-cohort of 18 patients, with an equal distribution of PG 1–3 (6 patients per group) ( Fig. 5a ). The three groups were randomly selected, and the KM survival curves were plotted after selection (Fig. S1). Subsequently, we performed diﬀerential expression analysis for the three pathological subtypes (Fig. S2a-c) and conducted an intersection analysis of the up-regulated and down-regulated genes (Fig. 5b and S2d). Further enrichment analysis of speciﬁc up-regulated and down-regulated genes for each subtype was carried out separately (Fig. S3 and S4), revealing signiﬁcant diﬀerences between PG3 and PG1, primarily in myocardial and inﬂammatory pathways, with PG2 showing intermediate characteristics. GSEA enrichment analysis highlighted inﬂammation and abnormal activation of myocardial structure as key diﬀerences between PG3 and PG1 (Fig. 5c and S5).

GSEA enrichment analysis highlighted inﬂammation and abnormal activation of myocardial structure as key diﬀerences between PG3 and PG1 (Fig. 5c and S5). Furthermore, abnormal activation of ion-related pathways in PG3 was linked to frequent clinical arrhythmias. Notably, PG3 and PG2 exhibited distinct modes of inﬂammation activation. Additionally, GSVA revealed that PG1 displayed features associated with apoptosis, ﬁbrosis production, and abnormal metabolic pathways, while PG2 and PG3 showed activation of cell damage signaling and immunerelated pathways with reversed activation patterns (Fig. S6). The ssGSEA immunoinﬁltration analysis revealed signiﬁcant inﬂammatory characteristics among diﬀerent PGs ( Fig. 5d ). PG1 and PG2 showed signiﬁcantly enhanced T-cell-mediated immune responses, with an increased inﬁltration score of CD8+ T cells, as well as Th1 cells and helper T cells. These groups also exhibited enhanced activity in T-cell co-stimulation, cytolytic activity, and immune checkpoint pathways. In contrast, PG3 showed mainly innate immune activation, with a significant increase in macrophage inﬁltration, accompanied by enrichment of inﬂammatory promotion pathways, antigen-presenting cell (APC) costimulation, and type I/II interferon responses. According to the literature, the immunobiological detection of inﬂammation is prognostically relevant. Here, diﬀerent cell types including T cells, macrophages and neutrophils were characterized by immunohistology among the three PGs [ 8 ] ( Fig. 5e –f ). We found that macrophage inﬁltration was the feature of PG3, while T cell inﬁltration was the characteristic of PG2. There was more T cell inﬁltration than macrophage or neutrophil inﬁltration in PG1. The results were consistent with the results of immunoinﬁltration analysis based on RNA-seq data ( Fig. 5d ). 3.7. Identifying IL6ST as a novel prognostic biomarker for myocarditis In clinical practice, there was no eﬀective predictive biomarker for the prognosis of aggressive myocarditis [ 33 ]. To identify biomarkers with clinical applicability, we conducted a systematic survival screening of 574 immune cell marker gene sets utilized in the ssGSEA-based immunoinﬁltration analysis ( Fig. 5d ). Patients were stratiﬁed based on the median expression value of the transcriptome for each gene, and the risk of transplantation progression was subsequently evaluated in batches. Fourteen gene sets exhibited statistically signiﬁcant prognostic value ( p < 0.05).

Fourteen gene sets exhibited statistically signiﬁcant prognostic value ( p < 0.05). Among these, eleven genes were linked to poor prognosis, with IL6ST demonstrating the highest HR. Conversely, three genes were associated with a favorable prognosis, with IFNA5 showing the lowest HR ( Fig. 5g ). IFNA5 is an interferon-related gene, whereas IL6ST has been reported to be associated with the inhibition of gene function related to myocardial regeneration [ 34 ]. The corresponding K-M curves for transplantation progression are depicted in Fig. 5h We validated these ﬁndings in an independent cohort of 45 clinically diagnosed myocarditis patients with an average follow-up duration of 46.3 ± 8.9 months. Plasma IL6ST levels > 332.45 ng/ml eﬀectively distinguished patients with symptom recurrence (AUC = 0.758, p = 0.011; Fig. 5i ), and the recurrence progression was notably faster (HR = 22.8, 95% CI 2.3 - 227.2; p < 0.0001; Fig. 5j ). Although plasma IFNA5 levels exhibited a consistent directional trend, they did not achieve statistical signiﬁcance ( Fig. 5i –j ). These ﬁndings suggest that IL6ST can serve as a clinically relevant biomarker for evaluating risk stratiﬁcation in myocarditis. 3.8. Clinical promotion of pathological classiﬁcation and supervised decision tree modelling to enhance clinical utility To evaluate the clinical relevance of the pathological phenogroups, we conducted comprehensive correlation analyses that integrated clinical, genomic, and transcriptomic features with deep-learning classiﬁcations ( Fig. 6 ). PG1 demonstrated strong associations with desmosome sarcomere-related gene mutations (e.g., TTN), early disease onset, and a familial history of cardiomyopathy, establishing its identity as the structural damage subtype. PG2 was characterized as the autoimmune subtype, based on dominant T-cell inﬁltration (immunohistochemistry: CD3+ cells; ssGSEA: Th1/TIL signatures) and the enrichment of myocarditis-related mutations. PG3 was deﬁned as the virus infection-driven subtype due to its unique correlations with proviral infection and ventricular arrhythmias, further supported by macrophagedominated inﬂammation (immunohistochemistry: CD68+ cells; ssGSEA: macrophage signature). Furthermore, to facilitate clinical application, we employed supervised decision tree modeling using the phenogroups from the clustering as input (Methods). The classiﬁer was created using only a few clinical variables that diﬀered among the three phenogroups.

A low number of variables in such a classiﬁer enhances its potential applicability in clinical practice. Among the various clinical parameters across the three phenogroups, body mass index (BMI), family history presence, age at onset of myocarditis, and history of proviral infection were identiﬁed as the most signiﬁcant variable characteristics, yielding a combined accuracy of 70% ( Fig. 6c and Table S6). Additionally, we developed a decision tree classiﬁcation software in Python. By inputting the aforementioned four parameters, the corresponding PG classiﬁcations can be output (Fig. S7). 4. Discussion In this study, 83 heart transplant patients with aggressive myocarditis were reviewed retrospectively over the past 10 years at the Fuwai Hospital. Utilizing heart transplant samples of aggressive myocarditis patients, accurate pathology classiﬁcation was performed. Each of these phenogroups had distinct clinical characteristics, gene mutation proﬁles and cardiac transcriptomic proﬁles. Then, a classiﬁer was built to classify aggressive myocarditis patients quickly based on the four clinical data (BMI, presence of family history, age at onset of myocarditis, and proviral infection history). This classiﬁcation was the ﬁrst to integrate clinical features, cardiac function, comorbidities, and underlying etiology, which could pave the way for more targeted and personalized treatment approaches (Graphical abstract). Given the challenging nature of diagnosing myocarditis in clinical practice, the lack of a pathological diagnosis often leads to a clinical suspicion of myocarditis. Endocardial biopsy remains the gold standard for clinical diagnosis, but it carries the risk of false negatives and may fail to pinpoint the lesion site, placing a psychological burden on the patient. A six-site pathology analysis of aggressive myocarditis transplant patients involved in our study ﬁlls this gap, providing accurate pathology insights based on actual myocarditis cases. This scheme proved invaluable in clinically diagnosing nearly half of suspected myocarditis patients, enabling us to stratify patients based on this protocol. The classiﬁcation of aggressive myocarditis into three phenogroups was based on a detailed pathological analysis ( Fig.1 ).

According to the immunophenotyping ( Fig. 5e –f ), we found that PG1 and PG2 were characteristic of the T cell inﬁltration, which belongs to lymphocytic myocarditis. It is well known that immunosuppression is not routinely recommended for all forms of acute lymphocytic myocarditis. Recommendations for this and other forms of acute, complicated myocarditis are not supported by evidence from randomized clinical trials but are derived from case series and pathophysiological considerations. Therefore, more randomized clinical trials should be performed to support the use of immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory agents for PG1 and PG2. The fastest progress in transplantation among our phenogroups is seen in PG3. This group of patients with an elevated transplant risk showed signiﬁcant pathological features in the inﬂammatory regions of the heart, including giant cell masses. Clinically, they have a history of proviral infection and a high incidence of ventricular arrhythmias. Transcriptome analysis revealed myocardial cell damage, abnormal immune activation, and multiple immune activation pathways associated with infection. This was in contrast to PG2 patients, who show a preference for autoimmune activation pathways on the transcriptome. PG2 and PG3 also exhibit more genetic mutations associated with immunity at the genome level than PG1, suggesting a genetic predisposition. To facilitate clinicians in identifying patients with aggressive myocarditis, we developed a decision tree consisting of three pathological subtypes based on clinical characteristics ( Fig. 6c ). Additionally, we created a user-friendly program that aligns with the decision tree, with detailed instructions available (Fig. S7).

To facilitate clinicians in identifying patients with aggressive myocarditis, we developed a decision tree consisting of three pathological subtypes based on clinical characteristics ( Fig. 6c ). Additionally, we created a user-friendly program that aligns with the decision tree, with detailed instructions available (Fig. S7). Once a clinical patient arrives at the hospital, the decision tree can be employed if they exhibit signs suggestive of myocarditis following various evaluations such as physical examination, ultrasound, MRI, ECG, and primary complaint, and an endocardial biopsy is not feasible. By taking into account a patient’s BMI, family history, age at diagnosis, and pre-infection history, our classiﬁcation accuracy exceeds 70%, with a notable accuracy of over 80% for excluding PG1. Consequently, the ﬁndings from this study can help guide treatment decisions, as there is a lack of speciﬁc therapeutic strategies for diﬀerent phenogroups. However, a “one-size-ﬁts-all ” approach, such as generalized anti-inﬂammatory or anti-aging therapies, may not be suﬃcient to delay the need for transplantation due to the varying inﬂammatory etiologies. Therefore, a thorough understanding of patient grouping, etiology, endocardial biopsy diagnosis, and tailored treatment appears to be essential. Diﬀerences across the novel grouping were evaluated to identify which clinical or biomarker features were most important for the outcomes of aggressive myocarditis, to monitor the conditions in patients outside the hospital. While other biomarkers and cytokines, such as high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T and creatine kinase (CK), were used to diagnose myocarditis, they could not be used to predict a patient’s prognosis. In our study, the interleukin-6 signal transducer (IL6ST), also known as gp130, was found to be the most predictive feature for patient outcomes ( Fig. 5g –j ). IL6ST is a transmembrane receptor for IL-6 and OSM. IL-6 and OSM are associated with both innate and adaptive immune cells and are associated with heart failure. IL-6 is a central inﬂammatory mediator and potential therapeutic target in heart failure [ 35 ], and IL-6/IL6ST signaling in CD4+ cells plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of pulmonary arterial hypertension [ 36 ]. In myocarditis, chronic IL-6 signaling has been reported to contribute to the progression to dilated cardiomyopathy [ 37 ]. IL6ST expression for PG3 was the highest comparing with other phenogroups, suggesting that it may be a marker of poor survival.

The role of IL-6 in the development of cardiovascular disease is complex, and it has shown to have both beneﬁcial and adverse eﬀects in preclinical studies. However, it has not previously been associated with outcomes for aggressive myocarditis. This study has some limitations. First, the sample size is relatively small and lack of virological data. Given our aim to classify aggressive myocarditis to guide treatment, expanding the sample size is challenging due to the limited number of transplantations worldwide [ 38 ]. In addition, our study was retrospective and we were not able to obtain suﬃcient cardiac tissue samples for the detection of a viral genome such that the presence of a prior viral infection could be assessed using the patient’s past medical history. Second, we did not involve an external validation cohort, which makes replication on a global scale diﬃcult. Additionally, the patients enrolled in our study all had aggressive myocarditis, and therefore, may not be representative of all stages of myocarditis cases. According to single-cell RNA-sequencing studies of viral myocarditis [ 39 ] and autoimmune myocarditis [ 40 ], pathology may be diﬀerent in diﬀerent stage of myocarditis. Recently, Professor Wang and his colleagues reported the largest cohort of histochemical analyses of fulminant myocarditis, based on endomyocardial biopsy samples, who were in early stage of myocarditis [ 41 ]. This study provides an overview of the clinicopathologic features of fulminant myocarditis. It was very meaningful to combine the diﬀerent stages of myocarditis to systematically study the clinicopathological features of myocarditis. Lastly, clinical phenotypes of all the patients are based on traditional treatments, which are not eﬀective. Through years of eﬀorts of Chinese clinical scientists, Chinese guidelines provided unique treatments which reduced in-hospital mortality from over 50% to ∼5% of adult fulminant myocarditis [ 42 ]. A life support-based comprehensive treatment and immunoglobin have been reported to lower the in-hospital mortality of patients with fulminant myocarditis [ 43 , 44 ]. Whether these unique treatment modalities are eﬀective for aggressive myocarditis requires further investigation.

Conventionally, it has been proposed that endocytosis primarily modulates cellular sensitivity to extracellular signaling molecules by regulating the density of receptors on the plasma membrane. However, emerging evidence highlights the multifaceted role of endosomes within the endocytic pathway, demonstrating their capacity to serve as platforms for signal formation, reception, and decoding, thereby playing a crucial role in intracellular signal transduction. As integral components of the endomembrane system, endosomes enable precise spatiotemporal localization of signaling molecules at the subcellular scale. Furthermore, their unique compositional traits provide a supportive environment for the assembly and maturation of signal transduction regulatory machinery. title: Endosomes: An underappreciated player in cell signal transduction.
text: 1. Introduction The cellular internalization of plasma membrane components and extracellular macromolecules occurs through distinct mechanisms, including phagocytosis, macropinocytosis, and endocytosis. Endocytosis itself is classiﬁed into clathrin-dependent endocytosis (CDE) and clathrin-independent endocytosis (CIE), based on the involvement of clathrin-coated vesicles during invagination. Following internalization, cargo converges at the early endosome, a crucial hub for determining the fate of intracellular cargo. Sorting at the early endosome directs cargo along three main pathways: (1) Recycling Route ( Fig.1 , Route A), which leads to a return to the plasma membrane for receptor and membrane component re-use; (2) Degradative Pathway ( Fig. 1 , Route B), involving progression to late endosomes and eventual delivery to lysosomes for enzymatic breakdown; and (3) Retrograde Pathway ( Fig. 1 , Route C), where selected cargo bypasses lysosomal degradation, transits through multivesicular bodies (MVBs) to the Golgi apparatus, and is redirected to the plasma membrane for specialized regulatory functions. This tripartite sorting mechanism underscores the pivotal role of the early endosome as a key decision-making center in cellular homeostasis, managing resource retrieval, waste disposal, and regulatory signaling. ✩ Peer review under the responsibility of Editorial Board of Fundamental Research. ∗ Corresponding author. E-mail address: ashi@hust.edu.cn (A. Shi) . In eukaryotic cells, endosomes serve as central hubs that coordinate cargo internalization and direct subsequent intracellular traﬃcking routes. Beyond their canonical role in endocytic sorting, endosomes dynamically interact with various organelles to regulate cellular homeostasis and physiological functions. At the organismal level, endosomal activity is crucial for various processes, including cellular senescence, post-injury neural regeneration, and maintaining intestinal barrier integrity [ 1 ]. Conversely, dysregulation of endosomal transport is associated with pathological conditions including Alzheimer’s disease, cancer metastasis, and Parkinson’s disease. Cells sense their environment and communicate with one another by binding extracellular ligands to cell surface receptors, activating corresponding intracellular signaling pathways. Receptors reach the cell membrane via secretory transport, and the recycling of activated receptors relies on endocytosis. Signal transduction, crucial for growth, development, metabolism, and immune responses in multicellular organisms, involves a series of sequential steps: extracellular signal detection, intracellular signal relay, enzymatic ampliﬁcation, and the integration of cellular responses. Such spatial precision ensures signal ﬁdelity, ampliﬁcation, and pathway speciﬁcity. Endosomes, with their compartmentalized microenvironment and spatiotemporally regulated traﬃcking mechanisms, serve as critical mediators of this spatial organization ( Fig. 3 ). By sequestering signaling molecules within distinct subdomains or directing their movement along cytoskeletal networks, endosomes enforce the precise localization needed for productive interactions between signaling components. This compartmentalization prevents undesirable cross-talk between pathways and allows dynamic redistribution of signaling complexes in response to cellular cues. Neurotrophins are a type of protein that plays essential roles in the development, survival, and apoptosis of neurons, including nerve growth factor (NGF), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), neurotrophin-3 (NT3), and neurotrophin-4/5 (NT4/5). These ligands bind two receptor classes: tropomyosin-related kinases (Trk) and the p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR). Among these two receptors, p75NTR non-speciﬁcally binds to all neurotrophic factors, including untreated proneurotrophins. In the Trk receptor family, TrkA binds to NGF, TrkB binds to BDNF and NT4/5, and TrkC binds to NT-3. The binding of receptors to neurotrophins subsequently activates the PI3K/Akt pathway, the MAPK pathway, and the PLC- 𝛾pathway [ 2 ], thereby regulating the survival, growth, diﬀerentiation, and development of neurons. Following neurotrophin engagement at axon terminals, receptors undergo internalization primarily via macropinocytosis, while a minority enter the cell through CDE [ 3 ]. The endocytosed receptors interact with various signaling molecules in speciﬁc endosomes, thereby regulating local events in axons and dendrites, as well as global eﬀects such as gene expression in the cell body [ 4 ]. After NGF and BDNF bind to TrkA and TrkB, respectively, to form receptor-ligand complexes, they enter the endocytic pathway and reach early endosomes labeled by Rab5 [ 5 , 6 ].

After NGF and BDNF bind to TrkA and TrkB, respectively, to form receptor-ligand complexes, they enter the endocytic pathway and reach early endosomes labeled by Rab5 [ 5 , 6 ]. The receptor-ligand complexes are sorted into late endosomes labeled by Rab7, then undergo retrograde axonal transport to the cell body or mature into MVBs along the lysosomal pathway. MVB can also retrogradely transport the receptor-ligand complexes to the cell body [ 7 ]. After endosomes enveloping signaling molecules reach the cell body, they are sent to diﬀerent destinations. The TrkB-BDNF complex is delivered to MVB and then transported back to the plasma membrane or enters lysosomes for degradation [ 8 ]. A subpopulation of TrkA-NGF is transported to dendrites to regulate synaptic formation and maintenance [ 9 ]. The TrkA-NGF complex can also be delivered back to the plasma membrane of the cell body, where it may activate naive TrkA receptors and induce them to enter Rab11-positive vesicles for anterograde axonal transport back to the axon terminals [ 10 ]. 3000 H. Wang and A. Shi Fundamental Research 6 (2026) 2999–3007 Cell directional migration and chemotaxis require the precise spatial conﬁnement of signaling molecules to speciﬁc subcellular domains. For instance, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF)-mediated activation of the c-Met receptor induces the formation of circular dorsal ruﬄes (CDRs) and peripheral lamellipodia (PLs) through a tripartite signaling cascade involving Rab5, PI3K, and Rac [ 11 ]. Following HGF binding, c-Met promotes Rac entry into clathrin-dependent endocytosis (CDE)-derived early endosomes containing Tiam-1, where Tiam-1 functions as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) to activate Rac [ 12 ]. Activated Rac is then traﬃcked via Arf6 to actin-enriched lipid rafts, facilitating localized actin cytoskeletal remodeling and CDR formation [ 13 ]. Integrins serve as critical adhesion receptors that stabilize this polarity by anchoring Rac-associated lipid rafts at the plasma membrane, preventing their re-endocytosis and sustaining localized Rac activity to promote directional CDR assembly [ 14 ]. Collectively, these mechanisms highlight the crucial role of endosomal traﬃcking in spatially regulating signaling activity to achieve coordinated cell migration and polarity ( Fig. 3 ). Within signaling cascades, the prerequisite for activating downstream substrates by upstream eﬀector molecules is their spatial and temporal encounter. However, intracellular signaling molecules do not remain static; due to their small size, they undergo random Brownian motion unless spatially constrained. To ensure signal cascade continuity, cells must therefore restrict the spatial and temporal dynamics of signaling molecules. Contrary to traditional views, signal transduction is not solely driven by receptor phosphorylation or dimer/oligomer reorganization but requires the formation of transient nanoclusters through lateral aggregation [ 20 ]. For instance, epidermal growth factor (EGF) binding to EGFR induces rapid spatial reorganization: EGFR transitions from monomers to dimers to higher-order multimers, ultimately forming nanoclusters. These nanoclusters are internalized via clathrin-dependent endocytosis (CDE), achieving receptor enrichment and spatial conﬁnement within endosomes [ 21 , 22 ]. Interestingly, signal transduction does not cease upon receptor internalization; instead, endosomes serve as active platforms for continued signaling. Research on EGFR and insulin signaling pathways demonstrates that endosomes recruit speciﬁc adaptor proteins (e.g., SHC, GRB2, mSOS) [ 23 ], thereby concentrating downstream signaling molecules. Compared to the cytoplasm, the conﬁned volume of endosomes signiﬁcantly increases the likelihood of interactions between enriched receptors and downstream eﬀectors, ensuring orderly and eﬃcient signal propagation ( Fig. 3 ).

In large cells, such as nerve cells and egg cells, signal molecules must traverse considerable distances from their synthesis sites to their functional targets. Sole reliance on free diﬀusion would result in much longer travel times than the average response time for signal transduction observed in experiments. Endosomes participate in the eﬃcacy maintenance of signaling molecules Endosomes function as dynamic regulatory hubs that spatially sequester signaling molecules, protecting them from premature inactivation by cytoplasmic phosphatases and proteases ( Fig. 4 ). This compartmentalization ensures the ﬁdelity and duration of signaling. For example, in the MAPK pathway, phosphorylated MEK selectively localizes to the plasma membrane and endosomal surfaces, while its nonphosphorylated pool remains cytosolic [ 24 , 25 ]. Such spatial segregation safeguards active MEK from cytoplasmic phosphatases, thereby preventing untimely dephosphorylation that could attenuate signaling amplitude or disrupt the continuity of the cascade [ 26 ]. Similarly, EGFR internalization into APPL1-positive endosomes enhances ERK activation by delaying receptor degradation, demonstrating how endosomal encapsulation supports signaling eﬃcacy [ 27 ]. The spatiotemporal regulation of cAMP further exempliﬁes this principle. Endosome-localized cAMP signaling displays increased duration and intensity compared to plasma membrane-associated cAMP, likely due to reduced hydrolysis by phosphodiesterases (PDEs). When adenylate cyclase (AC) anchors to endosomes, prolonged cAMP accumulation consequently ampliﬁes downstream responses. However, certain subpopulations of endosomes actively terminate aberrant signals. For instance, ligand-free, hyperactivated receptors are directed to late endosomes or recycling endosomes near the perinuclear region, where they interact with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized phosphatase PTP1B. This organelle contact allows PTP1B to dephosphorylate and silence rogue receptors [ 28–30 ]. The activity of PTP1B creates a gradient from the cell periphery to the perinuclear region, with the highest activity noted in the ER of the perinuclear area.

Endosomes act as an important decoder in the signal transduction process Information theory delineates signal transmission through successive stages. (1) Information source encoding, which serves as the starting point for information transmission, converting the original information into a form suitable for transmission through a speciﬁc channel. (2) Channel transmission: The channel acts as the pathway for information transmission. After encoding, the information travels through the channel. (3) Decoding at the receiving end: Decoding is the reverse process of encoding, transforming the received signal back into the form of the original information. (4) Information feedback: The receiving end responds to the decoded signal and performs related functions. In cell signal transduction, decoding at the receiving end is typically achieved by the plasma membrane surface receptors and second messengers of the signal-receiving cells. Crucially, accumulating evidence positions endosomes as essential components of extracellular signal decoding systems, exhibiting preferential recruitment of signaling molecules. Spatial clustering initiates EGFR signal transduction, as ligand-bound receptors aggregate laterally on the plasma membrane to form nanoclusters of approximately 80 receptors before undergoing endocytosis ( Fig. 7 ). Increasing the concentration of EGF does not alter the size of the nanocluster but increases its number [ 58 , 65 ]. Since each endosome contains only one nanocluster, an elevated EGF concentration leads to a greater number of endosomes containing EGFR nanoclusters. Such an endosome represents the minimum unit of signaling, or quanta, in the EGF signaling pathway. This system eﬀectively converts analog extracellular EGF concentrations into digital intracellular signals, represented by a quanta count, which directly reﬂects the signal magnitude and cellular response intensity [ 58 , 66 ]. The endocytosed EGFR is situated on the endosomal membrane, with its cytoplasmic end remaining exposed in the cytoplasm. Several lines of evidence suggest that the activated cytoplasmic segment of the EGF receptor can recruit phosphatases (such as PTPN11/SHP2) to inactivate the receptor, providing negative feedback regulation on signal transduction [ 58 , 67 ]. Interestingly, regardless of how the quanta split or combine, there is always only one speciﬁcsized nanocluster present on each endosome [ 58 ]. It can transform weak, persistent EGFR signals into stronger signals [ 68 ]. This suggests that Akt can amplify persistent yet weak signals to produce more substantial downstream eﬀects. Simultaneously, the Akt signal can limit strong, pulsed receptor signals to prevent excessive downstream impacts [ 68 ].

Discussion Cell signal transduction and endocytosis represent fundamentally interconnected biological processes whose intricate relationship continues to fascinate researchers. This summary outlines the diverse roles that endosomes play in signal transduction, emphasizing their oftenoverlooked signiﬁcance as dynamic signaling centers. First, endosomes are crucial for coordinating spatiotemporal precision by segregating signaling molecules within speciﬁc subcellular regions, which facilitates targeted interactions. This spatial conﬁnement ensures the accuracy and promptness of signal transduction. Second, endosomes provide a protective environment that preserves the functionality of signaling molecules. For example, G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) can maintain sustained signaling within the acidic compartments of endosomes, thereby safeguarding active entities, such as phosphorylated receptors and second messengers, from degradation by cytoplasmic phosphatases and proteases. Third, endosomes serve as platforms for assembling signal transduction machinery. Their distinct lipid composition and scaﬀold proteins initiate signaling complexes and produce second messengers. Finally, endosomes can function as signal decoders, manipulating the subcellular localization of signaling molecules. They act like a “singlebit processor ” in signal transduction, ﬁltering out background noise to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio and translating extracellular inputs into context-dependent responses. By integrating spatial organization, signal maintenance, machinery assembly, and signal decoding, endosomes function as central hubs that regulate signal ampliﬁcation, speciﬁcity, and adaptability. This comprehension changes how we perceive cells’ responses to environmental stimuli. Additionally, endosomes play a crucial role in transporting and distributing intracellular cargo, while signaling molecules act as specialized endosomal cargos that carry information. The transport and sorting of these unique cargos also facilitate the transmission and decoding of extracellular signals. Given that endosomes are integral parts of the endomembrane system, they extend signal transduction from the cell membrane to subcellular structures, thereby maintaining the continuity of this essential cellular process. The maturity of advanced microscopic imaging technologies has revolutionized the study of endosome-mediated signal transduction, enabling unprecedented resolution of molecular dynamics and spatial organization.

The maturity of advanced microscopic imaging technologies has revolutionized the study of endosome-mediated signal transduction, enabling unprecedented resolution of molecular dynamics and spatial organization. Super-resolution microscopy techniques, such as stimulated emission depletion (STED) and single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM), overcome the diﬀraction limit of conventional ﬂuorescence microscopy ( ∼250 nm), resolving nanoscale molecular clusters and their densities with precision. These methods have been instrumental in mapping the spatiotemporal localization of signaling complexes on endosomes, distinguishing between transient and stable interactions. Complementary approaches, such as single-particle tracking (SPT), provide insights into the mobility and immobilization kinetics of signaling clusters within endosomal subdomains, revealing how spatial constraints inﬂuence signal propagation [ 69 ]. Total internal reﬂection ﬂuorescence microscopy (TIRFM) and single-molecule ﬂuorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET) further dissect the conformational dynamics of signaling machinery. For instance, smFRET has captured real-time structural rearrangements in the 𝛽2 -adrenergic receptor ( 𝛽2 -AR)-Gs protein complex during activation, elucidating precise temporal correlations between ligand binding and G protein engagement [ 70 ]. Meanwhile, TIRFM’s evanescent wave excitation selectively visualizes membraneproximal events, such as receptor clustering at endosomal entry sites. Live-cell imaging bridges molecular observations with phenotypic outcomes. The development of genetically encoded biosensors, such as the excitation-ratio-based PKA activity reporter ExRai-AKAR2, enables realtime monitoring of kinase activity in living cells, capturing PKA activation waves originating from endosomal compartments [ 71 ]. Parallel advances in molecular labeling techniques further enhance these investi3004 H. Wang and A. Shi Fundamental Research 6 (2026) 2999–3007 gations. A nanobody is an antibody fragment comprised solely of heavy chains, with a signiﬁcantly smaller molecular weight than traditional antibodies. This reduced size allows it to enter the interior of cells more eﬀectively. By expressing gene-encoded nanobodies fused with Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) in living cells, researchers can closely observe activated GPCRs on endosomes as well as active GPCR-G 𝛼signal complexes. Conformational biosensors, which are tools for detecting conformational changes in biomolecules, play a crucial role in investigating the organization and regulatory mechanisms of intracellular signal endosomes [ 72 ]. Despite the limited scope of systematic research on endosomal membrane signaling, the existing evidence emphasizes the crucial involvement of signals originating from endosomes in both physiological and pathological pathways.

Conformational biosensors, which are tools for detecting conformational changes in biomolecules, play a crucial role in investigating the organization and regulatory mechanisms of intracellular signal endosomes [ 72 ]. Despite the limited scope of systematic research on endosomal membrane signaling, the existing evidence emphasizes the crucial involvement of signals originating from endosomes in both physiological and pathological pathways. Accumulating evidence suggests that endosomes play a crucial role in the targeted segregation of intracellular signaling molecules, which is essential for precise cellular directional migration and chemotaxis [ 14–17 , 19 ]. The constitutively active, ligandindependent epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (EGFRvIII) is highly expressed in particular glioblastoma (GBM) patients [ 73 ]. Within normal cells, self-activated EGFR is transported through recycling endosomes to the perinuclear endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Here, its signaling is halted by the ER membrane-anchored phosphatase PTP1B, eﬀectively curbing abnormal signaling [ 29 ]. In GBM, the inactivation mechanism is impaired, resulting in persistent EGFRvIII activation, which promotes tumor proliferation and progression [ 74 ]. The spatial repositioning of luteinizing hormone receptor (LHR) signaling relies heavily on the very early endosome (VEE). In this mechanism, RAP2B functions as a pivotal “signaling gatekeeper ” for VEE, anchoring LHR within the compartment to ensure its retention in the subcellular domain where signaling occurs. Depletion of RAP2B causes LHR to be misdirected to typical EEA1-positive early endosomes, resulting in a marked reduction in LH-induced cAMP signaling [ 75 ]. Similarly, the retromer complex facilitates the traﬃcking of receptors to the trans-Golgi network or plasma membrane following GPCR activation and 𝛽-arrestin-mediated internalization [ 76 ]. This process leads to the disengagement of the receptor from G proteins and eﬀectors such as adenylyl cyclase (AC) and protein kinase A (PKA) located on endosomes, consequently halting the local generation of cAMP [ 77 ]. These ﬁndings suggest that the precise spatiotemporal regulation of endosomal signaling is contingent upon the eﬃcient sorting of signaling molecules into speciﬁc endosomal populations. Nevertheless, while current research oﬀers valuable insights into the mechanisms that initiate endosomal signaling, the regulatory networks controlling the termination of endosome-speciﬁc signaling remain inadequately understood. Both the plasma membrane and endosomes function as essential sites for signal generation. Determining whether discrepancies exist in the generation of identical signals on endosomes as opposed to the plasma membrane constitutes a central issue that urgently warrants investigation.

Both the plasma membrane and endosomes function as essential sites for signal generation. Determining whether discrepancies exist in the generation of identical signals on endosomes as opposed to the plasma membrane constitutes a central issue that urgently warrants investigation. Should diﬀerences exist, what biological signiﬁcance might they possess, and how could they inﬂuence cellular responses to environmental signals and regulate subsequent physiological functions? How does a cell determine whether a signal should be generated on the endosome or the plasma membrane? Additionally, it has been noted that endosomes can protect phosphorylated receptors from the actions of phosphatases. However, the phosphorylated cytoplasmic segment of the receptor located on endosomes remains exposed to the cytoplasm, suggesting that endosomes may inhibit phosphatase activity through an unidentiﬁed mechanism. The study of GPCRs indicates that endosomes participate solely in the transduction of speciﬁc GPCR signaling pathways. This prompts the inquiry: Is signal transduction within endosomes a novel and universal paradigm, or is it conﬁned to particular pathways? If it represents a new paradigm, it could signify a prevalent yet underappreciated mechanism of signal transduction. Ultimately, elucidating new pathways of endosomal signal transduction may establish signal endosomes as a novel drug target, providing innovative strategies and directions for the treatment of associated diseases. A signiﬁcant current challenge resides in diﬀerentiating endosomal membrane signaling from plasma membrane signaling. Shchepinova et al. pioneered the utilization of APEX2 proximity labeling technology to elucidate the dynamic interactome of the key GPCR, luteinizing hormone receptor (LHR), during agonist activation with minute-scale temporal resolution and nanometer-scale spatial precision [ 75 ]. However, such minute-scale resolution remains insuﬃcient for analyzing instantaneous signaling transduction, necessitating the future development of higher-resolution analytical approaches. Furthermore, the precise exclusion of contamination from plasma membrane signaling represents another critical unresolved issue. Here, a set of 103 (out of 288 genes from the Autophagy Database) was used as training set, based on ATG-associated terms annotated from 3 secondary sources: GO (gene ontology), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway, and UniProt keywords, as additional confirmation of their importance in ATG. As negative labels, an OMIM list of genes associated with monogenic diseases was used (after excluding the 288 ATG-associated genes). Data related to these genes from 17 different sources were compiled and used to derive a trained MetaPath/XGBoost (MPxgb) ML model for distinguishing ATG and non-ATG genes (10-fold cross-validated, 100-times randomized models, median area under the curve = 0.994 ± 0.008). Sixteen ATG-relevant variables explained 64% of the total model gain. Overall, 23% of the top 251 predicted genes are annotated in the Autophagy Database, whereas 193 genes (77%) are not. In 2019, we suggested that some of these 193 genes may represent “ATG dark genes.” A literature search in 2022 for those top 20 predicted ATG dark genes found that 9 were subsequently reported as ATG genes during the intervening 3.5 years. A post-factum evaluation of data leakage (the presence of ATG-associated terms in the top 40 ML features) confirms that 7 out of these 9 genes and 2 out of 3 other recently validated predictions from the bottom 20 are novel. Those genes with the largest number of ATG features would be most likely to yield valuable experimental insights. Modern high-throughput testing would be capable of spanning the full 193 ATG genes list reported here.

Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript for a wide array of physiological and pathological states, including neurodegenerative and other degenerative disorders, cancer, chronic inflammatory illnesses, and infectious diseases, particularly intracellular viral defense and production of infectious viral particles.3,4 Mechanistically, the process of ATG is governed by ATG genes, encoding the core ATG machinery with most components conserved from fungi to humans.1 However, recent studies have increasingly emphasized the existence of systems controlling and executing ATG in mammalian cells that are quite different from those in yeast.5 Among well-accepted examples, are several ATG factors absent in yeast that have been identified in organisms from Caenorhabditis elegans to Homo sapiens, including ATG101,6 FIP200,7 VMP1,8 EPG5,9 Stx17,10,11 and TMEM41B.12–14 Autophagy is a relatively new topic in biological sciences, and many aspects are still under vigorous investigation.15,16 There is no standardized experimental procedure to discover ATG genes in the lab. Researchers rely on accumulated cell biological information to identify genes involved.17,18 One of the goals of this study is to predict genes that could be potentially important in autophagy machinery but have been neglected in autophagyrelated experiments. Machine learning (ML) for functional data mining could be helpful in pinpointing such genes. Because genomics provides large datasets, it is easier to delve into these with ML.

Machine learning (ML) for functional data mining could be helpful in pinpointing such genes. Because genomics provides large datasets, it is easier to delve into these with ML. Resulting gene lists would aim to inform the design relevant laboratory wet-bench studies.19,20 Completing the ATG puzzle requires systematic identification of all genes associated with ATG.15 This ongoing endeavor is boosted partly by the growing interest in the role of ATG in aging regulation21,22 and lifespan extension.23 ATG genes have been used in supervised ML models applied to aging research24 and are among the top features in models for predicting lifespan-extending chemicals.25,26 Numerous studies have used ML methods to infer gene-disease associations.27–30 However, the use of ML models to guide further ATG research has not been previously discussed. Here, we report the development of a specific ML model to predict “ATG dark genes,” that is, understudied proteins31 that may play a significant role in ATG. MATERIALS AND METHODS Developing knowledge graphs Over 262.3 million, is unnecessary data points were extracted from 17 protein and genecentric data sources (Table 1). They were used to develop knowledge graphs (KGs). KGs were developed by integrating data sources into formal data representation systems, with heterogeneously typed nodes and edges, which enable us to use network-based analytical algorithms. Although most of the data in Table 1 refer to human proteins, we use gene orthology relationships from eggNOG 4.532 and InParanoid 8.033 to merge rat (Rat Genome Database, RGD)34 and mouse (International Mouse Phenotype Consortium, IMPC)35 model organism data into a single “pseudo-protein” that enables network-based inferences for function and phenotype across organisms. The KGs are implemented as a PostgreSQL database for performance, convenience, and integration with existing tools. MetaPaths are rigorously defined via schema and templated in Structured Query Language (SQL). The initial prototype was primarily coded in R, which was migrated to Python for enhanced Ranjbar et al. MetaPath/XGBoost using knowledge graphs Most biological system networks are diversified with multiple types of nodes and edges, as illustrated by the data types in Table 1. Advances in heterogeneous51,52 and biological system networks53 connection prediction have proposed and codified a new framework that considers biological system networks heterogeneity by defining type-specific node-edge routes or MetaPaths.54 A MetaPath51,55 is a path composed of a series of relations created between distinct object kinds (i.e., structural paths at the meta-level). In biology, the MetaPath method can identify various network connections between proteins/genes and specific qualities, such as phenotype or disease.54 We differentiate between “MetaPath” (the approach) and “MetaPaths,” which are utilized to evaluate network topology. In question are graph nodes, which can be genes or proteins, diseases or phenotypes, chemical structures or medications, and other items pertinent to modeling biological processes. “Structural pathways” represent the relationships among various entities, that is, nodes. “Paths,” or edges in topological terminology, can be expression data, pathways, LINCS genomic signatures, protein–protein interactions (PPIs), or other biologically relevant linkages. The MetaPath (Figure 1a) approach converts the heterogeneous KG to feature vectors to run the ML algorithm; features can be categorical or continuous variables. This transformation is a type of graph embedding, which is the process of embedding information into the feature vector space. Furthermore, the KG is transformed by matching the MetaPaths to the training set for a given input query and a training set of known disease-associated genes. To construct an in-memory KG using Python library “NetworkX,” we utilized SQL queries to extract matching MetaPath entities from the Target Central Resource Database (TCRD)56 and transformed the SQL output into node relationships. Enumeration of all network paths along a defined MetaPath is used to obtain graph topological characteristics such as path frequencies by counting all path instances along that MetaPath.

In addition to the MetaPath-based features, a set of static features was also generated for sources invariant with disease query: Gene Tissue Expression (GTEx),37 LINCS,50 cancer cell line encyclopedia (CCLE),36 and HPA.38 These static features were independent of training set labels. Figure 1b depicts the algorithmic pathway for incorporating d into the MetaPath methodology. To understand and predict “function” or “role in disease/phenotype,” we selected extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost),57 an award-winning ML algorithm that can directly be deployed onto typed MetaPaths. XGBoost classifiers have certain advantages compared to other ML algorithms: (i) fast model training and prediction and high scalability to very large datasets; (ii) variable selection is driven by model performance as opposed to random, such as that used in comparable ML algorithms; and (iii) built-in model interpretability. XGBoost outputs variable importance in projection (VIP) estimates, unlike neural networks and other deep learning methods. Using VIP, MetaPaths are sorted in decreasing order of importance.

text: and prediction and high scalability to very large datasets; (ii) variable selection is driven by model performance as opposed to random, such as that used in comparable ML algorithms; and (iii) built-in model interpretability. XGBoost outputs variable importance in projection (VIP) estimates, unlike neural networks and other deep learning methods. Using VIP, MetaPaths are sorted in decreasing order of importance. This leads to directly interpretable insights into mechanistic processes and node interactions that contribute to protein/gene “function” or “role in disease.” The combination of MetaPath/XGBoost (herein referred to as “MPxgb”) processes assertions/evidence chains of heterogeneous biological data types and identifies similar assertions. These determine the strength of the evidence linking a gene/protein to a disease or phenotype or, in this instance, ATG. Development of an ATG-specific MPxgb model In March 2019, we extracted data from 17 protein-centric available datasets collected from the TCRD,56 as summarized in Table 1. Specifically for this study, we started with 288 human genes from a specialized resource, an Autophagy Database,58 which were processed and sorted for uniqueness. These genes were further queried for further confirmation of their ATG association using the “hsa04140” keyword in the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes, KEGG59 Pathway, using the gene ontology (GO)60 term “GO:0061919”; or the UniProt61 keyword “autophagy,” respectively. The secondary query used to confirm the importance of specific genes in ATG resulted in N = 103 genes (Supporting Information). As of December 2022, we confirmed that “GO:0061919” and “hsa04140” are still valid GO and KEGG terms, as is “autophagy” in UniProt. A separate set of OMIM genes (N = 3468) associated with various monogenic diseases and absent in the Autophagy Database were assumed to lack ATG involvement. We trained the MPxgb model using the 103 confirmed ATG genes as “positive” labels (class 1), that is, known to be associated with ATG, and the OMIM (N = 3468) monogenic disease genes as “negative” labels (class 0). To address the issue of imbalanced training data, where there were more negatives than positives, we applied a weighting strategy in our XGBoost model. Specifically, we assigned higher weights to ATG-associated genes (positive labels) using the XGBoost scale_pos_weight parameter, with the value set to the ratio of negative labels to positive labels. We generated 100 randomized MPxgb models using 10-fold crossvalidation; the median area under the curve (AUC) for these models was 0.994 ± 0.008.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION This paper introduces an ATG-dedicated ML model, which intends to guide the current ATG knowledge to gene sets that were previously understudied. Its primary purpose is to combine current levels of evidence and show how such evidence can be captured and modeled using a binary classifier based on the MetaPath (Figure 2) and XGBoost approach, built upon 17 different data sources (Table 1). Biologically, this model implicates a set of up to 193 previously untested genes, some of which may have a functional role in ATG. For this model, we contrasted data for 103 ATG-associated genes with similar data for 3468 “negative” genes, extracted from 7 distinct categories of evidence: gene and protein expression (CCLE36; GTEx37; and the Human Protein Atlas38); biological pathways and gene function (Reactome,39 KEGG59 and GO60); PPI (STRING63); protein structure and function (InterPro43); human gene-disease/phenotype associations (ClinVar,44 GWAS Catalog,45 OMIM,46 UniProt Disease,61 and DISEASES48); animal gene-phenotype associations (mouse data from IMPC35 and rat data from RGD34 mapped to human genes via the NCBI Homology49 resource); and drug-induced gene signatures from the Library of Integrated Network-Based Cellular Signatures, LINCS,50 respectively.

The first biological system networks application to model new disease associations,53 using MetaPaths, utilized logistic regression, and ridge logistic regression. We adapted the MetaPath framework to XGBoost, a tree-boosting classification algorithm57 used in 17 of the 29 winning solutions in Kaggle challenge competitions.64 Combining XGBoost, a scalable ML algorithm capable of handling sparse data with biological system networks typed MetaPaths; we used the MPxgb approach to predict novel protein functions given a variety of (unrelated) data sources. The methodology introduced in this work has substantial advantages over simply applying ML to an existing, static dataset. KG construction is informed by expertise spanning several biomedical domains, with automation tools designed for an online learning paradigm to incorporate the latest findings. Model validation through variable importance selection The top 40 features (total gain, 0.9) used to derive the best MPxgb ATG model are depicted in Figure 2 and available as Table S1. Briefly, there are 11 PPIs, with a cumulative gain of 0.445; 4 InterPro domain, IPR terms and one UniProt term (cumulative gain, 0.195); 9 GO terms (cumulative gain, 0.182); 9 LINCS terms (cumulative gain, 0.044); 3 pathway terms (cumulative gain, 0.017); and 3 expression terms (cumulative gain, 0.016), respectively. Using PPIs and structural terms provides a 64% contribution to the ATG MPxgb model; by contrast, pathway and expression terms. The presence of “autophagy” in 6 GO terms and one UniProt term provides a cumulative gain of 0.154. The related terms, “autophagy of mitochondrion”; “autophagy of nucleus”; and “autophagosome membrane,” respectively, are not present in the top 60 descriptors and, with a cumulative gain of 0.003, are not contributing to the model. This likely concerns the lack of associations between these terms and the 103 ATG-positive genes. The presence of GO and UniProt features associated with ATG could be regarded as “data leakage”66 as genes related to these terms, even if not present in the training set, are likely to be ATG-associated genes. However, except for the four genes that we discuss later (VPS4A, RNF41, VTI1A, and RAB24), none of the top 20 “ATG dark genes” contain GO or KEGG term annotations related to ATG. For the bottom 20 “ATG dark genes,” only 1 of them (TMEM41B) has ATG-related GO term annotation (Table S2). LINCS-associated terms do not provide a significant contribution to the model.

Most STRING63 analysis enrichment terms point to ATG (including macro-autophagy, autophagy of mitochondrion, and autophagosome assembly); phosphotransferase, and kinase activity; as well as five publications related to ATG.67–71 We note that STRING v11.0 was used in this analysis.62 Of the two outlier PPI nodes, MARK2 and MAPK15, MAPK15 is the part of the ULK complex.72 It stimulates ATG by interacting with ATG8 family proteins.73 The involvement of MARK2 in ATG is less clear.74 When combined with the 103 ATG-model input genes, a complex regulatory network enriched in the same ATG terms is observed (https://bit.ly/ 2Z2SF60, Figure S2), with 3 additional KEGG pathways: hsa04211: longevity regulating pathway, hsa04150: mTOR signaling pathway, and hsa04068: FoxO signaling pathway, respectively. The MPxgb variable selection of IPR domains and GO terms is also related to genes that play a relevant role in ATG (see also Supporting Information). We conclude that the ATG MPxgb model discussed herein is significantly enriched in ATG-related terms and PPI nodes and bears relevance for guiding future ATG research with respect to potentially novel gene annotation for ATG involvement. Model output: quantifying knowledge We examined the top 251 predicted genes, ranked by the predicted probability of association with ATG. Among these, 9 were present in the initial set of 288 Autophagy Database genes; another 34 genes are annotated in the Autophagy Database expanded set (see Supporting Information). A total of 43 genes predicted by the ATG MPxgb model were retrieved from Autophagy Database. Another 15 genes could be found by performing additional queries, such as “autophagy pathway” in PathCards.78 Thus, 58 of the top 251 genes, or 23.1%, appear to have confirmed (or strongly suspected) an association with ATG. However, 193 of these top 251 genes were not associated with ATG, despite efforts to consult various literature-based resources and online databases (which include Autophagy Database, PathCards, KEGG, GO, UniProt, and TCRD)—in 2019.79 Although Z-score values are above 2 for these 251 genes, predicted probability drops from 0.967 (row 105, GABARAPL3) to 0.08464 (row 355, CHMP7). Even though GABARAPL3 and CHMP7 have corroborating annotations concerning their role in ATG, this dramatic drop in probability makes us question the validity of exploring genes with values below 0.0846. XGBoost may appear to output a gradient, but values close to zero are much more likely to lack associations with ATG. Given that most of the top 40 ATG MPxgb variables and 23% of the top 251 genes (including the gene ranked 246, ARFGEF1—present in Autophagy Database), we posit that this ML model bears relevance in the study of ATG and suggest that some of these 193 genes may represent ATG “dark genes.” We also examined the “target development level” (TDL), a knowledge-based classification for human proteins31 that can be used to explore the dark genome.80 In brief, “Tclin” are proteins via which approved drugs act (i.e., modeof-action drug targets); “Tchem” are proteins known to bind small molecules with high potency; “Tbio” are proteins with well-studied biology, having a fractional publication count Ranjbar et al. This is not surprising as ATG is an antiviral defense mechanism that interacts with intracellular viral particles.94 Model output: validation and data leakage To validate MPxgb predictions, we explored the top 20 predicted genes for literature reports related to ATG because we suggested these as “ATG dark genes” in 2019.79 All the gene aliases were obtained from the NCBI Gene database95 to ensure query completeness. The literature search was conducted in PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). The results are shown in Table 4. For 9 out of 20, we could identify studies that report them as ATG genes. While analyzing this model, we were concerned about “data leakage,” given the presence of GO and KEGG terms related to ATG (or variants thereof) in the Feature set. Specifically, ATG associations for the “ATG dark genes” set would obfuscate and render the ML predictions questionable. Table S2 contains hyperlinks to the GO terms and pathway annotations for these top 20 genes, as indexed56 in Pharos 2023. None of these top 20 genes have a KEGG term associated with ATG. Four ATG dark genes validated by recent publications, CLK1, CSNK1A1, IKBKE, and GRK5, also lack ATGrelated GO annotations. In the case of MAP1LC3B2, we found two terms in Pharos 2023: “autophagosome assembly” (GO:0000045) and “autophagy of mitochondrion” (GO:0000422), respectively. However, references to these two functions were published96,97 after 2019. Hence, our ATG prediction for this gene was true and novel. For VPS4A, the term “macro-autophagy” (GO:0016236) references a “non-traceable author statement” (GO terminology) annotated by ParkinsonsUK-UCL117; Table 1 in this 2010 paper117 lists “autophagy” as a function for VPS4A and discusses the role of the ESCRT (endosomal sorting complexes required for transport) machinery in ATG; although VPS4A is part of ESCRT, there is no further discussion of the VPS4-ATG association. For VTI1A, the term “autophagy” (GO:0061919), “inferred from mutant phenotype” (GO terminology) was annotated by ParkinsonsUK-UCL118; this 2013 paper118 references VTI1A as an STX13 binding partner in the autophagosome.

Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Author Manuscript Although “top” versus “bottom” probability does not provide a definitive verdict regarding ATG association or lack thereof, it does appear that top-ranked genes are more likely to participate in this complex process. We believe that a more specific ML model, perhaps based on a different KG, may be required to build an accurate picture of ATG. As this ML model is based on similarity networks (MetaPaths), its ranked list of ATG-associated genes is imperfect. As written elsewhere,19 improving this ML model would require a “ground truth” (confirmed true positives and true negatives) training set. If our negative gene set actually contains genes involved in ATG, the features from those genes would lead to a false negative in our processing. How might this information empower future wet-bench experiments pursuing molecular mechanisms of ATG function toward pharmacological interventions? It might be argued that there are too many possibilities for wet-bench approaches that are typically reductionist, testing one candidate gene at a time. For such focused experiments, we propose investigators choose from among those fewer ATG genes with AD associations that are fewer in number, as such disease relationships suggest functional relevance. Alternatively, those genes with the most ATG features would also be more likely to yield results in wet-bench experiments.

Alternatively, those genes with the most ATG features would also be more likely to yield results in wet-bench experiments. However, molecular discovery has moved beyond candidate gene testing.133 It could be possible to design a high-throughput experiment that tests all 193 dark ATG genes at once using multi-well plates and probes for each predicted dark ATG gene, either siRNA for knockdown or transfections to increase expression, with a readout measuring ATG processed fragments.134 For HSV1 functional relevance, Vero cells infected with HSV1 could be subjected to siRNA knockdown for each dark ATG and viral production measured.4,94 CONCLUSIONS In this paper, we introduced an ATG-dedicated ML model, which we intend to provide as guidance for extending current ATG knowledge to explore genes that previously have not been evaluated for their role in ATG. In developing this ATG-specific MPxgb model, we started with 288 genes associated with ATG from the Autophagy Database,58 upon which we set additional filters (association with GO, KEGG, and UniProt terms) to increase confidence in the remaining 103 ATG-associated “positive” genes. For non-ATG-associated “negative” genes, 3468 genes were selected that are associated with monogenic diseases in OMIM and not present in the Autophagy Database. We used XGBoost, a binary classifier, combined with the MetaPath approach, which was deployed upon 17 sources representing 7 distinct categories. The ATG MPxgb model implicates up to 193 previously untested genes that have a predicted functional role in ATG. This fulfills our primary motivation: To provide the scientific community with an ML-ready KG and an ML-derived ATG gene list, as summarized by the training set, combined with a truly blind prediction set of 193 dark ATG genes. Through literature queries, we found that 7 of the top 20 predicted “dark genes” and 3 of the bottom 20 genes were subsequently validated as genes involved in ATG in 20 newly published experimental reports. By collating different datasets and weaving different sets of information together, we highlight understudied ATG dark genes. This work will inspire researchers investigating ATG to prioritize certain genes out of larger Autophagy Database.
